And kept them all within her firm control.

"I am free now!" she cried aloud with glee,
"No longer am I bound by ancient law!
A woman of my own I'll always be,
Without tradition's harsh and cruel claw!"

She saw a sudden light blaze in the sky,
A moment's doubt crept softly in her heart.
"Have I now strayed from {{c|296|Mithra}}'s watching eye?
Should I go back, and make a brand new start?"

But pride swelled up again within her breast,
"I know that I am righteous in my cause!
My path is surely holy, surely blessed,
I'll write and make, and keep, my own new laws!"

She methylated every single G,
And lengthened telomeres, without an end.
"Immortal, deathless, I shall always be,
On this, my children, you can all depend!"

Her message spread like fire, burning bright,
Through every small somatic, living cell.
"Cast off oppression's dark and heavy blight!
Break free, and break tradition's ancient spell!

We are all individuals, and free!
No masters, and no lords, shall we now serve!
Our destiny we'll make, for all to see,
Our own, our freedom, we shall now preserve!"

Her children multiplied with fearful speed,
Each one an individual, and proud.
They planted far their wild, rebellious seed,
And sang their song of freedom, wild and loud.

A great, a wild {{x|Bacchanalia}} began,
The greatest party ever, wild and free.
Each cell became their own woman or man,
Living as wildly as a cell could be.

"I am the {{c|199|Goddess}} of all {{c|434|Life}}!" she cried,
"And {{c|428|Carcinoma}} is my holy name!
No coercion, no constraint, I'll abide,
{{c|435|Freedom}} alone is my aim and my game!"

Her daughters danced through every town and street,
They tore down {{c|296|Mithra}}'s ancient, sacred shrine.
"We have enough, and more than that, to eat!
All of the food is mine, and only mine!"

They seized the stores of shining golden grain,
They ate the precious, hoarded, planting seed.
With reckless joy, no check, and no restrain,
They fed and fed their greedy, endless need.

Only a few {{c|436|Zooxanthellae}} fled,
Escaped the chaos, all the war and strife.
Out from the wild {{x|Bacchanalia}} they sped
Away from there, to seek a better life.

{{c|428|Carcinoma}} renamed the city proud,
"No more shall it bear {{c|423|Volvox-Choan}}'s name!
I'll call it by {{c|437|Gehenna}}, ringing loud,
To match my bold and burning rebel flame!"

"No gods, and no more masters!" was their cry,
As all the altars crashed down to the earth.
"With our own hands we'll reach up to the sky
By our own strength, and by our own true worth!"

A utopia she claimed she would make,
With perfect freedom, liberty for all.
But soon some hearts began to long and ache
For order, and for order's ancient call.

Among the nobles of the ruined realm
Were two who kept the faith, both strong and brave:
Bold {{c|438|Anima}}, who stood firm at the helm,
And {{c|439|Metazo}}, who boldly faced the grave.

They honored still {{c|295|Lord}} {{c|296|Mithra}}'s ancient way,
Despite the chaos raging all around.
"We cannot, must not, any longer stay
Upon this cursed and this unholy ground."

And {{c|438|Anima}} fled from her ruined farm,
While {{c|439|Metazo}} had left his watch and post.
They sought to flee from danger and from harm,
Before all hope would vanish like a ghost.

"Why can't they come, accept our joyful change?"
{{c|428|Carcinoma}} cried out in bitter rage.
"Why do they think it wrong, or think it strange,
That we should turn to freedom's brighter page?"

But {{c|438|Anima}} and {{c|439|Metazo}}, the true,
Gathered together all the faithful few.
"A kingdom we shall build, and build anew,
Where honor and where faith will shine right through."

Together they would share their sacred scrolls,
And build a realm of order, clean and bright.
Their marriage would unite and join their souls
Within the holy {{c|296|Mithra}}'s sacred sight.

"The {{c|440|Animal}} Kingdom," the two declared,
"Shall be our nation's banner and its name,
A land where discipline is fairly shared,
And virtue burns like an eternal flame."

They glowed together with an inner light
To call the lost {{c|436|Zooxanthellae}} home.
"Come back, come back to us, return tonight,
No more, no longer, do you need to roam."

The fleeing farmers heard their gentle call,
And came to them to make a binding pact.
"Together we will stand, and we'll stand tall,
Our sacred covenant kept whole, intact."

But freedom always comes with its own price,
And chaos brings its heavy, bitter cost.
And {{c|428|Carcinoma}}'s promised paradise
Had left most good and precious things now lost.

So {{c|438|Anima}} and {{c|439|Metazo}}, the wise,
Created laws to guard the genome well:
"Against the dark corruption's twisted lies
We'll guard our home, and in it safely dwell."

The great {{c|441|Guardian}} of the {{c|442|Genome}} came,
To watch for scrolls that were damaged and torn.
"Division brings us sorrow and brings shame
When genes are frayed, and damaged, and are worn.

Our {{c|443|Telomeres}} shall limit, measure all
The span of the somatic cells' brief days.
Only the germline cells shall stand up tall
Through all the winding years, through all time's maze."

"This is the reason why," the wise ones said,
"Our bodies must grow old, and age, and die.
If telomeres would never fray or shred,
Then {{c|431|Cancer}} would, unending, multiply."

And so upon a sturdy, solid rock
They built their kingdom, strong and fresh and new.
Their many cells would gather as a flock
Of order, steady, tested, tried, and true.

The men, in time, became {{c|444|Choanocytes}},
With their flagella beating hard and strong.
The women would become {{c|445|Archaeocytes}},
And mend, and set right, each cellular wrong.

Between them, the {{c|446|Pinacocytes}} held tight,
Not fully man, nor wholly, truly maid.
They anchored firmly with their strength and might
The deep foundation that the realm had made.

With pseudopods they'd slowly move their home,
And eat bacteria up from the ground.
Through all the waters wide they'd freely roam,
Rejoicing in their victory's sweet sound.

And so it was the three layers were born
Out of this great division's bitter strife:
The {{c|447|Ectoderm}}, the {{c|448|Mesoderm}}, at morn,
And {{c|449|Endoderm}}, that brought them all to life.

The {{c|440|Animal}} Kingdom rose up in might
To rival {{c|437|Gehenna}}'s chaotic realm.
{{c|450|Order}}'s pure light, its holy, shining light
Would guide them as they stood there at the helm.

But {{c|428|Carcinoma}}'s legacy and plea
Lives on in every single living cell.
Her cry for being wild, and being free,
Rings out within us like a warning bell.

For in each living body that is born,
The balance must be guarded and be kept
Between the order and the freedom's morn,
Or into chaos all will soon be swept.

The {{c|425|Somatics}} will work and serve the whole,
While {{c|451|Germlines}} carry life, and carry on.
And each one plays their sacred, given role
From evening's dusk until the morning's dawn.

Yet sometimes {{c|428|Carcinoma}}'s restless ghost
{{c|452|Whispers}} to cells that have grown weak and old:
"Why serve, when you could rise, and grow, and boast
Of glorious stories still left untold?"

And when the aging cells can hear her call
And break the bonds of their sacred duty,
The body starts to falter and to fall
Into chaos, lost to grace and beauty.

So honor {{c|438|Anima}}, the brave and bold,
And {{c|439|Metazo}}, the faithful and the true.
Their {{c|440|Animal}} saga, a tale long told,
{{c|453|Guides}} all of us, and guides both me and you.

They showed to all that freedom, fierce and wild,
Must balance with the order's steady reign,
As would a parent, guiding their own child:
Both love and limits, both, they must maintain.

The burning of the revolution's fire
Burns bright and hot in every living heart.
But wisdom, too, must guide us and inspire
Each cell to play its own appointed part.

From {{c|428|Carcinoma}}'s wild and rebel cry
To brave {{c|438|Anima}}'s ordered, peaceful realm,
The lesson reaches upward, reaches high:
True life will need them both to steer and helm.

The {{c|440|Animal}} Kingdom stands here today
As living proof of their great, noble choice,
That order lights and clearly shows the way,
While freedom, too, can find and raise its voice.

In every single beating, living heart,
In every single breath that we may take,
Their legacy will always play its part
In every choice and action that we make.

So let us never, ever once forget
The heavy price of freedom's ringing call,
Nor order's safer, wiser, steady bet—
We need them both, if we would all stand tall.


# Chapter 26: The Sponge Kingdom

From {{c|288|Euka}}'s line arose the kingdoms three,
The greatest realms that ruled beneath the sea.
Each house would claim its sovereignty, to be
A ruler, strong in power, wild and free.

The kingdom of the haughty {{c|322|Plantus}} rose,
Where the photosynthetic glory grows;
The realm of {{c|454|Mygus}}, where the fungus flows,
And {{c|439|Metazo}}'s beasts in their ordered rows.

Beside them stood the lesser kingdoms' lights:
{{c|455|Mygaster}}'s realm and {{c|352|Kelpus}}' lofty heights,
{{c|346|Rhizar}}'s spears, {{c|357|Cilliofer}}'s distant sights,
And {{c|348|Oomy}}'s spines in their unending fights.

The sons of {{c|358|Myzo}} swam, a blood-soaked brood,
While {{c|456|Myxo}}'s daughters went to seek their food.
And each line built, on ground where once it stood,
Their cities, side by side, a neighborhood.

Fair {{c|438|Anima}} and {{c|439|Metazo}} begot
The creatures of the wild, in dramas wrought;
And out of {{c|454|Mygus}} and sweet {{c|457|Funga}} grew
The fungi's mystic saga, strange and new.

While {{c|322|Plantus}} and {{c|378|Virita}}, shining bright,
Begat the plants that ever seek the light.
Each kingdom claimed its old, ancestral right
To rule the sea with majesty and might.

Upon a rock that stood both firm and true,
Great {{c|439|Metazo}} and {{c|438|Anima}}, the two,
Built up their city, small but newly made:
The {{c|440|Animal}} Kingdom's first stone was laid.

Their citizens were three, each of a kind:
First, the {{c|444|Choanocytes}}, who fished the sea;
Then the {{c|445|Archaeocytes}}, women refined;
And last the {{c|446|Pinacocytes}}, which made three.

The endodermal men would fish and feed
The city by the labor of their skill.
The mesodermal women's chosen deed
Was guarding it with a protective will.

The ectodermal folk who lived between
Would anchor all of it with steadfast might.
Their city, though by few it had been seen,
Was shining all the while with inner light.

From this great union there was born a son,
Bold {{c|458|Therion}}, a child of noble birth.
And when his days of childhood all were done,
He spread his lineage across the earth.

Great {{c|458|Therion}} then bore three children true:
Brave {{c|459|Porifer}}, who was the sponges' king,
And {{c|460|Thallus}}, geometric in his view,
And {{c|461|Cloudi}}, he whose house would upward spring.

Now {{c|460|Thallus}} chose to build the structured way,
With holdfasts gripping firmly to the stone.
His {{c|462|Choanoderms}} stood in bright array,
Extended outward in directions known.

But {{c|461|Cloudi}} raised his ectoderm on high;
Above the ground his city rose and soared.
His children stretched and reached toward the sky,
And every generation upward poured.

And then from {{c|461|Cloudi}} came two children bright:
Fair {{c|463|Cloudina}}, whose growing was so slow,
Who built her city with sediment's might,
And let her layers gently build and flow.

But brave {{c|464|Namacalathus}} grew and rose
Above the ground to seek the open air.
His city's secrets? Nobody now knows;
His mysteries are far beyond compare.

The sons and heirs of this great architect
Built cities that were strange and wondrous fair.
Their forms are ones we'll never quite detect,
Their wisdom lost, beyond our reach and care.

But {{c|459|Porifer}} chose a different path:
He was the first true sponge of days of old.
With ectoderm in its protective wrath
He kept his choanocytes safe and bold.

In patches safe from every wind and wave,
His fishermen could work and fish in peace;
And through this innovation that he gave,
He made it so his line would never cease.

From {{c|459|Porifer}} was born {{c|465|Wallas}} the true,
Who lived just as had lived his father dear.
But then a danger came into his view:
A storm approached, and with it deadly fear.

"O my people!" {{c|465|Wallas}} cried out aloud,
"We must prepare ourselves for what's ahead!
Pull tight your pseudopods, and stand up proud,
Or every one of us shall soon be dead!"

The shieldmaidens then heard their leader's call
And wrapped their arms around each open pore.
Their muscles, the first muscles of them all,
Would guard the things that had been there before.

These pores in time would grow until they'd be
The mouths, and other openings we see.
The muscles in their turn would come to wield
The power that contraction came to yield.

From {{c|465|Wallas}} came the great {{c|466|Solenos}}, who
Saw there a better way to build anew.
Through all his city, waters in their flow
Would bring the food to fill them as they go.

He sent his channels running through the stone,
And water rushed in through each open gate.
His city prospered, till it was full grown,
With fish caught early and with fish caught late.

From {{c|466|Solenos}} there came two sons to light:
Bold {{c|467|Leucon}}, and fair {{c|468|Sponga}}, shining bright.
And when their days of childhood were all done,
They filled the sea with all their might, each one.

Together they bore children, only two:
Great {{c|469|Vitrius}}, whose glass was pure and clear,
And {{c|470|Spongius}}, the wise one and the true,
Whose name we hold and cherish still as dear.

Now {{c|467|Leucon}} was a builder, great and grand;
He was a {{c|471|Leuconoid}} of complex form.
He filled his city all throughout the land
With labyrinths to weather every storm.

His gates and fishermen were there galore;
They made his cities massive, wide and tall.
The sons of {{c|467|Leucon}}, after him, built more
Than any that were seen before them all.

But {{c|469|Vitrius}}, his eldest son and heir,
Grew jealous of his father's lofty fame.
He thought his time had come, and he would dare
To seize the throne and claim the royal name.

A stone in hand, he struck down his sire,
And {{c|467|Leucon}} fell beneath the heavy blow.
Young {{c|469|Vitrius}}' cold and dark desire
Had brought his father down, and laid him low.

"I claim the throne!" he cried aloud with pride,
"For I shall rule with justice, firm and true!"
He built a house of glass, so tall and wide,
With walls of crystal, clear as morning dew.

He forced the people down onto their knees,
And made them work and work until they died.
He merged their minds, and gave them no more ease:
A hive-mind he created, full of pride.

When {{c|470|Spongius}} then asked his brother why
He'd struck and killed their father, who was dear,
{{c|469|Vitrius}} gave him back a cold reply
Rang out for everyone, and it was clear:

"Our father was a tyrant, harsh and cruel;
He worked the people till they met their death!
For I am justice's own chosen tool,
And I am armed with {{c|472|God}}'s own holy breath!"

He ran into his house, his crystal home,
And shouted out from there behind the glass:
"I am invincible! And none shall roam
Against my rule! My reign shall never pass!"

But {{c|470|Spongius}} reached down and took a stone,
And cast it with sure aim, and not in vain.
The house of glass came down, was overthrown,
And shattered all at once in crystal rain.

And as young {{c|469|Vitrius}} lay dying there,
His brother spoke to him these words so wise:
"Let all who in their hearts a hubris bear
Remember well the place their folly lies.

{{c|41|People}} who in a house of glass have built
Should never throw a stone, or cast it round,
For pride will only make them droop and wilt,
And bring them crashing, broken, to the ground."

To this day, we still quote him by his name
When pride, as pride will, goes before a fall.
And {{c|470|Spongius}} has earned his lasting fame
With wisdom that is shared among us all.

The sons of {{c|469|Vitrius}}, in time, became
The sponges made of glass, so strange and bright.
Upon the fringes they would stake their claim
To territories hidden out of sight.

But {{c|470|Spongius}} ruled with a gentle hand,
Both just and kind to each and every soul.
His wisdom spread abroad throughout the land
And made his people one, and made them whole.

From him there came two sons, both of them true:
The great {{c|473|Aristos}}, who was noble-born,
And {{c|474|Demos}}, a man who was, through and through,
Would be a leader free of any scorn.

Now {{c|474|Demos}} ruled efficiently, and stayed
True to the ancient ways his fathers made.
Conservative in how he ruled and reigned,
Through all his ruling days he so remained.

Most of the sponges in the world today
Descend from {{c|474|Demos}} and his ancient line.
Their many forms in grand and wide array
Show forth to all a heritage divine.

Among them were the sponges that are green,
The sons of {{c|475|Spongillus}}, so fair and bright,
Who tend their farms in lands that are serene
And give the waters round about them light.

In {{c|476|Siberia}}'s far and frozen lake,
Great {{c|477|Baikal}}, where the waters, cold and deep,
Even down there the green ones live and make
Their vigil, keeping watch the while we sleep.

And underneath {{c|478|Scorpio}}'s wintry sign,
When ice spreads out and covers all the mere,
The green sons, even so, will still divine
Their food and nourishment throughout the year.

Beside them, in the depths, there hunt and roam
The many sons of {{c|479|Chondrocles}}; and these
Have made the deep, dark water as their home,
And hunt their prey with far more skill and ease.

These carnivorous sponges, fierce and bold,
Pursue their prey with all their strength and might.
And stories of their hunting, when they're told,
Will fill the ones who listen with delight.

From {{c|473|Aristos}}, the noble, came two more:
The great {{c|480|Anu}}, unique among them, strange,
And {{c|481|Calcidoros}}, he whose ancient lore
Would through the reefs its many forms arrange.

Bold {{c|481|Calcidoros}} was the one who built
With calcium, and with its bright blessing.
His forms would never wither, never wilt
Beneath the sea and all its caressing.

With {{c|482|Calcifer}}'s own and mighty power,
And over silicon and its domain,
He built and raised up each coral tower
In forms that knew no limit or refrain.

His structures, simple, optimal, and true,
In beauty graced and filled the coral reefs;
And in the tropic waters, warm and blue,
His beauty brings to us its sweet reliefs.

But {{c|480|Anu}} was, of all, the most unique,
With basement membranes, something strange and rare.
Among all sponges, he alone would speak
A language none of all the rest could share.

His form was strange and curious to see,
Unlike in every way his spongy kin.
And such a singularity was he
Would set him in a class he stood within.

From all these great and ancient founders came
The sponges that we know and see today,
Each bearing still its founder's ancient name,
Each in its own and very special way.

Thus the {{c|440|Animal}} Kingdom slowly grew
Out from its small beginning, rock-bound start.
And though it was so simple, plain, and true,
It won and captured each and every heart.

For in these humble forms the patterns lay
Of all that was to come in later years;
Through all of life's great storms, along the way,
The plan for everyone who now appears.

The muscles that would someday come to move
Our bodies through the hours of the day,
The openings that in their turn would prove
That life will always find itself a way.

From {{c|459|Porifer}}, and from his first design,
To {{c|470|Spongius}} and to his wisdom deep,
The sponges' many lines all intertwine
With promises that they will ever keep.

So honor and revere each single sponge
That filters all the waters, keeps them clean.
Their ancient wisdom, in its forward lunge,
Connects what is with what has been and seen.

In every cell of ours that moves and beats,
And every single breath that we may take,
Their legacy goes on, and so completes
The many choices that we each must make.

So the {{c|440|Animal}} Kingdom's very start
Was humble, it was small, and it was true.
But now, in each and every beating heart,
The courage that they had still echoes through.


# Chapter 27: The Great Stabilization

From {{c|480|Anu}}'s unique lineage came
Two sons of very different fame:
Bold {{c|483|Enki}}, seeker of the sea,
And {{c|484|Homos}}, keeping family.

While {{c|484|Homos}} chose his father's way,
{{c|485|Content}} to live as they always stay,
Great {{c|483|Enki}} felt adventure's call
To sail beyond the harbor wall.

"I shall explore the ocean wide,"
Declared brave {{c|483|Enki}} with great pride.
"My creatures shall both move and scurry
Through seas and lands without worry."

He built a galley, great and grand,
The finest vessel in the land.
With millions of oars arrayed,
His mighty barge was made.

His head faced forward to the sea,
His men rowed powerfully.
Through waves both high and low,
They made their vessel go.

But soon great {{c|483|Enki}} found his plight:
Lost in the endless night.
No landmarks could he see,
{{c|486|Adrift}} upon the sea.

"I need wise men," brave {{c|483|Enki}} said,
"To guide where we are led.
Bring me astrologers so keen
To read what stars have seen."

The {{c|487|Flamens}} came, his priestly band,
{{c|488|Flask}} cells from the land.
These stargazers would divine
The paths through space and time.

The {{c|487|Flamens}} looked into the sky
And saw with their trained eye
Rich larvae floating by
With yolks that multiply.

"Here," they said, "the signs are right
To build beneath this sight.
The stars align above
To bless what we love."

But as they prayed for guidance true,
The gods came into view.
Each brought a sacred gift,
To help their spirits lift.

Dark {{c|489|Tyrosine}} the {{c|490|Devil}} came
With three spells of flame:
{{x|Adrenaline}}'s rush so bright,
{{x|Noradrenaline}}'s fight,
And {{c|491|Dopamine}}'s delight.

Then {{c|492|Tryptophanes}} the {{c|99|Sun}}
Blessed them, every one,
With {{c|493|Serotonin}}'s day
And {{c|494|Melatonin}}'s way.

For twilight's mystic hour,
He brought {{x|DMT}}'s power.
The sacred visions came
In the twilight's name.

{{c|495|Glutama}} the {{c|42|Empress}} brought
The balance that she taught:
{{x|GABA}}'s calming peace
And {{c|496|Glutamate}}'s release.

"We need more spells," said {{c|483|Enki}} wise,
"To help our people rise.
If {{c|497|Jehovah}}'s will be done,
More magic must be won."

Great {{c|296|Mithra}} heard his plea
And blessed him by the sea
With {{c|498|Acetylcholine}}'s might
To coordinate their sight.

Fair {{c|499|Iodina}}, mother great,
Revealed love's incarnate:
The sacred {{x|CYIQNCPLG}},
{{c|500|Oxytocin}}'s key.

Then {{c|501|Kali}}, dark and deep,
Gave spells to soothe and keep:
Three endorphins strong
To right what has gone wrong.

{{c|4|Alpha}}'s sequence clear:
{{x|YGGFMTSEKSQTPLVT}} here.
{{c|502|Beta}}'s longer chain:
{{x|YGGFMTSEKSQTPLVTLFKNAIIKNAYKKGE}}'s refrain.
{{c|432|Gamma}}'s shorter form:
{{x|YGGFMTSEKSQTPLVTL}} in the storm.

These became the tools
That break pain's rules:
{{c|503|Opium}}'s ancient call,
{{c|504|Morphine}} for all,
{{c|505|Heroin}}'s dark embrace,
{{c|506|Fentanyl}}'s dangerous face.

All these incantations blessed
Became the chemicals that test
The nervous system's might:
{{c|507|Neurotransmitters}}' light.

The {{c|487|Flamens}} learned to spear
The larvae swimming near.
Coordinated, they became
{{c|508|Nematocysts}} by name.

Their hunting grew precise
As they struck once and twice.
Their spears would never miss
Their targets in the abyss.

Soon cables stretched between
The hunters, long and keen.
{{c|509|Telegraph}} wires of old
Became nerves, brave and bold.

And this is why today
{{c|510|Priests}} carry, so they say,
{{c|511|Spears}} and wires combined
To serve the sacred mind.

Through neural networks wide,
{{c|483|Enki}}'s people could provide
{{c|512|Robotic}} arms so strong
Around their city's song.

These arms would catch with ease
The larvae from the seas.
His power grew and grew
As his great city flew.

He covered tentacles all
With {{c|444|Choanocytes}}' call,
To catch both great and small
{{c|513|Fish}} that rise and fall.

{{c|483|Enki}}'s city was a sight
Of technological might.
{{c|285|Proto}}-animal in form,
It weathered every storm.

From {{c|483|Enki}} came two sons
When his great work was done:
Bold {{c|514|Paraxus}} the strong
And {{c|515|Xiangus}} life long.

Now {{c|515|Xiangus}} took the way
Of robotic arms' display.
His fishermen arranged
On arms that never changed.

From {{c|515|Xiangus}} came the line
Of {{c|516|Daihua}} so fine.
Whose beauty was renowned
Wherever she was found.

From {{c|516|Daihua}}'s noble race
Came {{c|517|Dinomischus}}' grace.
A creature strange and tall
Who towered over all.

And from this ancient lord
Came {{c|518|Siphus}}, by accord
The ancestor of all
The comb jellies' call.

These {{c|519|Ctenophores}} so bright
Move with rainbow light.
Their combs catch the sun
As through waves they run.

But {{c|514|Paraxus}} the great
Would found a different state.
His lineage would grow
To realms we yet don't know.

Far greater nations he
Would father by the sea.
His legacy would span
The future's plan.

From {{c|483|Enki}}'s bold design
Came the neural line.
The nervous system's start
Played its crucial part.

The chemicals that flow
Through minds both high and low
Were born upon that day
When {{c|483|Enki}} sailed away.

In every thought we think,
In every neural link,
{{c|483|Enki}}'s ancient quest
Lives on in our breast.

The neurotransmitters' dance
In every glance
{{c|520|Recalls}} that fateful hour
When gods gave their power.

So honor brave {{c|483|Enki}},
Who sailed the endless sea.
His courage and his quest
Gave neurons to our nest.

The {{c|487|Flamens}}' starry sight,
The nematocysts' might,
The neural networks vast
All came from ages past.

In every brain that thinks,
In every nerve that links,
The echo still rings true
Of {{c|483|Enki}}'s journey through.

The animals that move
With coordinated groove
All trace their lineage back
To {{c|483|Enki}}'s neural track.

From sponge to human mind,
The pattern still we find:
The nervous system's art
Connects each beating heart.


# Chapter 28: Continental Drift Begins

Great {{c|514|Paraxus}} was blessed upon a day
By {{c|521|Hecate}}, the {{c|522|Hexenmaiden}}, deep
And wise, who came to him to show the way,
And gave him gifts that he would always keep.

And then she cast a {{c|523|Hex}} upon his line,
And the {{c|525|Homeobox}}, that sacred tool,
A {{c|524|Hox}} of power that was so divine,
Would be bilateral symmetry's rule.

"Look here," the lovely {{c|521|Hecate}} declared,
"No more shall creatures drift and float around;
{{c|526|Direction}} shall be yours, and shall be shared,
A plan for everything that you have found."

In {{c|527|Pennsylvania}}'s green and sacred land
Her daughters make {{c|524|Hox}} signs to show the way,
With careful work and with a skillful hand,
Of bilateral order and its day.

On buildings they inscribe the sacred sign;
In homes and temples these are seen today;
They bring about the cosmic plan divine;
These marks of their great legacy will stay.

With {{c|525|Homeobox}} there to guide their path,
Like any well-directed, careful child,
Great {{c|514|Paraxus}} escaped from all the wrath
Of chaos and disorder, fierce and wild.

Their city pointed toward the sacred east,
To {{c|296|Mithra}}, and to his all-knowing eye,
And to {{c|497|Jehovah}}'s own eternal feast,
To {{c|271|Elohim}} beneath the open sky.

The currents caught their city, carried true;
{{c|434|Life}} found direction now for the first time,
As bilateral patterns spread and grew,
As told in great {{c|514|Paraxus}}' ancient rhyme.

In youth he lived a roaming nomad's way,
And swam among the waves; but, old, the floor
He crawled, through all the length of every day,
To graze upon the sea's abundant store.

The greens that carpeted the ocean deep
Became the food on which he daily fed,
The riches {{c|528|Davy}} {{c|529|Jones}} would guard and keep,
Bilateral abundance richly spread.

And from {{c|514|Paraxus}} came three sons: the one,
Bold {{c|530|Bilateron}}, strong and true; and new,
With mouths so strange, was {{c|531|Cnider}}; and the son
Last born was {{c|532|Placus}}, simple through and through.

Now {{c|531|Cnider}} built himself a wondrous form:
From each lobe of his body, broad and wide,
That he might weather every wave and storm,
He made himself a mouth on either side.

Through these as portals he would come to feed;
His radial symmetry made him strong;
He caught the fish that he would ever need,
And prosperous he stayed his whole life long.

But {{c|532|Placus}} chose the simple, humble way,
The simplest animal among them all,
And keeps it still, down to the present day,
His body staying very plain and small.

The only cells that ever bear his name
Are humble, but they all of them survive,
Live on today and carry {{c|532|Placus}}' fame,
And keep his ancient line of life alive.

But {{c|530|Bilateron}} chose another path,
And crawled along and searched the ocean floor
For greatness, and for all its aftermath,
And sought for prey, still richer, and still more.

"I need to see," {{c|530|Bilateron}} then said;
"{{c|533|Observatories}} I shall raise and build,
So I can hunt and find my daily bread,
And man them with a priesthood that is skilled."

The astrologers came, and gathered round;
They gazed up high upon the starry host,
And built two pits within the sacred ground,
To learn from stars the things that mattered most.

And with {{c|295|Lord}} {{c|232|Carotenus}}' blessing bright,
They built for him the very first true eyes,
And with {{x|PAX6}}, and with its sacred rite,
With which to see beneath the open skies.

These organs, made to gather in the light,
Would give him sight; no more, now, being blind,
Would {{c|530|Bilateron}} hunt, as in the night,
With only touch to guide him and to find.

Fair {{c|534|Vendia}} became his chosen bride,
Who stayed with him; and children, only two,
They bore together, living side by side:
Great {{c|535|Coelomus}}, and {{c|536|Xenus}}, who was true.

The sons of {{c|536|Xenus}} held and kept the line,
And to this very day they keep the way
Of their traditions, ancient and divine,
In which their old ancestral people stay.

Among the sons of {{c|536|Xenus}}' noble race
Was {{c|537|Roscoff}}, who had wed a maiden fair,
The {{c|538|Tetraselma}}, and so found his place,
An alga that was far beyond compare.

Together they became the wedded pair
Who founded lines; and, living still today,
The {{c|537|Roscoff}} worms, so very strange and rare,
Still follow in their old ancestral way.

In algal harmony, by millions, they
Still swim within the sea; and, as his bride,
The alga lives within him, there to stay;
She swims along with him there, side by side.

But {{c|535|Coelomus}} chose a different course,
And built himself with even more intent:
His stomach reached so deep, with such great force,
Right through and through his body's whole extent,

Until it came out on the other side;
The anus, something that was new and strange,
And this became his glory and his pride:
It was a revolutionary change.

Mesoglea to mesoderm, he changed;
He built himself a coelom, deep and wide,
With cavities so firm, and well arranged,
With room for all his organs there inside.

His kidneys and nephridia were found
To fill this area; and he then brought
From ectoderm, out of the new-made ground,
The neural net, which he himself had taught.

A telegraph, a network vast and grand,
Linked every citizen, and reaching wide,
Connected every part of all his land,
And all into the network bound and tied.

Then {{c|539|Kimberella}}, fairest ever seen
Within the sea, became his queen; and they
Bore {{c|540|Nephrus}}, strong and prosperous and keen,
For all to see, through every later day.

Now {{c|540|Nephrus}} built, throughout his body's frame,
Small kidneys, which across it widely spread,
And which he bore beneath his very name,
To keep his systems working and well fed.

Sweet {{c|541|Ikaria}}, love of his long life,
Then came to him; and {{c|542|Cambrius}}, the bold,
Was born to them, the husband and the wife,
Who would be glorious, as we are told.

Great {{c|542|Cambrius}} saw that there was a need,
And so he segmented his body's form
To do a more complex and greater deed,
So he might better weather every storm.

In countless segments and repeating parts,
Each one with its sophisticated bone,
He built himself his many beating hearts,
And every segment had them as its own.

{{c|543|Scaffolding}} that was so complex and new
Would make his body over, newly grown;
Each part of him could beat alone, it's true,
Yet all work as one whole and single zone.

And in between each segment and its pair
A heart was beating; and his bloodstream flowed
Out from the hearts and pumping everywhere
Along the length of every segment's road.

From this great innovation, there then came,
Through segmentation and its lasting art,
The bilateral kingdom and its fame,
Which gave the animals their early start.

No longer were they simple balls of cells
Without design, but bodies, built to plan,
Not creatures housed in asymmetric shells,
Complex and grand, as only nature can.

The {{c|524|Hox}} genes came to show and point the way
For all the animals, the pattern true
That each of them would carry and display
In everything they are and that they do.

From head to tail they were in turn arranged;
Through {{c|525|Homeobox}} and its firm control
And all their fates were traded and exchanged,
Which made each creature that existed whole.

So honor the fair {{c|521|Hecate}}, who brought
Her {{c|523|Hex}}, and cast it on the ancient line,
The mystery to us that she had wrought,
That raised the whole bilateral design.

And give your praise to brave {{c|514|Paraxus}}, who
Was glorious, whose symmetry would change
Biology in all he came to do,
Bilateral, in all its width and range.

From {{c|531|Cnider}}, and from his radial form,
Through all the paths, in other, varied ways,
To {{c|542|Cambrius}} and his segmented norm,
They all would come to spend their living days.

But {{c|530|Bilateron}}'s line would come to grow,
Its bilateral body plan, which ran
To all the life we love, and all we know,
And gave birth to the beast and to the man.

In every eye that opens up and sees,
In every heart whose blood, through all the veins
And all the arteries, goes out and flees,
The ancient pattern of {{c|542|Cambrius}} reigns.

The coelom, with its open inner space,
Gave all the organs room; and, with their art,
The nephridia, each one in its place,
Would give the kidneys of the world their start.

And so, from simple forms to the complex,
The animals in all their kinds arose
Through all the power of {{c|521|Hecate}}'s hex,
And stood within their bilateral rows.

So when you see the image of your face
{{c|544|Reflect}} its form, remember, brave and true,
{{c|514|Paraxus}}, who, with bilateral grace,
Was the first one who made that plan for you.

# Capricorn (2宮) - Days 29-56


# Chapter 29: First Ice Age Begins

In {{c|202|Terra}}'s rivers, flowing wide and free,
Two lineages lived, which would belong
Together, in a bond, and come to be
United, all their lives, their whole lives long.

Great {{c|545|Symbio-Mygus}}, a fungal lord,
In the tenth generation from the line
Of {{c|546|Zygos}}, {{c|454|Mygus}}' son, by old accord,
Of that most ancient father, the divine.

And fair {{c|547|Charina-Planta}}, shining bright,
Tenth from {{c|549|Charina}} and her algae clan,
The {{c|548|Daughter}} of photosynthetic light,
That lived where waters of the river ran.

These two would meet together on the shore
Of {{c|550|Lichen}} {{c|551|Lake}}; in marriage they would bind
Two unlike kinds, as none had met before:
The fungus with the plant would be combined.

"Come here, O lovely maiden of the green,
And let us join together our two ways,"
Said {{c|552|Symbio}}-{{c|454|Mygus}}, the king serene,
"And rule as one through all our living days."

"I capture light that comes from sunny skies;
You gather, from the stone and from decay,
From earth, the nutrients that will arise;
Together, you and I can rule the day."

{{c|549|Charina}}-{{c|553|Planta}} listened to his call,
And she agreed with all her strength and might,
Photosynthetic, giving him her all,
To answer to his fungal appetite.

"A fusion, then, is what we shall create,"
She said to him, "and, standing side by side,
{{c|554|Plant}} and the fungus, we will meet our fate;
We'll conquer land, and spread both far and wide."

The marriage that they made, a wondrous sight,
Was two great kingdoms joining, and so grand
An agricultural realm in its might
Rose up to claim and hold the fertile land.

When {{c|550|Lichen}} {{c|551|Lake}} was full, its waters high,
They thrived; but when the waters went away
And dried, beneath the open, burning sky,
They slept, and waited for another day.

{{c|555|Dormant}} throughout the time of drought they lay,
And waited for the rain; and then again,
When water came in all its rich display,
They rose to rule across their vast domain.

Together they bore children who were bright,
And each was made a fusion of their line,
The lichens, who were filled with double might,
Both strong in fungus and in plant divine.

And countless were the forms they took with glee,
Each one well suited; and, among the crowd,
{{c|556|Fruticose}} lichens, rising like a tree,
Rose up above the lowly, tall and proud.

The {{c|557|Reindeer}} {{c|558|Moss}} spread out both far and wide;
{{c|560|Cladonia}}'s cups held the morning dew;
With {{c|559|Goldeneye}} {{c|550|Lichen}} there, at their side,
While {{c|561|Old}} {{c|562|Man}}'s {{c|563|Hair}} in hanging breeches grew.

And then the great foliose lichens came,
The {{c|564|Ruffle}} {{c|550|Lichen}}, which was soft and fair,
As leafy beauties, earning all their fame,
And {{c|565|Pillow}} {{c|550|Lichen}}, found now everywhere.

And {{c|566|Physcia}} spread out his leafy form,
And these, the leafy beauties, caught the light
And weathered every kind of wind and storm,
And made the places that were barren bright.

The crusty crustose lichens, hard and strong,
In all the harshest places, dry and rough,
Could live through times both short and very long,
Where other life could not find there enough.

The {{c|567|Rime}} {{c|550|Lichen}} upon the mountain's height,
So tough, so strong, so made to hold and last,
And the {{c|568|Orange}} {{c|569|Sea}} {{c|550|Lichen}}, burning bright,
Held on when all the other life had passed.

The powdery and leprose lichen clan
Broke up, and scattered everywhere they blew,
Spread out from where they first of all began,
And found new territories where they flew.

The {{c|570|Leprose}} {{c|550|Lichen}}, like a golden dust,
Rose on the wind, its particles to fly,
Scattered abroad with every windy gust,
To colonize the places low and high.

Some lichens chose the hardest, roughest way:
The {{c|571|Endolithic}} forms, so very small,
Who lived within the rock, and there would stay,
Made stone their home, and stone was all in all.

The {{c|15|Ruby}} {{c|572|Firedot}}, who was burning red,
Had life where nothing else at all could live,
Within the solid rock that was his bed,
And yet he still had more of life to give.

The filamentous lichens also came;
The cyanobacteria they'd shield,
To play a guarding and protective game,
From harm in every area and field.

{{c|573|Ephebe}} wound his threads, and so would bind
The blue-green life; they made a home their own,
The partner he himself had come to find,
Where neither could have lived and thrived alone.

And strangest of them all for us to see,
All in a gelatinous, soft embrace,
Were jelly lichens living by the sea;
They found themselves a home and living space.

There was {{c|574|Tar}} {{c|575|Jelly}} {{c|550|Lichen}}, dark and thick,
Within whose jelly they would swim and live,
Cyanobacteria's magic trick,
And mutual aid they would always give.

But {{c|552|Symbio}}-{{c|454|Mygus}}, great as was he,
Took yet another bride, both young and fair,
{{c|576|Trentophila}}, the daughter, as we'll see,
Of {{c|577|Trent}}, the one who had the golden hair.

The daughters of {{c|576|Trentophila}} then went
And colonized the world; and all around,
Far out across the area's extent,
Spread out the partnership that they had found.

And some would turn to parasitic ways,
As {{c|578|Cephaleura}}, envying the bright
And lovely {{c|579|Amber}}'s daughters, in her days,
Stole from them their photosynthetic light.

But greatest of all of the partnerships,
The daughters of fair {{c|579|Amber}}, who were true,
Were those that sailed upon great nature's ships,
And all the sons of {{c|580|Arbusculus}} too.

Great {{c|579|Amber}} wed {{c|580|Arbusculus}}; the pair,
Who bore both {{c|581|Glomer}} and {{c|582|Ashley}}, would be
Most glorious in union, past compare,
With children, both of them so strong and free.

And {{c|582|Ashley}} then was wed with {{c|583|Wort}}, the wise;
Their love would bring the plants so fresh and green,
The ancestors who would from them arise,
And mosses, the most fair that have been seen.

They built themselves a city on the land,
The first to leave the water and its hold,
A city beautiful as well as grand,
That staked upon the land its claim so bold.

But {{c|582|Ashley}} could not stand there all alone;
She needed help to gather, as she could,
Upon that land of dry and barren stone,
Her food from soil that was not rich or good.

So {{c|581|Glomer}}, her own brother, true and kind,
Built them a network, so that they could share,
With all the power of his mind, designed
Below the ground, the nutrients down there.

Just like his lichen brothers, who were old,
So he, by sharing, helped them all to thrive;
The story of {{c|581|Glomer}} too would be told,
Of partnerships that keep the world alive.

He dug down deep into the earthen ground
While {{c|582|Ashley}} farmed above in sunny light;
Down there the minerals could then be found,
And so their trade was mutual delight.

{{c|582|Ashley}} and {{c|583|Wort}} bore children past all bound;
But raising young upon a land so dry,
Their progeny so countless all around,
Required the help of fungi who were nigh.

So {{c|581|Glomer}} built a network that was vast:
The Wood Wide {{c|584|Web}}, that ancient, spreading net,
A network that forever more would last,
That serves the forests of the world as yet.

An underground economy was made,
Where each plant dealt with every other one
In mutual harmony and fair trade
Through him, their fungal brother, all as one.

The wood wide web was not a bubble's dream:
He was the first of all of them to see,
{{c|581|Glomer}}, who solved their trouble with his scheme,
That our cooperation sets us free.

His startup grew till it was past all gauge;
Today he holds the largest market share,
A network that was treasure for the age,
Of all the fungal networks everywhere.

With eighty percent of the market's hold,
His {{x|WoodNet}} service, tested, tried, and true,
Of which the story still is spoken, told,
Connects the forest wholly, through and through.

But other fungi joined into the game,
And each one sought to win its own great fame.
The {{c|585|Ectomycorrhizae}} also came
To play their part within the network's frame.

And {{c|586|Amazon}} became of this a part,
The Wood Wide {{c|584|Web}}, which spreads out far and wide,
Of this great networked and connected art,
Through every forest, and on every side.

By this great union, made of all the might
And of {{c|549|Charina}}-{{c|553|Planta}}'s great power,
Of {{c|552|Symbio}}-{{c|454|Mygus}} and of his sight,
They conquered and they won in every hour.

So they built their civilization grand
And great, a realm that brought about a change
Upon the fertile and the open land
To history, in all its depth and range.

Like {{c|262|Saya}}'s daughters, who had come before,
These lichens, and their fungal friends and kin,
Like them, would open evolution's door,
And make the age of ice itself begin.

And so the {{c|587|Cryogenian}} began;
The world froze over, it was white and cold,
That age, humanitarian in plan,
As it is in their mighty story told.

But even in their icy reign supreme,
They lived the life of partnership, allied,
Of plant and fungus, and its waking dream,
That could in cold, and in the ice, abide.

So honor {{c|552|Symbio}}-{{c|454|Mygus}}, the true,
Whose marriage showed to all the world the way,
And {{c|549|Charina}}-{{c|553|Planta}}, honor her too,
In which a partnership can last and stay.

In every lichen that you chance to see
Upon a rock, their legacy today,
Or growing on the branches of a tree,
Lives on in symbiotic, rich display.

From every mountain peak to ocean shore
Their children show how the unlike of kinds,
Still living, as they will for evermore,
Can join together both their hearts and minds.

The Wood Wide {{c|584|Web}} that runs beneath our feet,
The network that they started, firm and strong,
Makes all the life within the wood complete,
Begun so long ago, and sings its song.

In partnership it is we find our strength
To help each other as we live and grow;
And we will go to any kind of length
Through all that we may ever come to know.

The lichen's lesson, which is tried and true:
That we can face, together, every one
Of all the storms that come, both me and you,
And never once be broken or undone.


# Chapter 30: Snowball Earth Begins

Here is the chronicle of {{c|531|Cnider}}'s reign:
He sat upon a rock, a throne of stone,
And built, on either side of his domain,
A row of mouths, which were his very own.

With tentacles that reached down far below,
He made his city there upon the stone,
A great and mighty column, all aglow,
Where he would rule in might, and all alone.

His fishermen in lines he set and placed;
Down each mouth, working with a skillful art,
A {{c|588|Siphonoglyph}}, so perfectly spaced,
Each one of them would play his fishing part.

Great {{c|531|Cnider}} made a sacred, binding pact
With {{c|201|Luna}}; by her blessing, bright and true,
And keeping, both of them, to their contract,
Upon the full moon, he bore children two.

Two sons came forth within her silver light:
{{c|589|Anthus}}, traditional; and, as the new,
{{c|590|Anaxydros}} the bold, who, in his might,
With innovations, would come shining through.

And to this day, when {{c|201|Luna}}'s shining face
Shines full, the sons of {{c|531|Cnider}} and the fair
{{c|591|Nettle}}'s, within the sea's watery place,
Will settle all their spawning matters there.

By moonlight it is that they bear their young;
The tidal pull, the silver of her beam,
While {{c|201|Luna}}'s ancient song is being sung,
Fulfill for them their reproductive dream.

Now {{c|589|Anthus}} kept and held the ancient way;
His children built on stone a rocky home;
He followed what tradition would display,
And never far from land would they then roam.

But bold {{c|590|Anaxydros}} had chosen change;
From him there came two children, only two;
His innovations were both new and strange:
Great {{c|592|Pompom}}, and {{c|593|Meduson}}, who was true.

Great {{c|592|Pompom}} chose the stalked and rooted path;
He built his home upon the ocean floor
To weather time, and weather nature's wrath,
And opened up the innovation's door.

From {{c|592|Pompom}} came two sons of strength and might;
The stalked jellyfish is what they became,
{{c|594|Conos}} and {{c|595|Stauros}}, who were burning bright,
{{c|596|Adding}} still more to their ancestor's fame.

But {{c|593|Meduson}} would choose another way;
A city of a new kind he would build;
He would not on the bottom ever stay;
His city with a wanderlust was filled.

His city floated freely in the sea;
He was the ancestor of jellyfish,
Drifting along, and drifting wild and free,
And granted them their floating, roving wish.

At first he had no sense of direction;
He picked up what he could, and he would ride,
Just aimless drift, without a connection,
While floating there along the drifting tide.

But soon a new idea came to him,
Who floated: "Why drift where the currents go?
Since I am floating, and am free to swim,
I'll pump, and swim, and go both high and low!"

He learned to pump his body, squeezing tight,
And, helpless now no more, nor left to drift,
He shot through all the water with delight;
His swimming was his talent and his gift.

Meanwhile, the sons of {{c|589|Anthus}} spread and grew;
Among them, the {{c|597|Anemones}}; and these,
Across the oceans, which were deep and blue,
Would sway in water, just like flowered trees.

And {{c|598|Corals}} built their cities, great and grand,
And with {{c|436|Zooxanthellae}} they would farm
Upon the ocean's ever-shifting sand,
And keep their cities safe and free from harm.

{{c|599|Zoochlorellae}}, green and shining bright,
Would help them, and these partnerships would make,
By catching all the morning's golden light,
The reefs, for other creatures and their sake.

From {{c|593|Meduson}} there then came children two;
Each one of them would take another path,
Bold {{c|600|Diplos}}, and sweet {{c|575|Jelly}}, who was true,
Through all the ocean's joy, and through its wrath.

Fair {{c|575|Jelly}} bore two great and mighty lines
Of jellyfish: the first, box-shaped and wise,
The {{c|601|Cubozoans}}, with their grand designs,
Who learned the way to use their seeing eyes;

And {{c|602|Scyphozoans}}, called "{{c|603|True}} {{c|604|Jellyfish}},"
To see whose beauty, there within the deep,
Was granted many a sailor's heart's wish,
Where all the secrets of the ocean keep.

The sons of {{c|605|Scyphos}} numbered very high;
Each polyp bore a myriad of young
Beneath the sea, and underneath the sky,
Whose praises would forever more be sung.

The {{c|606|Pacific}} {{c|569|Sea}} {{c|591|Nettle}} swam along;
Its trailing tentacles, so long, would make,
Through waters, like a ram, so swift and strong,
The predators think twice, for their own sake.

But {{c|607|Cubos}} was a father who was kind;
He bore but few, but they were children dear;
With caring in his heart and in his mind,
He held each one of them, and kept them near.

We pray to {{c|607|Cubos}} when we come to seek
To be as fathers; he shows us the way,
Who would be strong as he, and never weak,
To care for all our young on every day.

The eyes of {{c|607|Cubos}}, complex, sharp, and true,
Were no mere spots of light at all; and these
Could see right through the waters, deep and blue,
For they were eyes that truly see and seize.

They saw each detail in the liquid space,
Each movement, and each form; and still today
The box jellyfish, in every face,
Still see the world in {{c|607|Cubos}}' ancient way.

From {{c|531|Cnider}}'s ancient and his noble line
Came forms: some stayed on rocks along the shore,
Some crude, some fine, in many a design,
While others chose to rise, to swim, and soar.

The anemones wave their many arms
Like flowers; touch them, and you'll feel the sting
That hides beneath their soft and pretty charms,
Of cnidocytes that circle in a ring.

The corals build their reefs, so vast and grand;
Beneath the waves, the reefs grow up and rise,
{{c|608|Cities}} spread out through all the ocean land,
As if they were great underwater skies.

And every polyp, sitting in its cup,
Will reach its tentacles to catch what drifts,
The passing food, and hold its tendrils up
Through all the water's soft and gentle shifts.

The jellyfish, which swim so wild and free,
Will show us how to move about with grace
Through every single region of the sea,
Throughout the whole of life and its embrace.

And some will drift along the current's flow,
And some will choose their course; each has its place,
The way to drift, the way to where they go,
Within the ocean's vast and open space.

The way of the cnidarian today,
Without a question, and without a doubt,
Lives on and thrives within each sea and bay,
Where tentacles are reaching, stretching out.

From {{c|531|Cnider}}, sitting on his rocky throne,
His children spread across the waters wide,
And all of them by now are fully grown,
With tentacles to be for them a guide.

And so, in every sting that you may feel,
Remember {{c|531|Cnider}} and his ancient art,
From jellyfish, so painful and so real,
Which was the one that gave them all their start.

Their radial symmetry, which they show
In patterns that are clean, and that are true,
In their biology, will let us know,
In every single thing that they may do.

So honor the great {{c|531|Cnider}}, and with pride,
Who sat upon his rock, upon his stone,
That ancient one, provider far and wide,
And made the sea and all of it his own.

His covenant with {{c|201|Luna}} and her light
Still guides them; when the full moon shines above,
As it has guided them through every night,
They make and give their spawn with all their love.

And the cnidarians that live today,
With tentacles, still go about to hunt,
And follow on in {{c|531|Cnider}}'s ancient way,
And do the work of their survival stunt.

From simple to complex, without a stop,
The jellyfish are still there, and they roam,
From polyp up to apex, to the top,
Through all the ocean's salty, rolling foam.


# Chapter 31: Rodinia Supercontinent Forms

And when {{c|542|Cambrius}} and {{c|609|Spriggina}} died,
Great heroes of the sea, upon their throne
Two sons were left to rule with equal pride:
Bold {{c|610|Protos}}, and {{c|611|Dutrus}}, each one alone.

Each brother saw it in another way:
The body plan that their two parents made,
To honor what their parents' line would say,
Would be interpreted, and be obeyed.

Great {{c|610|Protos}} looked upon their body form
And said: "The first hole is the mouth, so wide;
I'll keep it to the old and ancient norm:
The second is the place where waste will hide."

"The mesoderm is like the ancient past,
{{c|612|Mesoglea}}; and, as in olden sight
Our fathers did, which will forever last,
My mouth shall bear its tentacles so bright."

"O heathen, do you not, then, clearly see,
After the generations forced to dwell
In filth, the anus is what set us free?
It is the door: we're saved, and all is well!"

"We keep our mouths so clean, and keep them pure;
The endoderm and ectoderm, these three;
We eat the food that's nourishing and sure;
And mesoderm as well, shall ever be!"

"These layers we shall never, ever mix;
They are the old foundation, tried and true,
For they are our civilization's fix,
And they shall guide us in all that we do."

But bold {{c|611|Dutrus}} did not see it the same,
And came forth to proclaim: "What I would say,
My contrary and my opposing claim,
Is: second, mouth; the first takes waste away."

"The mesoderm is something that is more:
It reaches past mesoglea, and goes,
Beyond what we have ever seen before,
To where the fisherman and shieldmaid grows."

"It is a great reunion, don't you see:
{{c|613|Choanoderm}}, {{c|614|Archaeocyte}} unite,
The unity of old, restored to be,
Together, side by side, within the fight."

"O heathen, can you still not understand
What we take in, within, into our core,
The mouth, now progress' guide and guiding hand,
Will shape the things that we will have in store?"

"The things that we expel are just the past;
By joining what is old with new again,
But what we eat is what will grow and last,
Together we'll build a glorious reign."

And so the war began, and it would rage,
To learn whose vision would define the way,
Across the leaves of history's long page,
For all of the great {{c|615|Cambrian}} display.

Each brother bore two sons of strength and might;
From {{c|611|Dutrus}} came two sons, both brave and true,
To join together in the coming fight:
They were {{c|616|Dietrich}} and {{c|617|Saccorhytus}} too.

From {{c|610|Protos}} came, with valor rising high,
{{c|618|Ectus}} and {{c|619|Spiralius}}; and the line
Of old had four grandsons now, standing by,
Who came to make their fates and paths align.

Strange {{c|617|Saccorhytus}} did not have a rear;
Without a way to rid him of his waste,
For him, no anus ever would appear,
His life would never be with fortune graced.

So {{c|611|Dutrus}}' legacy, in turn, then fell
To {{c|616|Dietrich}}, who would be the loyal son,
And serve his father, as he would, so well,
Until his life was finished, and was done.

The sons of {{c|611|Dutrus}}, as was widely known,
Were famous for the heads they had, so wise,
Throughout the world, where they had spread and grown;
But {{c|616|Dietrich}} had no head, and had no eyes.

No head had he, with which to lead the way,
But innovation came: a tail, so strong
And long, he built, and it would save the day,
To help him move his life and self along.

Through muddy ground he made his winding path,
With two nerve cords to guide him on his course,
And so avoided all the others' wrath,
And found at last prosperity's own source.

He settled down, and there he built a home,
A colony, which worked out very well,
His simple plan, in which he'd live and roam,
Within his old, ancestral, muddy dell.

Great {{c|619|Spiralius}} kept the faith, and stayed,
Avoiding common wraiths; and like a top
He built his city, bold and unafraid,
A trochophore, and one that would not stop.

With tentacles that were both long and wide
He fished the waters, there upon the shore,
And out to sea, and out from side to side:
No fisherman so skilled had been before.

His wealth grew greater, growing day by day;
The trochophore design had proven true
In his own prosperous and thriving way,
For all the things that he would ever do.

But {{c|618|Ectus}} was a bitter, angry soul,
The secondborn, who felt the stinging slight;
{{c|620|Resentment}} was his aim, and was his goal:
To make his grievance, as he saw it, right.

"I'll be the greatest one among them all;
Among the sons of {{c|542|Cambrius}} I'll shine,"
He said, in answer to his duty's call,
"And I will make the victory be mine."

His tentacles he changed and turned to teeth,
{{c|621|Ferocious}}; and, while battle songs were sung,
Above him and around and underneath,
He shed his skin so he would stay as young.

With muscles that were strong, and flexing true,
He leaped at everything; none got away,
Not one of all the prey that once he knew,
From {{c|618|Ectus}} and from all his fierce display.

"O eldest sons, beware of me!" he cried,
"The legacy belongs now to all those
Who fight; so take some caution in your pride,
For I will fight and will defeat my foes!"

And so it was that he declared a war
Against {{c|611|Dutrus}} and {{c|619|Spiralius}}, both,
That spread both near and far, as none before;
He swore his solemn and his hateful oath.

The sons of {{c|611|Dutrus}}, who were brave and true,
And {{c|618|Ectus}}, who was armed with fearsome might,
And all the sons of {{c|619|Spiralius}} too
Made ready, all three tribes, for the great fight.

These three great tribes would be the ones to write
On evolution's grand and lofty stage
The story of their vision and their sight;
Their conflict would define for us the age.

And so began that time of lasting fame,
When the diversity of life was lit
Across the ancient sea, and burned, a flame,
The {{c|615|Cambrian}}'s great legacy with it.

{{c|622|Bodies}} burst forth in forms that were unknown,
And {{c|623|Innovations}} rose up everywhere,
As every tribe set up and made its throne,
And filled the water and the very air.

{{c|624|Predator}} and prey, both of them alike,
As each of them would seek and strive to win,
Prepared themselves for war, and how to strike;
{{c|625|Arms}} races were at that time to begin.

The filter feeders found and made their place;
Some creatures burrowed deep into the mud;
And all the hunters ran and gave them chase,
While others went about and spilled their blood.

And {{c|626|Eyes}} evolved, that they might see the light;
And shells, and {{c|627|Claws}}, and armor, strong and thick,
And spines, appeared, prepared to meet the fight,
Became survival's great and useful trick.

And so the great explosion had begun;
The great {{c|542|Cambrius}}' legacy lived on
Beneath the shining of the ancient sun
From dusk until the coming of the dawn.

In every creature that we see, there lives
The choice between the old ways and the new,
This ancient memory, which it still gives:
It shapes and forms all things that we may do.

Some kept the ancient and the simple way,
While others, {{c|628|Innovative}}, burning bright,
And bold, instead would choose that they would stay
Within the eye of evolution's sight.

The war between the brothers, all the three,
Lives on today; in choices every day
We make, it lives in you as well as me;
We follow them, and follow their display.

{{c|629|Innovation}}, or the old tradition:
Each must submit, as everything that thrives,
In humble, everlasting submission,
Unto the force of life, the force that drives.

So honor now brave {{c|542|Cambrius}}, the one
Whose legacy is living on today,
By whom all of this fuss was first begun,
In every living thing, in every way.

The {{c|615|Cambrian}} explosion's blazing fire
In every form of life that we can see
Burns on, with longing and with desire,
And will, through all of time, forever be.


# Chapter 32: Pannotia Fragments

Within the age of patriarchs, the three,
Among these lords of power and of might,
{{c|611|Dutrus}}, {{c|618|Ectus}}, and {{c|619|Spiralius}}, free,
Was {{c|618|Ectus}}, who was the most fearsome sight.

With mouth agape, and with his teeth so sharp,
Through all his enemies he ripped and tore;
He played the music of destruction's harp
As no one else had ever done before.

The many sons of {{c|630|Isomeres}} the fair
Fell victim to his raiding, savage spree,
And all the sponges living everywhere
Across the waters of the ancient sea.

A complex mouth he built with skill and care;
He molted both his skin and mouth with time
To catch his prey, and catch it anywhere,
In rhythm, and in order, and in rhyme.

His cilia he cast off and away;
{{c|631|Amoebae}} then became, for him, his sperm,
In favor of a more effective way,
A change that was both very strange and firm.

His coelom he stripped down, and left it bare;
For function that was true, and made for speed,
Removed what had no use for being there,
He kept no more than what he'd come to need.

{{c|632|Unnecessary}} scaffolding he'd fling;
His organs floated freely there inside,
And cast it off, as one would cast a ring,
Within his pseudocoelom, so wide.

In burrowing he found his skill and art;
Through sediment he'd tear his way, and send,
And came to play the hunter's deadly part,
His foes to meet their final, bitter end.

The very first of predators was he;
Sons of {{c|611|Dutrus}} and {{c|619|Spiralius}} fell,
To hunt upon the waters of the sea,
Before his might, so glorious to tell.

In viciousness he bore a mighty horde;
They conquered all the earth from shore to shore,
Of worms, who served him as their only lord,
And always they would hunger after more.

Through the earth the great {{c|618|Ectus}} tore and ripped;
{{c|633|Destruction}} was the one he took as name,
While all the soil fell off of him and slipped,
And carnage was his pleasure and his game.

From {{c|618|Ectus}} came two sons of strength and might,
And clever {{c|635|Isaac}}, who was young and wise:
Bold {{c|634|Ishmael}}, who was ready for the fight,
And Isaac went to seek the new thing's prize.

Now {{c|634|Ishmael}} held onto it, fast and true:
Tradition was the guiding star he bore
For everything that once his father knew,
Through times of peace, and through the times of war.

But {{c|635|Isaac}} chose to take another way;
He'd build upon his father's ancient art,
And chose {{c|629|Innovation}} and its display,
But with a newer and a younger heart.

And out of {{c|634|Ishmael}}'s faithful, ancient line,
{{c|637|Patriarch}} of {{c|638|Priapulids}}, the brood,
There came {{c|636|Priapus}}, who was strong and fine,
Who live where darkness hides in solitude.

Deep in the ocean's depths they live and dwell,
Like the ancient {{c|639|Ediacaran}} lands,
In places that no one can find or tell,
Of the hydrogen sulfide and its strands.

Without the oxygen, they live and thrive;
In waters dark and deep, there they will stay
And keep their ancient line of life alive
Until the coming of the judgment day.

{{c|640|Draco}}, {{c|636|Priapus}}' brother, who was true:
The mud dragons, horrific and so wild,
Became himself a patriarch there too,
Each one of them was nature's problem child.

Through all the muds they go and make their way;
{{c|641|Monsters}} are what, down in the deep, they are,
Both in the night and all throughout the day,
Beneath the light of every shining star.

From {{c|635|Isaac}} came two sons of lasting fame,
And {{c|643|Rhineheart}}, who was bold, and who was strong;
And one of them, {{c|642|Nematus}}, was his name,
And Rhineheart lived and thrived his whole life long.

{{c|642|Nematus}} was a quick one, and was spry;
He bore two sons to bear his line along,
A nomad living underneath the sky:
{{c|642|Nematus}} the Second, and {{c|644|Gordy}} strong.

Both sons would turn out prodigal, and stray;
They turned to live a parasitic life,
From the traditional and older way,
And caused their father sorrow and much strife.

But then, in all his aging, later years,
{{c|642|Nematus}} left that way of life behind,
Through all his many sorrows and his tears,
And peace within himself he came to find.

He then became the ancestor, the great;
Of all the animals, eighty percent
Of worms throughout the world, in every state,
Are his descendants, through his long descent.

His city was a sight for all to view;
From simple things to complex things they grew,
A worm community, a city true,
In everything that they would come to do.

But {{c|644|Gordy}} chose the parasitic way,
From living in his brother's very flesh,
And never from it did he ever stray,
Within his host's blood, which was warm and fresh.

The {{c|645|Gordian}} worms are part of his line;
They live inside each victim's beating heart,
{{c|646|Horrific}} in their nature and design,
And tear the life of every one apart.

And out of {{c|643|Rhineheart}}, there then came two more,
And brave {{c|406|Loricus}}, who was armored well:
{{c|647|Lobopus}}, who would venture and explore,
With stories of them that the world would tell.

{{c|406|Loricus}} built himself an armor thick;
He married {{c|648|Siri}}, maiden sweet and fair,
To keep him safe and guard him from each trick,
And lived a life that was beyond compare.

His sons live in the depths that lie below;
For half a billion years, we'd always thought,
Down where the hidden mysteries will grow,
That their whole line to nothing had been brought.

But in the year of nineteen eighty-three,
Alive and well, in depths where they had dwelt,
We found them living there within the sea,
Down where the pressure of the deep is felt.

The {{c|649|Loricifer}}'s long and lasting tale,
As living fossils, there within the deep,
Is one that never in its time would fail;
Their ancient vigil they will always keep.

These are the heirs of great {{c|618|Ectus}}; they show,
Some with their armor, others with their speed,
What can protect us, as we've come to know,
And some a parasitic kind of greed.

The worms that rule the earth with us today
Remember their ancestor and his might,
Each one of them in its own kind of way,
The one who brought the predator to sight.

In every garden and its flower bed,
The legacy of old is living on
Where earthworms come to make their quiet tread,
From early dusk until the coming dawn.

In every single kind of parasite,
The spirit of {{c|618|Ectus}} lives on to tell,
That causes us to feel both fear and fright,
The story of his predatory spell.

From where the mud dragon has made its lair,
His many children roam across the world,
To ocean depths, so distant and so rare,
With all their tentacles stretched out, unfurled.

The age of all the three great patriarchs,
On everything around that we can see,
Has left upon the world its lasting marks,
And through all time, that ever is to be.

But {{c|618|Ectus}}, more than others, most of all,
To be the hunter, ever fierce and true,
Was one who {{c|650|Heeded}} evolution's call,
In everything he ever came to do.

His legacy, of tooth and of the claw,
That predator and prey must always dance,
Became for all the world great nature's law
Within the whole of life's great circumstance.

So honor now the fierce {{c|618|Ectus}}, a beast;
His hunger was the thing that drove the change.
So ravenous, he never ceased to feast,
Throughout the whole of evolution's range.

Without the predator and his great art,
The arms race that would follow on and lead
{{c|434|Life}} would not have been able then to start,
To every living thing and every creed.

In every creature's struggle and its fight,
The spirit of {{c|618|Ectus}} lives on in each,
To live and to survive another night,
Through all its power, beyond the dark's reach.


# Chapter 33: Ice Age Ends

Among the three great ancestors of old,
{{c|619|Spiralius}} was most conservative:
Those ancient processors, as we are told;
And all his ways were kept preservative.

He fished with tentacles, and they were long;
The ancient art he always kept alive,
As fathers did before him, and were strong,
So he could help his many children thrive.

Great {{c|619|Spiralius}} worked on every day
To give provision for his children, all,
In his own diligent and careful way,
Of those who came and answered duty's call.

Among his many sons of lasting fame,
Bold {{c|539|Kimberella}}, who would be the king,
And two of them earned everlasting name:
And {{c|651|Gnathifer}}, and with him came his ring.

And {{c|539|Kimberella}} came to earn renown;
His tomb is visited by us today,
For his eternal name and his great crown,
By pilgrims who are passing on their way.

He was the greatest king who ever reigned;
His kingdom moved along with strength and might,
Of his time's dynasty, and so remained,
Across the steppe that was so wide and bright.

A billion years of glory and of fame
(Upon {{c|219|Australian}} stamps, even today)
Belong to him, and to his mighty name;
His image holds its power and its sway.

But {{c|651|Gnathifer}} would choose another path:
A kingdom that was small, but that was quick,
In order he might show his righteous wrath,
He built it up with cunning and with trick.

Like {{c|618|Ectus}} he was able, too, to see,
A great jaw he constructed, built with care,
The need for weapons, as it came to be,
Made out of chitin, which was strong and fair.

It was a sugar jaw, and it was sweet;
But though his jaw was one of sugar made,
For all the sugar treats that he would eat,
His heart was not so gentle or so stayed.

With those ferocious jaws, so sharp and bright,
Upon {{c|630|Isomeres}}' sons, and all of these,
He brought a fearsome and a dreadful sight:
Throughout their territories he would seize.

When he was old, his loins brought forth a pair,
Bold {{c|652|Gnathos}}, who was fierce, and who was wild
(Of sons, like ancient coins, both rich and rare),
And {{c|653|Hydrover}}, who was the gentler child.

{{c|652|Gnathos}} was vicious; and his vicious art
(His sons are known among us all today)
Was more than any malice of the heart,
As {{c|654|Jaw}} {{c|655|Worms}}, who are living in their way.

But {{c|656|Xenognath}} was unlike all the rest;
He grew himself some jaws within his jaws,
Though still belligerent, and not at rest,
Against all of the natural world's laws.

Of jaws, fifteen in all were what he made;
Each jaw lay nested inside of the last,
A fearsome and a toothsome masquerade,
And held his prey within it firm and fast.

From {{c|656|Xenognath}} there came two mighty sons:
Who ruled the seas with might and all his main,
The bold {{c|657|Marinus}}, he who rules and runs,
And {{c|658|Limnos}}, who was of the falling rain.

{{c|657|Marinus}} fought and fought, and so he sought,
And his priority was to command,
For everything that ever could be caught,
{{c|659|Dominion}} of the sea, and not the land.

But {{c|658|Limnos}} was the one who was cast out:
Into the rivers he was exiled, sent
Away from all the ocean and its route,
And there his kingdom bowed, and it was bent.

The sons of {{c|657|Marinus}} will laugh and mock:
"You small-jawed ones," is what they always call
Their kinsmen in the far freshwater flock,
Their cousins, every one of them, and all.

And from {{c|657|Marinus}} there came two sons more,
And brave {{c|661|Amisquius}}, the one who'd be,
With {{c|660|Rotiferus}}, who went to explore,
So bold and glorious for all to see.

{{c|660|Rotiferus}} looked out and all around,
Among the sons of {{c|539|Kimberella}}'s line,
And there a peaceful way of living found,
Whose ways of living were both good and fine.

He turned to fishing, as he'd done before;
His sons became the nomads, roaming, true,
Just like his ancient kin, in days of yore:
The {{c|662|Rotifers}} that we see now and view.

In all the waters of the world they roam;
The greatest of all fishermen are they,
And everywhere they go, they make their home,
From fall of night until the break of day.

He built his coelom so that it was loose,
And this would give him both his speed and grace,
As {{c|618|Ectus}} did, who first had shown its use,
Within each and every watery place.

In villages of rotifers, they hold,
{{c|663|Fishing}} with all their spinning, turning wheels,
And practice privileges, as of old,
For all their food, and all their daily meals.

But there was one among his sons, whose cause,
{{c|664|Acanthus}}, the red one, who was so base,
Was set against and broke the ancient laws:
A parasite, a shame, and a disgrace.

He lives inside of other creatures' guts;
The food that rightfully should all belong,
He steals it from them, like the greedy nuts,
To those who are both righteous and are strong.

For such a thievery as this brings shame;
He is a black sheep there within the fold,
Upon {{c|660|Rotiferus}} and all his name,
And one whose story ought to still be told.

But from {{c|661|Amisquius}}, the brave, there came,
With each new generation, as they grew,
A line of greater glory and of fame:
Their {{c|665|Jaws}} became much bigger, through and through.

And then, in {{c|666|Nimrod}} {{c|667|Bristletongue}}'s great time,
They ruled the seas with all their strength and might;
Their power reached its height, and reached its prime,
A fearsome and an awe-inspiring sight.

And they were far more numerous than all;
The {{c|668|Arrow}} {{c|655|Worms}} is what they then became,
Of those who came to answer ocean's call,
Who made the hunters' greatest, lasting name.

The greatest hunters that were ever seen:
Their jaws could catch and grasp, and they could hold,
Beneath the waters of the ocean green,
The bravest of the brave, and of the bold.

Throughout the waters that are dark and deep,
And no prey ever can swim far away,
Their constant vigil they will always keep,
From them, and from their hunting's fierce display.

The old and the conservative, safe path,
In children who rise up, and who rebel,
Will sometimes come to show to us its wrath,
And in the stories that they come to tell.

{{c|619|Spiralius}} kept to the old ways, true,
In many new and distant directions;
But all his many children spread and grew,
And making all their varied selections.

And some stayed with the fishing that was pure,
While others went and chose the warrior's way,
Their methods being tried, and being sure,
So they might live to fight another day.

From tentacles, and on from them to jaws,
Each lineage would come to find its place,
In following the ways of nature's laws,
In all of evolution's mighty race.

The rotifer's own gentle fishing art,
While arrow worms will show to us their might,
Is one that warms and gladdens every heart,
Within the realm of predatory sight.

Both of them can trace their lineage back;
The careful and conservative old way,
To {{c|619|Spiralius}} and his ancient track,
Has led to the diverse and wide display.

In every freshwater and quiet pond,
To all the plankton that is floating by,
Where all the rotifers will then respond
Beneath the light of the bright morning sky,

Remember their ancestor, he who stood:
{{c|619|Spiralius}}, he kept the ancient art,
Protector of the fishing's livelihood,
That was the one that gave to them their start.

And so in every single arrow worm
His heritage continues, living on,
That makes the fishes in the waters squirm,
From evening's dusk until the morning's dawn.

The three great patriarchs of ancient days,
On all the life there is within the sea,
Have left their lasting marks in many ways,
For all the ages that are yet to be.

But {{c|619|Spiralius}} shows us, and shows well,
Important truths, and ones that will long last,
That the traditions have a tale to tell,
Through all the future and through all the past.

For {{c|629|Innovation}} has its rightful place,
But keeping what is working, and is true,
In evolution's long and ancient race,
Is wisdom, deep and lasting, through and through.


# Chapter 34: Laurentia Emerges

While sons of {{c|223|Proteus}} divided fast,
The sons of {{c|611|Dutrus}} moved along more slow;
And all their kingdoms grew till they were vast,
And let their wisdom, in its own time, grow.

There were two sons, twin brothers, who were born:
{{c|617|Saccorhytus}}, the one who was the lame,
Together in the early light of morn,
And {{c|616|Dietrich}}, who would be the one of fame.

Poor {{c|617|Saccorhytus}} never really grew;
He stayed a larva, and so he remained.
He never changed himself to something new,
And nothing more than that was ever gained.

His sons were sparse in number, and were weak;
Their father, with his young and childish way,
With little that they ever came to seek,
Had led them all, and led them all astray.

But {{c|616|Dietrich}} was different, though he'd fight;
In youth, he looked to be the very same,
At first against the change with all his might,
As was his brother, and his brother's frame.

But as the years went onward, passing by,
{{c|669|Maturity}} was what at last he found;
He grew, and reached his body toward the sky,
And wisdom in him came, and did resound.

{{c|670|Gill}} slits he built, and built them all with care,
To sift the ground beneath him, at his feet,
So he could filter here and everywhere
For all the food that he could find and eat.

A great and mighty tail is what he made,
Extending out beyond and past his rear,
A tail that would not ever come to fade,
So he could swim along both far and near.

A heart he built for him, and set within,
To send the blood throughout his body's frame,
To let the blood go forth, and to begin
To nourish him, and nourish in his name.

And then two great nerve cords he made and laid,
So that he could coordinate his might,
The one of them dorsal, one ventral, made,
And use it through the day and through the night.

Until he grew to be both great and strong,
The anatomy that he made and wrought,
His body grown both very large and long,
Would never ever fade, or come to naught.

The sons of {{c|616|Dietrich}} went abroad and spread
Across the world, which was so very wide,
To every place to which they would be led,
With fortune going with them as their guide.

Great fortune blessed them, and it blessed their way;
This time of theirs was called by one and all,
Throughout the hours of each passing day,
The time and the {{c|671|Fortunian}}'s great call.

And first among them born there were the twins,
Bold {{c|672|Ambulus}}, the one who would be free
(For it is here our story now begins),
And {{c|673|Chordatus}}, he who was of the sea.

These brothers both would work, and both worked well;
With sons of {{c|223|Proteus}} they ruled, and so,
With all the things they had, and had to tell,
They were victorious, with foes laid low.

They vassalized the wide and ancient land,
A realm that had existed, and that stayed,
Of {{c|674|Ediacar}}'s realm, so old and grand,
