Returned to burn the {{c|3516|Spanish}} empire through,
The pachakuti finally begun.

The {{p|Andes}} rose. From {{p|Cuzco}} to {{p|La Paz}},
From the altiplano's frozen breath
To the valley floors, the ancient cause
Brought sixty thousand to defy the death

That the empire promised every rebel soul.
{{c|3523|Quechua}}, {{c|3611|Aymara}}, mestizo, the poor
Of every color rallied to the whole
And incandescent vision: a world before

The {{c|3516|Spanish}} came--or a world that might yet be
When the chains were broken and the mita's weight
Was lifted from the shoulders of the free
And ancient peoples whom no colonial state

Had the right to grind to dust.

                                 At {{p|Sangarara}}
The rebel army met the {{c|3516|Spanish}} force
And broke it--the church itself the gharara
Of battle, when the powder magazine's course

Of flame exploded through the sacristy
And the {{c|3516|Spanish}} soldiers burned inside the nave--
Five hundred dead, the fire's ferocity
A sign, the {{c|3523|Quechua}} said, that even the grave

And sacred stones had turned against the crown.

But empires do not die from one defeat.

From {{p|Lima}} came the reinforcements' frown
Of twenty thousand men, the drum's hard beat

Of a professional army on the march.
And the alliance that {{c|3606|Tupac Amaru}} built
Was fragile--for beneath the rebel arch
The creole landowners felt their own guilt

And interest threatened: this was not merely war
Against the {{c|3516|Spanish}} king, but revolution
That might overturn the social floor
On which they too had built their institution

Of hacienda and of peonage.
They pulled away. The creoles chose the crown
Over the {{c|3523|Quechua}} future's open page--
Better the king they knew than the burning down

Of the colonial order that enriched them too.

{{c|3606|Tupac Amaru}} was taken in the field--
Betrayed, as prophets are, by the untrue
And fickle allies. In {{p|Cuzco}}'s square, the sealed

And terrible sentence was pronounced in May
Of seventeen-eighty-one. They cut the tongue
Of {{c|3612|Micaela Bastidas}} first--his wife, the stay
And strategist of the revolt--among

The crowd that wept. They killed his son before
His eyes. They tied his limbs to four horses
And tried to pull him apart--but the core
Of his body held, as if the {{x|Andean}} forces

Of the mountain stone had fused within his frame,
And the horses strained and could not tear
The {{c|3403|Inca}}'s body from the {{c|3403|Inca}}'s name--
Until the axe completed what despair

And horsepower could not do alone.

                                    They severed
His head and sent it south to {{p|Tinta}},
His limbs to the four corners, endeavored
To scatter him so thoroughly that no hint or

Memory could reassemble what they broke.
They banned the {{c|3523|Quechua}} language. Banned the wearing
Of the {{c|3403|Inca}} royal garments. Spoke
The decree that {{c|3403|Inca}} was a word past bearing--

Erased from law, from title, from the tongue.

But you cannot quarter a prophecy.

In {{p|Bolivia}} the fire leapt among
The {{c|3611|Aymara}} highlands, and the prophecy

Wore a new name: {{c|3613|Tupac Katari}}--
{{c|3614|Julian Apaza}}, who took his title from
Two thunderbolts: {{c|3606|Tupac Amaru}}'s rally
And {{c|3615|Tomas Katari}}'s martyrdom--

And laid siege to {{p|La Paz}} with forty thousand
Warriors who blocked the mountain passes
And starved the {{c|3516|Spanish}} city till the thousand
Corpses in the streets were the colonial masses

Who had starved the {{c|3611|Aymara}} for centuries.
{{c|3616|Katari}} too was taken, {{c|3616|Katari}} too
Was quartered--but he spoke the centuries'
Unbroken vow: "I die, but I return to you

As millions." And the millions came.

                                      For the name
Of {{c|3606|Tupac Amaru}} would echo through the age
Of liberation--{{c|3617|Bolivar}} claimed the flame,
And every rebel on the {{c|3618|Andean}} stage

Invoked the severed body that the horses
Could not tear apart, the prophecy
That no decree could silence, the forces
Of a mountain people's memory.

Honor {{c|3606|Tupac Amaru}}--whose blood
Was scattered to the four winds and the four
Directions of the {{c|3403|Inca}} world, the flood
Of royal crimson on the {{p|Cuzco}} floor

That seeped into the earth and fed the root
Of every revolution yet to come.
They quartered him, but from the living shoot
Of his sacrifice the millions would become

The thunderbolt he promised: I will return.
The {{p|Andes}} hold his name. The condor flies
Above the peaks where his scattered ashes burn,
And the sun that the {{c|3516|Spanish}} killed still rises.


# Chapter 249: The Northwest War

Now hear the forest speak.

                              In the country
Of the {{p|Wabash}} and the {{p|Maumee}}, where the trees
Grew thick as armies and the undergrowth's boundary
Was a labyrinth of shadow, root, and freeze

Of winter streams--the {{c|3619|Miami}} and the {{c|3620|Shawnee}},
The {{c|3621|Delaware}} and {{c|3622|Wyandot}} and {{c|3584|Ottawa}},
The {{c|3623|Ojibwe}} and {{c|3624|Potawatomi}}'s brawny
{{c|3625|Confederation}}--rose against the law

Of the new republic's hunger for the ground
Beneath their feet.

                     The {{x|Treaty}} of {{p|Paris}} gave
The {{c|3404|Americans}} a line drawn and unwound
Across the map--the {{p|Ohio}}'s wave

As boundary of the new nation's western edge.
But lines on maps are the empire's fantasy:
The nations of the forest held their pledge
To defend the land their grandfathers' dynasty

Had hunted since before the {{c|3244|English}} came,
And no treaty signed by distant {{c|3401|European}} hands
Could grant the {{c|3404|Americans}} a legitimate claim
To the {{p|Ohio}} country and its bands

Of sovereign peoples who had signed nothing.

The republic sent its soldiers west. The thing
It wanted was not peace but land--the cutting
And surveying of the forest, the clearing

Of the title, the erasure of the name
That every creek and ridge already bore
In {{c|3620|Shawnee}} and in {{c|3619|Miami}}--the same
Hunger that had broken down the door

Of every eastern nation now pressed west
With the weight of a {{c|3626|Republic}}'s manifest
And {{c|472|God}}-anointed greed.

                         They met the best
Military mind the continent possessed.

{{c|3627|Mihsihkinaahkwa}}--{{c|3628|Little Turtle}}--
War chief of the {{c|3619|Miami}}, whose tactical
Genius turned the forest to a girdle
Of destruction for every sabbatical

And blundering column the republic sent.
He read the woods the way a general reads
A map--each ridge and river-bend he lent
A military purpose, and the weeds

And thickets and the fallen timber's maze
Became his fortification, his redoubt,
His killing ground where the forest's haze
Of morning fog and shadow gave no route

Of safe retreat.

                  Beside him {{c|3629|Weyapiersenwah}}--
{{c|3630|Blue Jacket}} of the {{c|3620|Shawnee}}--brought the fire
Of a warrior's fury and a leader's awe
To the confederacy. And higher

Still, the {{c|3581|British}} at {{p|Detroit}} supplied
The muskets and the powder and the word
Of encouragement from the imperial side
That had lost the war but still preferred

The {{c|3561|Indigenous}} wall between the {{c|3484|American}} flood
And the fur-trade empire of the northern lakes.

In seventeen-ninety, {{c|3631|Harmar}} marched through mud
And forest with fourteen hundred men--mistakes

Compounding with each mile, the militia raw
And undisciplined, the column strung along
The trail like a serpent with a broken jaw--
And {{c|3628|Little Turtle}} struck. The primal song

Of the forest ambush: the musket's crack
From behind the trees, the warriors invisible
Until the killing began, the panicked pack
Of militia breaking, the indivisible

And lethal coordination of the allied nations
Moving through the woods like water through the stone.
{{c|3631|Harmar}}'s army shattered--two engagements'
Humiliation, then the long retreat alone

Back to {{p|Fort Washington}} with the dead
Left rotting on the trail.

                            The {{c|3626|Republic}} burned
With shame. And sent a larger force--{{c|3632|St. Clair}},
The governor, the general who had learned

Nothing from the forest's previous lesson.
Two thousand men marched north in the autumn rain
Of seventeen-ninety-one, the camp's aggression
Slackening with each cold and muddy day's refrain

Of desertion, sickness, dwindling supply--
Until the fourth of November found them camped
Along the {{p|Wabash}} headwaters, the sky
Still dark, the sentries sleeping, the stamped

And frozen ground a bivouac of the doomed.

At dawn {{c|3628|Little Turtle}} struck with everything.

A thousand warriors in the fog that loomed
Like the forest's own vengeance--the shattering

Of musket-fire from every side at once,
The camp dissolving into butchery,
The officers cut down in the opening stunts
Of a battle that was a masterwork, the summary

Of everything the forest nations knew
Of war against the invader's clumsy lines:
Six hundred {{c|3484|American}} dead, the avenue
Of retreat a gauntlet of the pines

And the pursuing warriors. {{c|3632|St. Clair}} escaped
On a packhorse, gout-ridden and disgraced--
The worst defeat the {{c|3484|American}} army gaped
At in its history, the taste

Of {{c|3561|Indigenous}} military genius on the tongue
Of a nation that would spend two centuries
Denying that such genius could have sprung
From the peoples it was determined to seize.

The {{c|3626|Republic}} reeled. But the {{c|3626|Republic}} had
What the confederacy did not: the endless
Reserve of men and money, the iron-clad
And industrial patience of a nation's relentless

Capacity to absorb defeat and return.

{{c|3633|Anthony Wayne}}--"{{c|3634|Mad Anthony}}"--was sent
With a disciplined and drilled army to burn
What {{c|3628|Little Turtle}} had built. He spent

Two years in preparation, forging soldiers
From the raw militia's undisciplined mass,
Building forts like stepping-stones, the boulders
Of a methodical advance through the grass

And forest of the {{p|Ohio}} country.

{{c|3628|Little Turtle}} read the wind. He saw
The change: this was no blundering foray
But a calculated war without a flaw

In its logistics. He counseled peace--
Negotiate, he said, while strength remains,
Before the final battle brings the lease
Of our sovereignty to its bloody strains.

But {{c|3630|Blue Jacket}} and the younger warriors chose
To fight--and {{c|3628|Little Turtle}}, loyal
To the confederacy, accepted what the prose
Of history would render as the royal

And tragic courage of the final stand.

At {{p|Fallen Timbers}}--where a storm had thrown
The ancient trees across the land
In a tangle of trunk and branch and stone--

The armies met in August, ninety-four.
The warriors had fasted for the fight
And many had gone home to eat before
The battle came--and {{c|3635|Wayne}} struck at the height

Of the confusion. The {{c|3484|American}} bayonet
Drove through the timber's maze, and the {{c|3581|British}} fort
That stood nearby refused to let
The warriors in--the final and most short

Betrayal: the allies who had armed the fight
Now shut the gate when the fight was lost.
The confederacy broke in the fading light
Of an August afternoon--and the cost

Was written at {{p|Greenville}} the following year:
The treaty that surrendered the {{p|Ohio}}
Country, two-thirds of a world held dear,
The hunting grounds and the village and the bio-

Graphy of a thousand generations sold
For twenty thousand dollars and the hollow
Promise of annuities--the cold
And annual reminder of the fallow

And diminished life that treaties leave behind.

Honor {{c|3628|Little Turtle}}--{{c|3627|Mihsihkinaahkwa}}--
The genius of the forest, whose refined
And devastating art of war could draw a

Nation to its knees, who gave the young
{{c|3626|Republic}} its worst defeat and proved
That the forest was not empty, that the tongue
Of every creek and ridge had moved

With the intelligence of peoples who
Could outthink, outfight, and outmaneuver
The invader's army--and who knew
That the forest, in the end, would never

Belong to those who could not read its name.
He lost. The numbers and the factories
And the {{c|3581|British}} treachery were the flame
That burned the confederacy. But the histories

Remember what the treaty tried to erase:
That the greatest military mind that ever fought
Upon this continent wore an {{c|3561|Indigenous}} face,
And the forest speaks the lesson that he taught.


# Chapter 250: The Civilized Trap

They did everything that was asked of them.

                                            This
Is the bitterest verse in all the book of wounds--
Not the story of the warrior's near-miss
Or the prophet's burning moon, but the platoons

Of scholars, farmers, lawmakers, and scribes
Who built republics in the settler's tongue
And met each demand of the invading tribes
Of {{c|2930|Europeans}}--and were still among

The dispossessed.

                  Five nations of the southeast:
The {{c|3636|Cherokee}}, the {{c|3637|Choctaw}}, the {{c|3638|Chickasaw}},
The {{c|3639|Creek}}--whom the {{c|3404|Americans}} called {{c|3640|Muscogee}}--the least
And last the {{c|3641|Seminole}}, whose law

And custom the republic named "civilized"--
A word that meant: you look enough like us
That we can almost see you. They revised
Their lives to fit the conqueror's calculus

And found the calculation was a lie.

The {{c|3636|Cherokee}} led the way. In the mountains
Of the southern {{p|Appalachians}}, where the sky
Meets the blue ridges and the fountains

Of a hundred rivers spring from laurel slopes,
They had held their country since the forest
Was young--and now they took the ropes
Of the {{c|3401|European}} system and the poorest

Gift of the conqueror, his alphabet,
And made it something the conqueror could not imagine.

{{c|3642|Sequoyah}}--{{c|3643|George Gist}} by his settler name, and yet
As {{c|3642|Sequoyah}} alone he fills the margin

Of history's page--sat for twelve years and thought.
He could not read the {{c|3244|English}} marks, but he
Understood the principle of what they wrought:
That sound could be made visible, that the free

And flowing river of the spoken word
Could be caught in symbols on a page and held
Forever--and he knew that what he heard
In {{c|3636|Cherokee}} could be as precisely spelled

As anything the {{c|3244|English}} tongue could write.

He did not borrow {{c|3244|English}} letters' sounds.
He listened to his language in the night
And broke the {{c|3636|Cherokee}} tongue to its compounds

Of syllables--eighty-six distinct, no more--
And gave each one a symbol. Some he drew
From the {{c|3244|English}} alphabet's forgotten store
Of shapes, but reassigned to the new

And {{c|3636|Cherokee}} sounds: D was not D but a,
R was not R but e, and S
Was not S but du--and in this way
The {{c|3244|English}} letters' shapes became the dress

Of a {{c|3636|Cherokee}} phonetic mind that worked
By syllable, not phoneme, and required
No years of school--the genius that lurked
In {{c|3642|Sequoyah}}'s system was that it aspired

To teach in weeks what {{c|3244|English}} took in years.

Within a single generation, the {{c|3636|Cherokee}}
Were a literate nation. The pioneers
Of their own modernity, the foray

Into the written word was not surrender
But transformation: the {{c|3636|Cherokee}} {{x|Phoenix}}
Rose in eighteen-twenty-eight, the tender
And defiant newspaper that links

A people's voice to the machinery of print--
Bilingual, bold, and edited by {{c|3644|Elias Boudinot}},
Its columns carried the {{c|3636|Cherokee}}'s glint
Of sovereign identity--the knot

Of a language written in its own script,
A thing that no other {{c|3561|Indigenous}} nation
Of the {{p|Americas}} had accomplished, equipped
By the genius of a single man's creation.

And they built a government. The {{c|3636|Cherokee}}
Constitution of eighteen-twenty-seven:
Three branches modeled on the {{c|3484|American}} way--
A principal chief, a senate, the leaven

Of a judiciary and a written code
Of laws that any {{c|3484|American}} jurist would
Recognize--the {{c|3636|Cherokee}} had strode
Into the world of written law and stood

As a republic among republics, a nation
With a capital at {{p|New Echota}}, where the court
Convened and the council held deliberation
In the language {{c|3642|Sequoyah}} had taught to sort

Into syllables of light upon the page.

The {{c|3637|Choctaw}} built their schools. The {{c|3638|Chickasaw}}
Established farms that rivaled, at that stage,
The plantations of their {{c|3484|American}} neighbor's law.

The {{c|3639|Creek}} rebuilt after the devastation
Of the {{x|Red Stick War}}--{{c|3645|Andrew Jackson}}'s first
Campaign of {{c|3561|Indigenous}} elimination,
Where he had used the {{c|3639|Creek}} allies' thirst

For peace against the {{c|3639|Creek}} resisters, then
Punished ally and enemy alike
With the {{x|Treaty}} of {{p|Fort Jackson}}'s pen
That seized twenty-three million acres--the strike

Of a rattlesnake that bites the hand that feeds.

And the {{c|3641|Seminole}} in {{p|Florida}}'s green maze
Of swamp and hammock--a nation whose deeds
Of resistance would outlast all the craze

For removal--but that is the next chapter's telling.

Here is the bitter center: they did everything.
They adopted the plow. They built the dwelling
In the {{c|3401|European}} style. They let the ring

Of the church bell sound across their towns.
They wrote constitutions, published newspapers,
Sent their children to the schools, wore the gowns
Of the {{c|3484|American}} republic's capers

And conventions--and it was not enough.
It was never going to be enough. The word
"Civilized" was a lock without a key, the bluff
Of an empire that had already transferred

The verdict from the courtroom to the ledger:
The land was worth more than the people on it.
Gold was found in {{p|Georgia}}'s {{c|3636|Cherokee}} acreage,
And the settler's hunger would not quit

For any constitution or gazette.

The more the {{c|3636|Cherokee}} became like the {{c|3404|Americans}},
The more the {{c|3404|Americans}} felt the threat
Of a people who disproved the talismans

Of racial destiny: if the {{c|3636|Cherokee}}
Could build a republic, write a constitution,
And govern themselves with a literate decree,
Then what excuse remained for the execution

Of the policy of removal? What remained
Of the comfortable fiction that the land
Was wasted on the savage, the unchained
And wandering brute who could not understand

The plow's purpose or the ballot's weight?

The {{c|3636|Cherokee}} disproved the lie. And for this
They would be punished with a greater hate
Than any warrior nation would dismiss--

Because they held the mirror up and showed
The republic its own face, and the republic
Could not bear the image. What it owed
To its own principles was a truth too thick

To swallow--and so it swallowed the {{c|3636|Cherokee}} instead.

Honor {{c|3642|Sequoyah}}--who gave his people letters
Without borrowing any foreign alphabet's thread,
Who forged a syllabary that unfetters

The {{c|3636|Cherokee}} voice from the tyranny of silence
And the colonizer's monopoly on the page.
Honor the {{c|3636|Cherokee}} {{x|Phoenix}}, whose defiance
In print was the most civilized outrage

That any nation offered any empire--
The proof, in black ink on white paper pressed,
That the word "savage" was the colonizer's liar
And the word "civilized" was the colonizer's jest.

They built everything they were told to build.
They became everything they were told to become.
And the reward for every promise fulfilled
Was the drumbeat of removal's drum.


# Chapter 251: The Last Confederacies

One more time.

                  One more time the vision came--
The dream of unity, the ancient fire
That {{c|3583|Pontiac}} had kindled, the claim
That only together could the nations aspire

To hold the line--and this time the dreamer
Was the greatest of them all.

                                {{c|3646|Tecumseh}}--
The {{c|3647|Shooting Star}}--whose name was the redeemer
Of a continent's last hope, whose prophecy

Was simple and was true and came too late:
"The land belongs to all. No single nation
May sell what every nation holds. The weight
Of the earth beneath our feet is the foundation

That no chief's signature can give away.
Sell the air. Sell the rain. Sell the river's flow.
But do not sell the land on which we pray,
For the land was here before us and below

Our feet it holds the bones of those who came
Before and those who yet will come--and no
Treaty signed by one can sign away the claim
Of all who walk upon the earth."

                                   And so
He walked. From the {{p|Great Lakes}} to the {{p|Gulf}},
From the {{c|3620|Shawnee}} towns of {{p|Ohio}} to the gulf-
Coast {{c|3639|Creek}} and {{c|3637|Choctaw}}, from the wolf-
Run forests of the north to the {{p|Seminole}} shelf

Of {{p|Florida}}'s green swamp, {{c|3646|Tecumseh}} carried
The message: unite or die. One confederacy
Of every nation, east and west, unmarried
To any {{c|3401|European}} king, the legacy

Of {{c|3583|Pontiac}} reborn in a greater flame--
Not merely war against the {{c|3581|British}} or the {{c|3404|Americans}},
But the refusal, absolute, to name
A price for the earth itself, the talismans

Of sovereignty held in common trust.

His brother walked beside him--{{c|3648|Tenskwatawa}},
The {{c|2776|Prophet}}, who had risen from the dust
Of alcoholism and despair, the raw

And broken man remade by vision's fire:
He had died and returned, he said, and the {{c|1470|Master}}
Of Life had shown him how the world entire
Could be healed--renounce the whiskey, the disaster

Of the {{c|3401|European}} trade goods, the poison
Of the metal world, and return to the ways
That the {{c|3591|Creator}} gave: the ancient season
Of the corn and the deer and the prayer's praise

Spoken in the tongue the {{c|3591|Creator}} understood.

At {{p|Prophetstown}}--{{p|Tippecanoe}}--they built
The capital of the confederacy: a wood
And bark metropolis where the guilt

Of tribal division was dissolved in prayer
And the warriors of a dozen nations gathered
To hear the {{c|2776|Prophet}} speak and to prepare
For the world renewed, the old ways lathered

Clean of the colonizer's filth.

                                 {{c|3646|Tecumseh}} traveled south.
While he was gone, {{c|3649|William Henry Harrison}}
Marched on {{p|Prophetstown}} with the drouth
Of a man who feared the garrison

Of united nations more than any army.
At dawn on the seventh of November,
Eighteen-eleven, he provoked the swarmy
And premature battle--the ember

That {{c|3648|Tenskwatawa}} fanned against his brother's
Strict command. The {{c|2776|Prophet}} promised magic:
The bullets would not harm, the warriors' mothers
Would see their sons return. The tragic

Miscalculation cost the confederacy
Its capital--{{p|Prophetstown}} burned,
The stores destroyed, the prophecy
Of invulnerability overturned

By the mundane arithmetic of lead.

{{c|3646|Tecumseh}} returned to ashes. But he did not break.

The {{x|War of Eighteen-Twelve}} became the thread
He seized: the {{c|3581|British}} and {{c|3404|Americans}} at stake

Again, and the {{c|3581|British}} needed allies
In the forests of the {{p|Great Lakes}} and the west--
And {{c|3646|Tecumseh}} gave them what no compromise
Could purchase: the greatest warrior and the best

Strategic mind between the {{p|Appalachians}}
And the {{p|Mississippi}}. At {{p|Detroit}}
He bluffed an {{c|3484|American}} general--{{c|3650|Hull}}'s equations
Of fear multiplied by {{c|3646|Tecumseh}}'s adroit

March of the same warriors past the same
Window three times, each time in different dress--
And {{c|3650|Hull}} surrendered {{p|Detroit}} to the claim
Of a force half the size of his own, the finesse

Of a mind that understood the theatre of war.

But the {{c|3581|British}} were not worthy of the alliance.
At the {{p|Thames}} in {{p|Ontario}}, the scar
Of the final battle, the {{c|3581|British}} defiance

Dissolved: {{c|3651|Procter}} fled with his cavalry
And left {{c|3646|Tecumseh}} and his warriors alone
Against {{c|3652|Harrison}}'s charge--the gallantry
Of a general abandoned, the stone

Of {{c|3646|Tecumseh}}'s last stand in the swamp
Where the horsemen came in waves and the musket's
Roar was the drumbeat and the stomp
Of a continent's last hope--the gaskets

Of the dream bursting--and {{c|3646|Tecumseh}} fell.

October eighteen-thirteen. The forest closed
Around his body. No one knew the well
Or hollow where his warriors composed

His final resting place--they hid him
From the {{c|3404|Americans}} who would have stripped
His skin for souvenirs--and the requiem
Of his confederacy's end was the ripped

And scattered fabric of the dream.

                                    But the thread
Was not yet fully severed.

                             {{c|3653|Black Hawk}} rose
In eighteen-thirty-two--{{c|3654|Ma-ka-tai-me-she-kia-kiak}}--
The {{c|3655|Sauk}} war chief who chose

To cross the {{p|Mississippi}} back to the east,
Back to the homeland at {{p|Saukenuk}} that the treaty
Of eighteen-four had signed away, the feast
Of the {{c|3484|American}} land-grab's receipt, the

Fraudulent mark of a drunken chief who signed
What no council sanctioned, what no nation chose.
{{c|3653|Black Hawk}} crossed with women, children, the resigned
And desperate families, the rows

Of the hungry and the dispossessed who only
Wanted to plant their corn on ancestral ground.
The {{c|3404|Americans}} called it war. The lonely
And starving band was hunted, hound by hound,

Through {{p|Wisconsin}}'s summer forests--and at {{p|Bad Axe}}
The steamboat {{x|Warrior}} and the militia's
Gun-line slaughtered women at the river's tracks
As they tried to swim across--the malicious

And deliberate murder of the fleeing, the surrender
Rejected, the white flag ignored, the tender
Bodies of children floating in the current's flow--
The {{p|Mississippi}} reddened in the undertow.

And in the south, the {{c|3641|Seminole}} refused.

Three wars--eighteen-seventeen to eighteen-fifty-eight--
The longest {{c|3561|Indigenous}} resistance, the abused
And indomitable people of the strait

And labyrinth of {{p|Florida}}'s swamps, where {{c|3656|Osceola}},
The young war chief who was never truly chief
But the soul of the resistance, the corolla
Of defiance in the cypress and the reef

Of saw-grass and saw-palmetto, fought the {{c|3484|American}}
Army to exhaustion. They took {{c|3656|Osceola}}
Under a flag of truce--the un-American
And faithless seizure of a warrior, the cola-

Nial treachery that {{c|3657|Jesup}} called diplomacy.
{{c|3656|Osceola}} died in prison. But the {{c|3641|Seminole}}
Fought on, and on, until the hypocrisy
Of the republic spent forty million whole

Dollars and fifteen hundred lives to remove
A nation that numbered fewer than four thousand souls.
Some never surrendered. Some refused to move.
Deep in the {{p|Everglades}}, in the watery shoals

And hammocks of the saw-grass wilderness,
A remnant held--the unconquered {{c|3641|Seminole}},
The only eastern nation whose address
Was never changed by the removal's toll.

Honor {{c|3646|Tecumseh}}--the {{c|3647|Shooting Star}}
Whose light crossed the continent and whose fire
Burns in every refusal to sell the land, the scar
Of his death the proof that the empire's desire

Cannot purchase what the earth itself has spoken:
That the land is not for sale, the covenant unbroken.

Honor {{c|3653|Black Hawk}}--who crossed the river home
And paid the price in blood for the simple right
To plant the corn and rest beneath the dome
Of the sky his fathers knew. Honor the night

Of {{p|Bad Axe}}, where the children died in the water.

Honor {{c|3656|Osceola}}--taken under truce,
The {{c|3641|Seminole}} whose unconquered daughter
And son still walk the {{p|Everglades}}, the noose

Of removal never tightened on their throats.
The last confederacies burned and fell and burned
Again--but in the ashes, the embers' notes
Still glow, and the lesson {{c|3646|Tecumseh}} learned

Still speaks: no single nation stands alone.
The land belongs to all, and the bones beneath the stone
Are the covenant no treaty can unmake--
And the {{c|3647|Shooting Star}} still burns for every nation's sake.


# Chapter 252: The Unsealed Book

Now seal the book.

                   No--the book was never sealed.
The book was always open. The book was written
In the corn and in the council fire, revealed
In every language the {{c|3591|Creator}} had smitten

Into being on this continent of tongues--
Three hundred families of speech, a thousand
Languages that named the world, the lungs
Of a hemisphere breathing the thousand

Names of {{c|472|God}} that no one needed to translate
Because the rivers spoke them and the mountains
Held them in their granite and the weight
Of ten thousand years of prayer at the fountains

Of the sacred springs--this was the book.
This was always the book.

                           Then, in one year,
a man in {{p|Palmyra}}, {{p|New York}}, would look
into a stone and see the plates appear:

the golden plates that {{c|3661|Moroni}} had sealed
within a hill, the record of a son
of {{p|Israel}} who crossed the sea, revealed
in "{{x|Reformed Egyptian}}," and so begun

with {{c|3402|Lehi}}, from {{p|Jerusalem}}, who came,
and {{c|3659|Nephi}}, who would sail across the sea:
the first book that would give this land a name,
its prophets, kings, its {{c|1497|Christ}}, its living tree.

{{c|1497|Christ}} came to Bountiful, and taught, and healed,
and blessed their children: the Redeemer's day
that this book also keeps, its promise sealed
to come again, and not to pass away.

It named the peoples here {{c|3658|Lamanites}},
of Laman's line, and darkened for the sin
their fathers did; and here the quarrel bites:
whose fathers were they? Jacob's, or the kin

who walked out of {{p|Beringia}}? The gold plates
said {{c|3402|Lehi}}; and the land said ice and coast;
and the one house of the dead, at its gates,
takes both: the tree has room for every ghost.

In March of eighteen-thirty {{c|3660|Joseph Smith}}
set out the book {{c|3661|Moroni}} had concealed,
and his eleven witnesses, forthwith,
signed that they saw the plates the hill revealed.

In that same year--eighteen-thirty--the {{c|3484|American}}
Congress passed the act that mattered most:
The {{x|Indian Removal Act}}. The plan

Of {{c|3645|Andrew Jackson}}--{{c|3662|Sharp Knife}}, the {{c|3636|Cherokee}} called him,
The man who had already devoured
The {{c|3639|Creek}} homeland, the general grim
Who had conquered {{p|Florida}} and towered

Above the ruin of every treaty signed--
Now held the presidency, and the weight
Of the {{c|3626|Republic}}'s westward hunger, refined
To a single policy, a single fate:

Remove them all.

                  Every nation east
Of the {{p|Mississippi}}--every {{c|3636|Cherokee}} farm
With its constitution and its printing-press feast
Of civilized achievement, every arm

Of {{c|3637|Choctaw}} governance, every {{c|3638|Chickasaw}}
Town with its elected council, every {{c|3639|Creek}}
Who had rebuilt from {{c|3663|Jackson}}'s earlier war--
Move west. The east is for the meek

And pale inheritors of a {{p|Promised Land}}
That {{c|472|God}}, the settlers said, had set aside
For the {{c|3484|American}} republic's hand
To cultivate. The darker peoples ride

The trail of exile to the territory
Beyond the {{p|Mississippi}}'s western shore,
Where the republic, in its transitory
Generosity, will promise them once more

A homeland "as long as grass shall grow
And water run"--the same words spoken
At every treaty, the eternal vow
That was eternally and instantly broken.

{{c|3664|John Ross}}--principal chief of the {{c|3636|Cherokee}},
One-eighth {{c|3636|Cherokee}} by blood and all {{c|3636|Cherokee}}
By every measure that a nation's day
Of governance could offer--fought the way

The {{c|3636|Cherokee}} had always fought since {{c|3642|Sequoyah}}:
With law, with language, with the written word.
He brought the case to the {{x|Supreme Court}}'s playa
Of jurisprudence, and the nation heard

The argument: the {{c|3636|Cherokee}} were sovereign.
No state could impose its laws upon the land
Of a nation that the federal covenant
Had recognized by treaty. The command

Of {{p|Georgia}}'s legislature to dissolve
The {{c|3636|Cherokee}} government and seize the soil
Was void--the {{x|Constitution}} would resolve
The question in the {{c|3636|Cherokee}}'s favor, the foil

Of states' rights against the treaty's sacred bond.

And {{c|3665|John Marshall}} ruled. The {{c|3666|Chief Justice}} found
That {{p|Georgia}}'s laws were void--the wand
Of the {{x|Constitution}}'s supremacy, the ground

Of {{c|3667|Worcester}} versus {{p|Georgia}}: the {{c|3636|Cherokee}}
Were a sovereign nation, and the {{c|3484|American}} state
Had no authority to decree
Their dissolution--the mandate of the great

And highest court was clear.

                              {{c|3663|Jackson}} laughed.

"{{c|3665|John Marshall}} has made his decision.
Now let him enforce it." The statecraft
Of the republic's highest vision

Reduced to a bully's sneer, the law
Of the land discarded by the land's elected king--
For what was a {{x|Constitution}}'s awe
Against the settler's hunger and the ring

Of gold discovered in the {{c|3636|Cherokee}} hills?
The {{x|Court}} had spoken. The {{c|3668|President}} refused.
And in that refusal, the republic kills
The principle that its founders had enthused

Upon every parchment page: that law,
Not power, would govern--that the covenant
Of written words would hold the tyrant's claw
In check. But the covenant was meant

Only for the {{c|3401|European}}'s liberty--
The {{c|3636|Cherokee}} learned what the {{c|3497|Haudenosaunee}} knew,
What {{c|3628|Little Turtle}} knew, what the entirety
Of the continent had learned was true:

The colonizer's law protects the colonizer.

The {{c|3637|Choctaw}} went first--the winter of eighteen-thirty-one,
Forced west through ice and snow, the miser-
Able caravans of the dispossessed, the sun

Hidden behind the clouds for weeks, the dead
Left unburied on the frozen road.
A {{c|3637|Choctaw}} chief looked back at what he'd fled
And spoke the words that history bestowed

Upon the exodus: "A trail of tears and death."

The {{c|3639|Creek}} followed. The {{c|3638|Chickasaw}} were sold
Into the march. And last, with labored breath,
The {{c|3636|Cherokee}}--in eighteen-thirty-eight, the cold

And calculated roundup: soldiers came
To every farm and every cabin door
And herded families at bayonet's aim
Into the stockades, where the filthy floor

Of the concentration camps awaited them.
They were allowed to carry nothing. The homes
They had built, the orchards, the literary gem
Of the {{c|3636|Cherokee}} {{x|Phoenix}}, the chromosomes

Of a civilization encoded in their schools
And courts and churches--left behind for the white
Settlers who rushed in like a pack of ghouls
Before the last {{c|3636|Cherokee}} was out of sight.

Sixteen thousand walked the trail. Four thousand died.
The children died first--the old died next--
The mothers carried the dead until the tide
Of grief became the only text

They could recite.

                   The same year, side by side:

In eighteen-thirty, as the act was signed,
the book came out; and in the year of tears,
in eighteen-thirty-eight, the same state's mind
drove out the Saints, from Missouri's frontiers.

Its governor signed Order Forty-Four:
the Saints must leave the state, or else be slain.
The same year, same republic, the same door:
the {{c|3636|Cherokee}}, the Saints, went west in pain.

The book did not move them. It was the land,
the farms the state had wanted, and the gold;
the book had sent four preachers out to stand
with Delaware and Shawnee, and they told

the chiefs: your fathers were the prophets' line,
your dead are kings and seers in what we read;
the {{c|3402|Lehi}} of your house is also mine.
That was the quarrel: who would hold the dead.

The book had called their skin's darkness a curse,
and they would turn "white and delightsome" when
redeemed; the Church would later change the verse
to "pure," in nineteen eighty-one, again.

It was one house's quarrel over skin,
and over fathers, and who keeps the name:
the {{c|3673|Mormons}} and {{c|3658|Lamanites}} are kin,
one people, and one altar, and one flame.

And so this book here in your hands lays bare
the plates again, and opens them with care:
the long walk out of {{p|Beringia}}, the tide
of corn, the mounds, the cities, and beside

them, {{c|1497|Christ}} in Bountiful and {{c|3402|Lehi}}'s sail,
the record of ten thousand years of prayer,
the quipu knots, the codex, and the tale
of every people who had once lived there.

This is the book that always stays unsealed,
the record that was never lost, the names
of every nation, every saint, revealed
to {{c|3660|Joseph Smith}} or to the council flames.

Here ends the {{x|Book}} of {{c|3402|Lehi}}, his and theirs:
the {{c|3402|Lehi}} of the plates, and of the land,
whose history was carved in mounds and prayers,
whose scripture is the earth on which they stand.

A hemisphere that never lay there blank
for any pen; a full and holy stage
where ten thousand years of prayer, rank on rank,
had made it holy, age on holy age.

The {{x|Trail of Tears}} was Jackson's; and the hate,
the {{x|Indian Removal Act}}, his hand.
But the peoples endure, and keep their gate;
the record is intact. The peoples stand.

This is that record. Remember every name.
Remember {{c|3646|Tecumseh}} and {{c|3606|Tupac Amaru}},
Remember {{c|3642|Sequoyah}} and the flame
Of every council fire from {{p|Cusco}} to {{p|Manitou}}.

Remember the {{c|3587|Guarani}} violins.
Remember the {{c|3497|Haudenosaunee}} {{x|Law}}.
Remember {{c|3628|Little Turtle}}'s discipline.
Remember {{c|3656|Osceola}} and the raw

And unconquered {{c|3641|Seminole}} in the swamp.
Remember the children in the {{p|Mississippi}}'s current.
Remember the {{c|3637|Choctaw}} chief who called it the stomp
And trail of tears, whose words are the deterrent

Against forgetting. Remember the {{c|3636|Cherokee}} {{x|Phoenix}}.
Remember {{c|3664|John Ross}} and the {{x|Court}} that ruled
For justice--and the {{c|3668|President}} whose cynics
And whose cruelty overruled.

The book is sealed--no. The book is never sealed.
The book is open, and you hold it now.
The real record of this hemisphere, revealed
By {{c|3661|Moroni}} and by the sacred vow

Of memory itself: that what was done
Shall be remembered, and the dead shall speak
Through every line, and the extinguished sun
Of every nation rises in the mystique

Of the word that refuses to be lost.

Honor them all. Honor the cost.
The {{x|Book}} of {{c|3402|Lehi}} ends. The record stands.
The continent remembers. Hold it in your hands.

---

# Virgo (10宮) - Days 253-280


# Chapter 253: The Chronicle of the Popes

Now count the keys. Not fathers, for these men
Were sworn to have no sons--and some had sons--
But hands on heads, the laying-on, and then
The next head bowed, the next, until it runs

Fifteen centuries from a fisherman to a king
Who cut the world in half with a line of ink.
Here is the chronicle. Here is the ring
Passed hand to hand. Here is the missing link

Between the {{p|Galilee}} and the age of sail.
Hear it as the old ones heard the kings of {{p|Ur}}:
One name, then one name, then the tale
Folded small, and then the next one. Here they were.

{{c|1093|Peter}}, the fisherman, who denied him three times
Before the rooster, and then did not deny,
Hung head-down in {{p|Rome}} for his crimes
Of saying the dead man lived. He asked to die

Upside down, unworthy of the cross
His teacher hung on. Then {{c|3675|Linus}}. Then {{c|3676|Cletus}}.
Then {{c|3677|Clement}}, writing letters to the loss
And quarrel at {{p|Corinth}}: be at peace, defeat us

Not by your schisms. Bishops of a buried sect,
Underground in the tufa where the dead were laid,
Their names scratched in the catacomb's neglect,
Martyrs by the dozen, bishops by the blade.

{{c|3678|Callixtus}}, a slave once, who had lost
A banker's money and been sent to the mill.
{{c|3679|Pontian}}, sent to die in the mines, the lost
Pits of {{p|Sardinia}}, who resigned there, still

The first to put the keys down. {{c|3680|Fabian}},
Chosen when a dove came down and settled on
His head in the assembly--a farmer, a layman--
Killed under {{c|2583|Decius}}. The dove was gone.

Then {{c|3681|Sylvester}}, and the world turned over.
{{c|2555|Constantine}} had seen a sign in the sun,
The unconquered sun, {{c|2554|Sol Invictus}}, the lover
Of soldiers, and he made the two suns one.

The persecuted became the palace. The tomb
Of the fisherman became a basilica of gold.
And four hundred years later, in some room,
A forger wrote that {{c|2555|Constantine}} had sold--

No, given--the whole {{p|West}} to {{c|3681|Sylvester}}'s chair.
The {{x|Donation}}. A lie that held a continent
For seven hundred years, until {{c|3682|Valla}} laid it bare
By its bad {{x|Latin}}. Remember what the forgers meant.

{{c|3683|Damasus}}, who set {{c|3684|Jerome}} to make one book
In the tongue of the street, the {{x|Vulgate}}. {{c|3685|Leo}} the Great,
Who rode out to the {{p|Mincio}}, and the look
Of him turned {{c|3686|Attila}} back from the gate.

{{c|2621|Gregory}}, who called himself the servant
Of the servants of {{c|472|God}}, and sent a monk to {{p|Kent}}.
And {{c|2834|Leo III}}, on {{x|Christmas Day}}, observant
Of nothing but the crown, who stood and bent

Over {{c|2677|Charlemagne}} at prayer in {{p|Saint Peter's}}
And set a crown on him that he had not asked for,
Emperor of the {{c|1004|Romans}}. Nearly every reader
Born of {{p|Europe}} descends from him. The door

Of every lineage in {{p|Europe}} opens there.
Then came the years of the great houses. Mark:
{{c|3283|Formosus}}, dug up, propped up in the chair,
Dressed in his robes, a deacon set to bark

His answers for him at the {{x|Cadaver Synod}}.
Condemned, his blessing fingers cut away,
Thrown in the {{p|Tiber}}. And the bishops nodded.
And then the house of {{c|3687|Theophylact}} held sway.

{{c|3275|Marozia}}, his daughter. Lover of a pope,
{{c|3688|Sergius}}, and mother of a pope, {{c|2537|John}},
And grandmother of a pope--a family's scope
To make and unmake the keys and pass them on

Exactly as the kings did: by the blood.
Her grandson {{c|3278|John XII}}, a boy of eighteen,
Who crowned {{c|3280|Otto}}, and died, so the story went, in the mud
Of a married woman's bed. The keys had been

A dynasty, a genealogy, a house.
And this book honors genealogies. It must
Say so plainly: the chair the church endows
With heaven was a household's. That is just.

And after them {{c|3689|Sylvester II}}, {{c|3690|Gerbert}},
Who brought the {{x|Arab}} numerals to the {{p|West}},
The abacus, the astrolabe, the expert
Of the year one thousand, when they guessed

The world would end, and it did not end.
Then 1054: the legates at the altar
Of {{p|Hagia Sophia}} in {{p|Istanbul}} send
A bull of excommunication. {{p|East}} and {{p|West}} would falter

Apart and never close. {{c|3691|Gregory VII}},
And the king {{c|3374|Henry}}, barefoot in the snow
Three days at {{p|Canossa}}, begging to be forgiven,
And the pope who made him wait, and let him go.

Urban at {{p|Clermont-Ferrand}}: {{c|472|God}} wills it. The cross
Sewn onto shoulders, and the road to {{p|Jerusalem}}
Paved with the slaughtered. {{c|3692|Innocent III}}, the boss
Of kings, who forbade the sack, and then watched them

Sack {{p|Istanbul}} anyway, a {{x|Christian}} city,
In 1204. {{c|3693|Celestine}}, the hermit, who could not bear
The keys, and gave them back. And then, without pity,
{{c|3694|Boniface}}: {{x|One Holy Church}}, and every soul is there

Subject to the {{x|Roman}} pontiff. Slapped at {{p|Anagni}}
By a {{c|3245|French}} king's men. Then the papacy
Packed up and moved to {{p|Avignon}}. The money
Of the {{x|Babylonian Captivity}}

Flowed seventy years to a palace on the {{p|Rhône}}
Till {{c|3695|Catherine}} of {{p|Siena}} wrote: come home.
They came home, and elected two. Then three. Each throne
Excommunicated the others. Which was {{p|Rome}}?

At {{p|Konstanz}} a council ended it,
Deposed them all, and crowned {{c|3696|Martin}}, one again,
Two years after it burned {{c|3697|Jan Hus}}, and lit
The fire that {{p|Bohemia}} would remember. Then

The scholars. {{c|3698|Nicholas}}, who built the {{x|Library}}
In the years the {{c|3107|Turks}} took {{p|Istanbul}} for good.
{{c|3699|Sixtus}}, who built the {{x|Chapel}}, where the very
Ceiling would be painted by a man who stood

On scaffolding for four years with his head bent back.
And at the end of the chronicle, {{c|3700|Rodrigo}},
{{c|3701|Borgia}}, {{c|3702|Alexander VI}}, and the black
Joke of his children, {{c|3703|Cesare}} and {{c|3704|Lucrezia}}, and the slow

Poison of the rumors. In 1493
He drew a line from pole to pole across the sea:
{{p|West}} of it for {{p|Spain}}, east for {{p|Portugal}}.
At {{p|Tordesillas}} the two kings moved it farther west,

And the world was divided by the heir of the fisherman
Between two crowns that had never seen most of it.
The {{c|3705|Taíno}} were not asked. Nor the {{c|3403|Inca}}. Nor the {{c|3706|Tupinambá}}. The plan
Was paper, and the paper was the writ.

Fifteen hundred years. A fisherman, a line.
Some were saints and some were murderers and most
Were keepers, and the chair they kept, divine:
The chair was holy. What passed was the ghost,

And with it, hands on heads, and then the name
Read out, the next name, and the keeping of the list.
That is what an institution is. The same
Way a family is. In {{p|Eisleben}}, a miner's son who would twist

The keys in their lock was already born. The chronicle closes.
The keys go on, unbroken, past this page.
Count them. Keep the list. The list is what the house is.
The age of the chronicle ends. Here begins the age

Of the reckoning.


# Chapter 254: The Sea Joins the World

Before this there were many seas. The {{p|Indian Ocean}}
Was a market as old as the {{c|3707|Pharaohs}}, where the dhow
Rode the monsoon out and back, a slow devotion
To the wind's two seasons, and the merchant's vow

Was kept in pepper and in cloth and in the gold
Of {{p|Kilwa}} and the cottons of {{p|Gujarat}}.
The {{p|Atlantic}} was an edge. The {{p|Pacific}} was untold.
Each sea had its own world, and that was that.

Then {{c|3211|Vasco da Gama}} sailed out of {{p|Lisbon}},
Four ships, the summer of 1497,
Swung wide into the empty ocean, beyond the reckon
Of the coast, three months without a sight of land, the heaven

Their only chart, the astrolabe their priest,
And came around the {{p|Cape of Good Hope}} in the cold
And up the coast of {{p|Africa}} to the east,
To {{p|Mozambique}}, to {{p|Mombasa}}, where they were told

To find a pilot at {{p|Malindi}}, and they found one,
A man who knew the monsoon like a psalm,
Whose name the chronicles dispute. He was the one
Who knew. He took them across the ocean's palm

To {{p|Kozhikode}}, in the May of 1498.
And here is the story to remember, here is the hinge:
They went into a temple, and they knelt, and they prayed
Before a goddess, and they did not cringe,

Because they thought she was {{c|1399|Mary}}. They thought the priests
Were {{c|2494|Christians}} of some old and broken rite.
They saw the saints on the walls with too many arms, the feasts,
The lamps, the holy water, and in the light

They saw what they had come to see. The {{c|3204|Hindus}} saw
Strangers bowing to the {{c|3708|Mother}}, and let them bow.
For one afternoon the world was joined, the law
Of every rite kept whole, in the one now

Of no mistake. Then trade. The {{c|3709|Zamorin}}
Was not impressed by their gifts: some cloth, some hats,
Some honey. The {{c|3710|Arab}} merchants laughed. And in
The end they sailed home with pepper, and with rats,

And with the scurvy, which killed more than half of them.
The pepper paid for the voyage sixty times.
And so the sea was opened, and the hem
Of the world was lifted. Hear the price, the crimes:

{{c|3711|Da Gama}} came again, with cannon. A ship
Of pilgrims coming home from {{p|Mecca}}, the {{c|3712|Miri}},
He took, and stripped, and burned. The women held up gold to buy their lives. The whip
Of fire took the children. Write it down. Be weary

Of anyone who tells this as adventure only.
{{c|3713|Albuquerque}} took {{p|Goa}}, and took {{p|Melaka}},
The strait the whole of {{p|Asia}}'s trade ran through, the lonely
Gate of the cloves. The ocean that was a bazaar

Became a toll road. Pay the {{c|3212|Portuguese}} or burn.
And {{c|3714|Cabral}}, sailing for {{p|India}} in 1500,
Swung too far west and found the coast of {{p|Brazil}}, the turn
Of a wheel that would roll over the {{c|3432|Tupi}} like thunder.

Then {{c|7|Magellan}}. A {{c|3212|Portuguese}} who sailed for {{p|Spain}},
Five ships from {{p|Sanlúcar}} in 1519, to find
A western road to the spice islands, to gain
For {{c|3253|Charles}} the cloves of {{p|Maluku}}, and to bind

The line the {{c|2825|Pope}} had drawn back round the world.
Mutiny in {{p|Patagonia}}, and the beheading,
The marooning. Then the strait, the cold, the curled
Fingers of the channel, thirty-eight days of threading

Through the rock and the williwaw, and then the open
Water so calm he called it peaceful: the {{p|Pacific}}.
Ninety-eight days across it, the ship's biscuit broken
To dust and worms, the leather of the rigging, the specific

Taste of rats, the men's gums swelling over their teeth.
And then {{p|Guam}}. And then the islands of the {{p|Philippines}},
Where {{c|3715|Enrique}}, his slave, a man from beneath
The winds of {{p|Melaka}}, bought at the scene

Of its conquest, spoke to the islanders, and was understood.
He had come home the long way round. He may have been
The first human being who ever stood
Again at his own beginning by going clean

Around the world. Remember {{c|3715|Enrique}}. Then {{c|7|Magellan}}
Baptized a king at {{p|Cebu}}, and wanted more,
And fought {{c|3716|Lapulapu}} on the beach at {{p|Mactan}}, and fell in
The shallows, April 1521. The shore

Kept him. {{c|3716|Lapulapu}} kept the island. And the fleet,
What was left of it, two ships, then one, the {{c|3717|Victoria}},
Under {{c|3718|Elcano}}, found the cloves at {{p|Tidore}}, a sweet
Cargo, and went on west, the long euphoria

And misery of the {{p|Indian Ocean}} and the {{p|Cape}}
And the {{p|Atlantic}} home, and came into {{p|Sanlúcar}}
In September 1522: eighteen men, the shape
Of skeletons, of two hundred and seventy. And they were

A day off. Their log said Wednesday. It was Thursday.
They had sailed with the sun and lost a day to it,
And the learned men of {{p|Venice}} worked out why. The {{p|Earth}}'s way
Of turning had been measured by a ship. Admit

What this means: the world is one thing now. One sea.
One sphere you can sail around, one market, one
Reckoning of days. The many worlds would be
One world, by cannon and by pepper and by sun.

Here begins the joining. It was done by force.
It was done in a temple, on a knee.
It was done by a slave who found his way back to his source.
Hold all three. The sea joins. The world will never again be free

Of the rest of the world.


# Chapter 255: There Is No Hindu, There Is No Muslim

In {{p|Punjab}}, the land of the five rivers, where the road
From {{p|Kabul}} came down to {{p|Delhi}} and the armies came down with it,
A storekeeper's clerk at {{p|Sultanpur Lodhi}} kept the load
Of grain and salt in order, every measure fit,

And counted out the rations: one, two, three,
Up to thirteen, and at thirteen, *tera*,
Which also means *yours*, he stopped, and could not see
To count past it: yours, yours, yours. The era

Of the ledger ended for him there. His name was {{c|3719|Nanak}}.
Born at {{p|Nankana Sahib}} in 1469,
A {{c|3720|Khatri}} boy, the son of {{c|3721|Kalu}}, an accountant. Back
Then the village schoolmaster wrote a line

For him to copy, and the boy wrote a hymn instead.
They married him. They gave him work. He gave the store away.
And around 1499, so the {{c|3722|janamsakhis}} said,
He went down to bathe in the {{p|Kali Bein}} one day

And did not come up. Three days. They dragged the stream.
They thought him drowned. And on the third day he came out
Of the water, and was silent, and then, as in a dream,
Or as from the far side of a dream, without a doubt:

*There is no {{c|3723|Hindu}}. There is no {{c|3385|Muslim}}.*
That was the first thing. Not a creed. A clearing of the ground.
The governor asked him: then whose path do you follow? Him,
Said {{c|3719|Nanak}}. {{c|472|God}}'s. And when the call to prayer came round

He went with the governor and the {{c|3724|qazi}} to the mosque,
And did not bow, and when they asked him why, he said:
Your body bowed, but your mind was in {{p|Kabul}}, at the kiosk,
Buying horses. And the qazi's was at home, where a mare had bred

And he feared the foal would fall into the well.
So he would pray with them, he said, when they were praying.
That is the story. Whether it is true, I cannot tell.
The janamsakhis tell it. It is worth the saying.

Then the journeys. Four of them, the {{c|3725|udasis}}, east and south
And north into the mountains and west to {{p|Mecca}}, with a friend,
{{c|3726|Mardana}}, a {{c|3385|Muslim}}, who played the rebab while from his mouth
The hymns came, a {{c|3385|Muslim}} minstrel and a {{c|3723|Hindu}}-born, without end

Walking. At {{p|Haridwar}}, where the pilgrims threw
The {{p|Ganges}} water east, toward the rising sun,
To reach their ancestors, he threw it west. What do you do?
They asked. I'm watering my fields in {{p|Punjab}}. If yours run

Up to the sun, mine can reach three hundred miles.
At {{p|Mecca}}, they say, he lay down with his feet toward the {{c|2744|Kaaba}},
And the keeper kicked him: you point your feet at {{c|472|God}}! He smiled:
Then turn my feet toward where {{c|472|God}} is not. And the ground, the robber

Of every certainty, would not turn. Again: a story. Hold it so.
What is sure is the hymns. Nine hundred and some
Of them, in {{c|3727|Punjabi}} and the mixed tongue of the poor, the slow
Music of the {{c|3728|Bhakti}} saints and the {{c|3729|Sufis}}, one

{{c|472|God}}, without form, without fear, without hatred, not born,
Not dying, self-existent, known by grace. *{{x|Ik Onkar}}*:
One. The {{c|3591|Creator}}. The {{x|True Name}}. And at dawn, every morn,
The {{c|3730|Japji}}, still sung. That is the scripture, where we are

Not guessing. Then {{c|3189|Babur}} came down from {{p|Kabul}} like the flood,
The first of the {{c|2985|Mughals}}, and sacked {{p|Eminabad}}, and the hymns
Of {{c|3719|Nanak}} are the witness: the city in its blood,
The women of good houses dragged out by their limbs,

{{c|472|God}}, he sang, had sent the {{c|3731|Mughal}} as death's own herald. He had seen it.
He did not write a war-song. He wrote a lament
And a reproach to {{c|472|God}}: did you not feel pain? He would mean it.
Then he settled. On the bank of the {{p|Ravi}}, he went

To {{p|Kartarpur}}, and farmed, and built a kitchen
Where everyone sat on the floor in one row, the high
Caste and the low, the {{c|3385|Muslim}} and the {{c|3723|Hindu}}, and no one rich in
That line, the *langar*, which feeds a hundred thousand a day now. Why

Does it matter? Because the meal was the doctrine.
To eat together was to be one thing. And when he grew old
He passed the guruship not to his sons, as a king would, nor to kin in
Any degree, but to {{c|3732|Lehna}}, a disciple, who did as he was told,

Who carried a bundle of wet grass on his head,
Who went into the mud. He named him {{c|3733|Angad}}, part of my own limb,
And bowed to him. The light passed from one lamp to the next, they said,
Not by blood, as {{c|3275|Marozia}}'s house had passed the keys. Not him.

In 1539 he died at {{p|Kartarpur}}, and this is how it goes:
That {{c|3204|Hindus}} wished to burn him and the {{c|2764|Muslims}} wished to bury,
And they argued over him, and when they lifted the cloth, the rows
Of flowers were all that lay there. They divided them, a very

Fair division, and each did as its custom said.
There is a shrine on each side of what is now a border.
The line of 1947 runs between the living and the dead,
And {{p|Kartarpur}} is in {{p|Pakistan}}, and for years the order

Of the states let pilgrims only look across the field
Through binoculars, till they opened a corridor.
He was a synthesis, and the synthesis was sealed
In a new community, which had to be a new thing, more

Than a bridge, because the bridge had nowhere left to stand.
That is the lesson of the clearing of the ground:
Say there is no {{c|3723|Hindu}} and no {{c|3385|Muslim}}, and the land
Will make a third thing of you. The third thing will be found,

And named, and given a border of its own.
It is still the clearest thing said in this age.
There is no {{c|3723|Hindu}}. There is no {{c|3385|Muslim}}. Sit on the floor. The bread is shown
To all. Eat. Turn the page.


# Chapter 256: The Red Heads

At {{p|Ardabil}}, under the mountain, a holy man
Named {{c|3734|Safi}} taught the inner way: the remembrance,
The breath, the circle of the dervishes, the plan
Of the soul's return. He died in 1334. His descendants

Kept the lodge, and the lodge grew rich on the gifts
Of the {{c|3735|Turkmen}} tribes, who came down from the high
Pastures of {{p|Anatolia}} to kiss the threshold. The rifts
Of two centuries widened. The sheikhs began to ride, and die

In battle. The brotherhood became an army.
The disciples wore a red cap with twelve folds,
One for each of the twelve imams, and the enemy
Called them {{c|3736|Qizilbash}}: the {{c|3737|Red Heads}}. Who holds

The cap holds the faith, and who holds the faith holds the sword.
And then a boy. {{c|3738|Ismail}}, a child of seven, hidden
On the shore of the {{p|Caspian}} after his father and his eldest brother were gored
And cut down in battle, came out of hiding, bidden

By the {{c|3737|Red Heads}}, and at fourteen he took {{p|Tabriz}},
In 1501, and crowned himself the {{x|Shah}},
And in the {{c|3739|Friday}} mosque he made them read the creed with these
Words added: *and {{c|2771|Ali}} is the friend of {{c|472|God}}*. The law

Of the land was now the {{x|Twelver}} faith, the {{x|Shia}},
In a country where most people were {{c|2777|Sunni}}. Those
Who would not curse the first three caliphs, the idea
Of the new state said, could die. And many chose

To curse. And some did not, and died. The boy
Wrote poetry in {{c|3347|Turkish}} under the name {{c|3740|Khatai}},
The {{c|3741|Sinner}}, and the poems said: I am the joy
Of {{c|472|God}}, I am His mystery, I am {{c|2771|Ali}}, come and see,

Come and bow down, I am the eternal one.
His soldiers believed it. They went into battle without armor.
That is the holy king: the cloth was spun
One thread, the saint and king, in one armor.

The brotherhood that sought the self in {{c|472|God}}
was crowned in him, and found the one it sought,
and made a nation by the creed and rod
of {{c|2771|Ali}}'s house, the heir {{p|Tabriz}} was taught.

He sent for teachers, and the scholars came
from {{p|Jabal Amil}}, on {{p|Lebanon}}'s hills,
to write the books and keep the mourning's flame
for {{c|2771|Ali}}'s line, as every old house wills:

So the faith of {{p|Iran}}, that seems so old,
with the {{c|3742|Ashura}} mourning, and the shrine,
is old: the house of {{c|2771|Ali}}, which a bold
young king set on a throne in one straight line

Of conquest; a century held it true.
Remember: it was the old faith, foretold.
Then {{p|Çaldıran}}, 1514. The {{c|3341|Ottoman}} {{c|3743|Selim}} knew
The {{c|3737|Red Heads}} would charge into anything, and so he rolled

His cannon to the front and chained them wheel to wheel,
And the boy who was {{c|472|God}} charged into the guns.
{{c|472|God}} lost. The {{c|3115|Ottomans}} took {{p|Tabriz}}. The steel
Of the old way, the cavalry, the believers, the sons

Of the {{c|3735|Turkmen}} tents, broke on the gunpowder.
They say {{c|3738|Ismail}} never smiled again, that he drank
And hunted and did not lead an army after.
He died at thirty-six; his house held rank.

The state stood, and that matters, and the faith;
His great-grandson {{c|3745|Abbas}} built {{p|Isfahan}},
The square, the blue domes, *half the world*, the wraith
Of the {{c|3737|Red Heads}} tamed into a standing army, the plan

Of a modern state. One more thing, for this book:
{{c|3738|Ismail}}'s mother was the daughter of {{c|3746|Uzun Hasan}},
The {{x|White Sheep}} khan, and of {{c|3273|Theodora}}, a {{c|3747|Komnene}}, who took
The name {{c|3748|Despina}}, a {{x|Christian}} princess of {{p|Trabzon}},

Daughter of the last emperors of the {{c|2519|Greeks}} by the {{p|Black Sea}}.
So the founder of {{x|Shia}} {{p|Iran}} was the grandson
Of a {{x|Greek Orthodox}} lady of the {{c|3749|Komnenoi}}.
The blood is mixed, as every house is: one.

Greek mother, Turkmen father: the house weaves.
Four hundred and some years later, in 1979,
The clergy that {{c|3738|Ismail}} imported took the eaves
Of the state itself, and ruled. Read the line

From {{p|Ardabil}} to {{p|Tehran}}: a mystic, a boy, a sword,
A scholar, a jurist, a revolution. Each one sure
It kept the old faith, each its own reward.
Say of the {{c|3750|Safavids}}: they would endure

as saints and kings at once; the sword was long,
and the longing for {{c|472|God}} sat on the throne
in the same red cap; and the nation's song
was woven in one lifetime, and was known

As it had always been. He believed it.
He did not lie; he was right; he was young,
And had been hidden, and was saved, and he received it:
{{c|472|God}}'s mystery, in the {{x|Turkish}} of his tongue.


# Chapter 257: Here I Stand

The miner's son from {{p|Eisleben}} was meant to be a lawyer.
His father {{c|3751|Hans}} had copper smelters and a plan.
But in 1505, on the road near {{p|Stotternheim}},
A thunderbolt threw him down, and the young man,

Terrified, cried out to {{c|3752|Saint Anne}}, the miners' saint:
Help me, and I will become a monk. He kept the vow.
He went into the {{c|3753|Augustinians}} at {{p|Erfurt}},
And fasted, and confessed, and could not tell how

To be righteous enough for {{c|472|God}}. He confessed for hours.
His confessor told him: go and sin something worth confessing.
He went to {{p|Rome}} and climbed the holy stairs on his knees
And at the top he thought: who knows if it is so? The blessing

Did not come. He taught the {{x|Bible}} at {{p|Wittenberg}},
In a small university in a small {{x|Saxon}} town,
And in the {{c|3754|Letter to the Romans}} he read: the just shall live
By faith. Not by the stairs. Not by the crown

Of works. Not by the money. And then the money came.
{{c|3755|Tetzel}}, a friar, was selling indulgences
Across the border, for the building of {{p|Saint Peter's}}
And for the debts of an archbishop, the expenses

Of {{c|3756|Albrecht}} of {{p|Mainz}}, who had bought his see:
*As soon as the coin in the coffer rings,
The soul from purgatory springs.*
The peasants of {{p|Saxony}} walked across to buy the things.

On the last day of October, 1517,
{{c|1062|Luther}} wrote out ninety-five theses for debate,
In {{x|Latin}}, for scholars: whether the pope can empty purgatory,
And if he can, why he does not, out of love, and not for the weight

Of the coins. Whether he nailed them to the church door
Is not certain. He sent them to the archbishop. What is certain
Is the press. Within weeks they were printed, and by the spring in {{x|German}},
And within months they were across the empire. The curtain

Of the {{x|Latin}} was torn. This is what {{c|3217|Gutenberg}} had made
Seventy years before without knowing: a voice
That could not be burned faster than it could be set in type.
{{c|3757|Hus}} had been burned. {{c|1062|Luther}} was printed. Choice

Of a weapon. In the next years his pamphlets
Were more than any author's in {{p|Europe}} had ever been:
*To the {{x|Christian Nobility}}*. *The {{x|Babylonian Captivity}}*.
*The {{x|Freedom of a Christian}}*. Small books, cheap, and seen

In every market, read aloud in every tavern
To men who could not read. The {{c|2825|Pope}} excommunicated him.
He burned the bull in a bonfire at the city gate.
And at {{p|Worms}}, in 1521, before the emperor, {{c|3253|Charles}}, grim

In his youth, with his {{x|Habsburg}} jaw, the lord
Of half the world, the monk was asked to recant.
He asked for a day. He came back, and he said: unless
I am convinced by {{x|Scripture}} and plain reason, I can't,

My conscience is captive to the {{x|Word of God}}.
And the printers, afterward, added: *Here I stand.
I can do no other.* He may not have said it.
It was printed. It became what he said. The hand

Of the press decides what the man said. Remember that.
Then a friendly kidnapping: {{c|3758|Frederick}} of {{p|Saxony}}
Had him seized on the road and hidden in the {{p|Wartburg}},
And there, as {{c|3759|Junker Jörg}}, in a beard, in a cell of agony

And ink, he translated the {{c|3760|New Testament}}
Into {{x|German}} in eleven weeks. Not the {{x|German}}
Of the clerks: the {{x|German}} of the mother in the house,
The children in the street, the man in the market. The sermon

Had been the priest's. Now the book was the household's.
And the language of the book became the language of the land.
{{x|High German}} is, in part, the language {{c|1062|Luther}} chose.
That is what it means for scripture to leave the priest's hand.

Now the other side. Hold both. In 1525 the peasants rose,
Reading the same book, finding freedom in it, and the princes
Slaughtered them, and {{c|1062|Luther}} wrote to the princes:
*Smite, slay, and stab.* A hundred thousand dead. He who convinces

The poor that the book is theirs had better be ready
For them to read it. He was not ready. And when he was old
He wrote against the {{c|2500|Jews}}, a book of fire:
Burn their synagogues, he wrote. Four hundred years later, the cold

Men of the {{c|3761|Reich}} would print it again. That is the press too.
The same machine. A voice that cannot be burned
Can be used to burn. {{c|1062|Luther}} married {{c|3762|Katharina von Bora}},
An escaped nun, smuggled out in a fish wagon; they turned

A monastery into a house of children and of students,
And beer, and table talk. The {{x|Church}} split in three:
{{p|Rome}}, and {{p|Wittenberg}}, and the others coming, {{p|Zürich}}, {{p|Geneva}}.
The keys the fisherman had passed were no longer the only key.

Every household with a {{x|Bible}} became a little church.
Every reader, a priest. That was the promise and the danger.
The register of souls the priests had kept would pass
To the state. The book would pass to the stranger.

Hold the one sentence that was surely his, before the printing:
Unless I am convinced, I cannot. The rest is the printers' saying.
A conscience in a hall. The press. The hymn. The praying.


# Chapter 258: The Lawgiver's Register

In the year {{c|1062|Luther}} burned the pope's bull at {{p|Wittenberg}},
In {{p|Istanbul}} a young man came to the throne of the world's
Greatest empire, from the {{p|Nile}} to the {{p|Danube}},
From {{p|Mecca}} to the {{p|Crimea}}. The flags unfurled

For {{c|3763|Suleiman}}, the tenth sultan of the house of {{c|3241|Osman}}.
{{p|Europe}} called him the {{c|3764|Magnificent}}. His own people
Called him {{c|3765|Kanuni}}: the {{c|3766|Lawgiver}}. Hold both names.
The conqueror and the clerk. The minaret and the steeple

Under one crown. He took {{p|Belgrade}} in 1521,
And {{p|Rhodes}} from the {{c|3767|Knights of Saint John}} the year after,
And let them sail away with honor. At {{p|Mohács}}
In 1526 he broke the {{x|Hungarian}} army, and the laughter

Of the young king {{c|3768|Louis}} ended in a stream
Where he drowned in his armor, fleeing. Half of {{p|Hungary}}
Became {{x|Ottoman}}. In 1529 he came to {{p|Vienna}}
And the rains and the walls turned him back. The hungry

Janissaries went home. That was the high-water mark.
Now the other face, the one the name {{c|3765|Kanuni}} carries:
The empire was a register. Every province, every village,
Every household was written in the {{c|3769|defter}}: who marries,

Who farms which field, who owes what, and of what faith.
The scribes went out and counted. The tax register,
The {{c|3770|tahrir}}, listed the {{c|2764|Muslims}} and the {{c|2494|Christians}} and the {{c|2500|Jews}},
Each by name, each by community. The sinister

And the generous are the same pen here. The non-Muslim paid
The {{c|3771|jizya}}, the head tax, and in return
Was let alone to pray: the {{c|3772|Orthodox}} under their patriarch
In {{p|Istanbul}}, the {{c|2615|Armenians}} under theirs, the concern

Of the {{c|2500|Jews}} in the hands of their rabbis, each community
Judging its own marriages and wills and quarrels
By its own law, its own book, its own courts.
Historians would later call it the millet system. The laurels

Are deserved and not deserved. It was not tolerance
As a modern means it. It was order. It was a ledger.
A man's religion was his legal address. You were born
Into your millet, and the state was the keeper and the hedger

Of the walls between them. You could not easily leave.
But you could live. When {{p|Spain}} expelled its {{c|2500|Jews}} in 1492,
The sultan's father's father took them in, and in {{p|Thessaloniki}}
They became the city's majority, and the printing presses grew,

And {{c|3773|Doña Gracia}}, the banker, fleeing the {{x|Inquisition}},
Came to {{p|Istanbul}}, and her nephew {{c|3774|Joseph Nasi}}
Became the sultan's friend, and later Duke of {{p|Naxos}},
And leased {{p|Tiberias}} to rebuild it, a refuge, a fantasy

Of return, three centuries early. And the other side:
The {{c|3235|devshirme}}, the levy of boys, the {{x|Christian}} sons
Taken from the villages of the {{p|Balkans}}, converted,
Trained, and made the sultan's slaves, the janissaries, the guns

Of the empire, some of them its viziers, its architects:
{{c|3775|Sinan}}, a levied boy from {{p|Anatolia}}, built the
{{c|3776|Süleymaniye}} on the hill above the {{p|Golden Horn}},
The mosque that answers {{p|Hagia Sophia}}. The register gave and took. See

Both. And in the harem, a captive from {{p|Ruthenia}},
{{c|3777|Hürrem}}, whom the {{p|West}} called {{c|3778|Roxelana}}, freed and married,
Against every custom of the house: a slave become a queen,
And for her sons' sake, they said, the heir {{c|3779|Mustafa}} strangled and buried,

In his father's tent, the father watching from behind a screen, the story says.
The {{c|3766|Lawgiver}} wrote the {{c|3780|kanun}} beside the holy law,
With {{c|3781|Ebussuud}}, his jurist, making the two agree:
Codes for land, for crime, for the army, for every flaw

Of an empire of sixty peoples. And he wrote poems,
Under the name {{c|3782|Muhibbi}}, the {{c|3783|Lover}}: *people think wealth
And power the greatest fortune, but in this world
There is nothing like the state of health.*

He died in 1566 in his tent at {{p|Szigetvár}}, in {{p|Hungary}},
Besieging a fortress, an old man of seventy-one,
And his vizier hid his death from the army for weeks.
The register went on. The census would be done

By every state that came after, every empire and republic,
Every nation that wanted to know who its people were,
And what they believed, and where to find them.
The millet became the census box. The pen, the stir

Of the scribe in the village, is where the modern state begins:
Not only in the guns. In the page that says who you are.
A faith as an address. A people as a column.
Hold the gift and the wound in the one ledger. Here we are.


# Chapter 259: The Register of Every Soul

Until now the dead were mostly nameless.
The kings were written, and the saints, and those
Who gave land to a monastery, and the blameless
And the guilty in the courts. The rest: the rows

Of fields, the children born and buried in a winter,
The marriages at the church door, the plague years,
Went into memory and out of it. A splinter
Of a name on a grave. A song. The sum of tears

Without a column. Then, in September 1538,
In {{p|England}}, {{c|3784|Thomas Cromwell}}, the king's vicar-general,
A blacksmith's son who had made himself the weight
Behind the throne of {{c|3374|Henry}}, sent an order, general

To every parish: keep a book. Write in it
Every christening, every wedding, every burial,
Every Sunday, in the presence of a churchwarden. Fit
The book in a coffer with two locks. The material

Of a people, written. And the people were afraid.
They said: it is for a new tax. They said: the king
Will charge us for our children. Through the {{p|West Country}} it was said
For a year, and men were ready to rise. It was not a tax. The thing

Was worse and better: it was a memory that did not die
With the old woman of the village. A record
That outlasted the parish clerk, the priest, the sky
Of that year. Not every parish obeyed. The word

Was enforced by fines, by bishops, by the slow
Habit of Sundays. In 1598 they were told
To copy the old paper into parchment books, and so
Many {{x|English}} registers begin with the year of the old

{{c|3785|Queen}}'s crowning, 1558, in a clean hand.
And across the water, at {{p|Trent}}, in the mountains of the {{p|Tyrol}},
The {{x|Catholic Church}}, answering {{c|1062|Luther}}, in its stand
Against the {{c|3786|Reformers}}, decided at its twenty-fourth session, the whole

Of {{c|3332|Christendom}} that kept the old faith must register
Its marriages, with witnesses, by name,
And its baptisms, with the godparents. No minister
Could marry a couple secretly anymore. The same

Book, the same page, from {{p|Lisbon}} to {{p|Kraków}}, to {{p|Lima}}, to {{p|Goa}}.
In 1614 the {{x|Roman Ritual}} added the dead,
And the {{c|3787|Book of the State of Souls}}: every household, who
Lived in it, who had made their {{x|Easter}} confession. The thread

Of the register ran out into every village of the {{x|Catholic}} world.
And the {{c|3788|Lutherans}} took it up, and in the {{p|North}}
It became the most thorough of all. In {{p|Sweden}}, unfurled
In the {{x|Church Law}} of 1686, the priest went forth

House by house each year with the roll of the household examination,
Who could read, who knew the catechism, who had moved,
Who was born, who married, who died. A nation
Written down to the last cottar. And this is proved

In this book's own blood. The ancestors of the writer of this scripture
Have a year and nothing else, a guess, until the parish
Begins to write. Then: *{{c|3789|Per Olofsson}}, born the fourth of April, 1696*.
A day. A real day, kept in a {{x|Swedish}} church. The varnish

Of the old guesses comes off, and the people underneath
Have birthdays. That is what the register gave:
Not the kings. The kings had always had their wreath
Of dates. The register gave the cottar, the herdsman, the slave,

The midwife, the drowned child, the girl who married at nineteen,
A day of their own. It is the democracy of the dead.
And the state learned to read it. What the church had seen
For the sake of souls, the state would read instead

For soldiers and taxes and, in the worst years, for blood.
A register that can find every {{c|3386|Christian}} can find every {{c|2510|Jew}}.
Hold that. The same book. And the {{c|3673|Mormons}}, in the flood
Of the twentieth century, would come to photograph them, through

Every archive in the world, the parish books of {{p|Europe}},
Microfilm in a mountain in {{p|Utah}}, to baptize the dead.
And from those films, the tree. And from the tree, the scope
Of a family reaching back to {{c|2896|Qarin}} and the kings it is said

To come from. All of it rests on a clerk on a Sunday,
In a cold church, with a quill, writing a name.
Honor him. He did not know what he was making. One day
Someone would read his hand, and say: there, that is where I came.


# Chapter 260: The Earth Leaves the Centre

For two thousand years the {{p|Earth}} stood still.
The {{x|Sun}} went round it, and the {{x|Moon}}, and the five
Wandering stars, and the fixed stars on their shell,
And the whole sky turned once a day, alive

Around us, the way a king's court turns around the king.
{{c|2265|Ptolemy}} had written it down in {{p|Alexandria}}:
Circles on circles, the epicycles, everything
Explained, predicted, measured. The criteria

Of the heavens were the same as those of heaven:
We were in the middle. God looked at us.
And it worked, almost. The calendar slipped. The seven
Lights were late or early. The astronomers made a fuss

And added circles. Then a canon of the cathedral
At {{p|Frombork}}, on the {{p|Baltic}} shore, a careful man,
{{c|3790|Nicolaus Copernicus}}, born in {{p|Toruń}}, a scholar, a medical
Doctor, a lawyer, an economist, who wrote a plan

To stop the debasement of the coin, who held a castle
At {{p|Olsztyn}} against the {{c|3055|Teutonic Knights}},
Who kept the accounts of his chapter: this unremarkable vassal
Of the Prince-Bishop of {{p|Warmia}} spent his nights

On a tower, with simple instruments, and his days
With the old books, and saw that the sky was simpler
If the {{x|Sun}} stood in the middle, and the {{p|Earth}} was one of the rays
Of the wheel, a planet among planets. A whisper

At first: a little handwritten book, around 1514,
Passed among friends. He did not publish. Thirty years.
He was afraid of being laughed at, he said. Between
The fear and the book, a young man appears:

{{c|3791|Rheticus}}, a {{x|Lutheran}} professor from {{p|Wittenberg}},
Who came in 1539 to the {{x|Catholic}} canon's house
And stayed two years, and talked him into it. The iceberg
Of the old sky cracked at last. The book was set in type, and the douse

Of cold water came from a friend: {{c|3792|Osiander}}, who saw it through the press
In {{p|Nuremberg}}, added a preface without a name,
Saying it was only a hypothesis, a way to compute, no less,
No more, not true. *{{x|On the Revolutions}}*. It came

Off the press in 1543, and the story says
A copy was put into his hands as he lay dying
Of a stroke in {{p|Frombork}}, on the twenty-fourth of May.
He may not have known it. The story, the comforting lying

Or the truth, is that the old man held the new sky
On his last day. And hold this too: he was not the first.
{{c|3793|Aristarchus}} of {{p|Samos}} had said it, long ago, and the why
Of his models, the little paired circles, had been rehearsed

At {{p|Maragha}}, in {{p|Iran}}, by {{c|3794|al-Tusi}} and his school,
Three centuries before, and in {{p|Damascus}} by {{c|3795|Ibn al-Shatir}},
Whose moon moved as {{c|2266|Copernicus}}'s moved. The rule
Of the transmission the {{x|Golden Age}} began, the clear

Water running from the {{p|House of Wisdom}} west, ran here too.
He still had circles. He still had epicycles. The sky
Would wait for {{c|3796|Kepler}}'s ellipses and {{c|2396|Galileo}}'s view
Through the glass. But the {{p|Earth}} was moving. Why

Does it matter for a scripture? Because the {{x|Gaiad}} begins
With the birth of the universe, and the long work of stars,
And the {{p|Earth}} is not the centre. It never was. The spins
Of the planets do not circle us. Our scars

Are not the sky's concern. And still, here is the strangeness:
On this one moving stone, small, off-centre, plain,
Life happened. It is not the place that makes the greatness.
It is what grew here. The {{x|Sun}} is the centre. The grain,

The fish, the bird, the child, the hand that wrote the book:
These are not at the middle of anything but our own regard.
Lifeism keeps that. The centre is not where we look
From. The centre is what we hold, and hold hard.

The {{x|Church}} put the book on the {{x|Index}} in 1616,
"Until corrected." It came off in 1835.
The {{p|Earth}} went on turning through the quarrel. Between
The two dates, every navigator, every child alive

Learned the new sky, and it was not a loss.
We are travelling. We were always travelling. The year
Is a journey round a star, and the cross
Of the seasons is our orbit. Count it, and be glad to be here.


# Chapter 261: The Farmers at Bure
