Of the holiday is joy, and it is commanded: *you shall rejoice*.
In a house you know is temporary. Under a roof
That lets in the stars and the rain. The choice
Of the sukkah is the choice to hope without proof

And not be destroyed when the proof does not come.
The barrels in {{p|Hameln}} were a sukkah. A hope, kept packed,
In a house where the stars came in. The sum
Of the story is not: the hope was a fool's. It is the fact

That a people who had just been massacred
Could still dance in the synagogue, and still pack the barrels, and still, when the hope
Turned to shame, unpack, and live, and wait. The word
Of the festival: rejoice in what does not last. The scope

Of his year was short. The joy was not wrong.
Sit in the hut tonight. It will not stand forever.
Sing anyway. The roof is thin. The night is long.
The barrels can be unpacked. The hope can be kept. Never

Let one year's dawn close the door of the world.
And never stop leaving the roof open to the stars.
Rejoice in the booth. The branches are curled
Over your head, and they let the light through the bars.


# Chapter 279: One Law for the Apple and the Moon

A child born early on {{x|Christmas Day}}, 1642, so small, his mother said,
He would have fit in a quart pot, at {{p|Woolsthorpe}} in {{p|Lincolnshire}},
The year {{c|2396|Galileo}} died. His father was already dead.
His mother left him with his grandmother. The fire

Of that boyhood never cooled: he made lists of his sins, and one was
*Threatening my father and mother Smith to burn them and the house over them.*
He went to {{p|Cambridge}} as a servant-student. And then, because
Of the plague, in 1665 the university closed, and the stem

Of the modern world grew in an orchard at {{p|Woolsthorpe}}.
Twenty-three years old, alone, for eighteen months, he invented
The calculus, and split white light with a prism into the rainbow's gorge,
And wondered, watching an apple fall, the story is remembered

Or told by his own old age, whether the force that pulled it down
Reached up as far as the {{c|198|Moon}}, and held it in its orbit,
And weakened with the square of the distance. The crown
Of the idea he kept to himself for twenty years. The sorbet

Of fame did not interest him. Then, in 1684, {{c|3979|Edmond Halley}}
Came to {{p|Cambridge}} and asked: if the force on the planets falls
With the square of the distance, what path do they follow? The rally
Of the answer: an ellipse. I have calculated it. The walls

Of his rooms were searched for the paper, and it was lost, and he promised
To do it again. Three years later the book came out:
*{{x|Philosophiae Naturalis Principia Mathematica}}*, the fifth of July, 1687, the honest
Size of it three books in {{x|Latin}}, paid for, as the last chapter told, without doubt,

By {{c|3980|Halley}}. Three laws of motion. A body at rest stays at rest.
A force changes motion in proportion. Every action has its reaction.
And one law of gravity, the same for the apple and the planets, the test
Of the sky the same as the test of the orchard: one attraction

Between every two masses in the universe, falling with the square
Of their distance. The {{c|198|Moon}}'s orbit. The tides. The comets' return,
So that {{c|3980|Halley}} could predict his comet would come back, and it did, there
In 1758, sixteen years after he had died. The burn

Of the old sky was over: the heavens were not made of a finer stuff.
They were made of world. The same law in the stars as in the hand.
That is the {{x|Gaiad}}'s first chapter, written in {{x|Latin}}. Enough
To know the universe is one: one law, one land.

And now the other {{c|3895|Newton}}. The one who spent more years
On alchemy than on physics, hunting the philosopher's stone,
Writing a million words on the transmutation of metals, the tears
Of mercury and the green lion. The one who, alone,

Denied the {{x|Trinity}} in secret, and calculated from the {{c|3993|Book of Daniel}}
That the world would not end before 2060. The one
Whose papers, sold in 1936, made {{c|3994|Keynes}} write that he was not the first
Of the age of reason: he was the last of the magicians. The sun

Of the new science and the moon of the old wisdom in one man.
And here is the thing to keep, after {{c|3896|Bureus}}: {{c|3895|Newton}} knew which was which.
He published the laws, which anyone could check. The plan
Of the alchemy he kept in a box. He did not make the switch

Of dream into proof. The box was opened after he died,
And the world was surprised. That is the right shape. Dream, if you dream.
Keep it in the box, labelled. Publish what can be tried.
He wrote: *I frame no hypotheses*, about the cause, the seam

Of gravity he could not explain. He knew what he did not know.
And he was cruel: to {{c|3981|Hooke}}, to {{c|3995|Leibniz}}, and, as {{x|Master of the Mint}},
To the counterfeiters he hunted himself, and sent to the gallows. So
Hold the whole man. Not a saint. A mind, and a temper, and a stint

Of loneliness that lasted his whole life. He wrote, of himself, near the end,
That he had been like a boy on the shore, playing with a smoother pebble,
A prettier shell, while the great ocean of truth lay all undiscovered. Attend
To that: the greatest mind of the age, and the ocean, and the treble

Of the waves on a beach. He died in 1727 and lies in {{p|Westminster}}.
*Nature and Nature's laws lay hid in night;
God said, Let {{c|3895|Newton}} be! and all was light.* The poet's tinder.
Better the shell on the shore. Better the boy. Better the ocean, and the sight

Of the apple falling, and the {{c|198|Moon}} held, by one thing.
The universe is one law. And the ocean is still there.
Pick up a shell. Check it. Keep your dreams in a box, labelled. And sing
For the orchard where the plague sent a boy, and he looked up, and saw it there.


# Chapter 280: One and Nothing

{{c|3996|Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz}}, born in {{p|Leipzig}} in 1646, the son
Of a professor of ethics who died when the boy was six,
Taught himself {{x|Latin}} from the books of his father's library, and won
A doctorate in law at twenty, and then refused the fixed

Life of a professor, and became a courtier, a diplomat, a librarian,
A historian of the house of {{p|Brunswick}}, a writer of letters, fifteen
Thousand of them, to everyone in {{p|Europe}} and beyond, the clarion
Of a mind that wanted to join every mind it had seen.

He found the calculus at the same time as {{c|3895|Newton}}, alone,
And wrote it in the signs we still use: the long S of the integral,
The *d* of the differential. And the quarrel over whose it was, the bone
Of the {{c|3974|Royal Society}}'s committee, as the earlier chapter told, the minimal

Justice of it came late. But this chapter is about two numbers.
In 1679 he wrote out a way of counting with only one and zero:
One, ten, eleven, a hundred. Two digits for all the numbers. The slumbers
Of the idea lasted twenty years. He saw in it, as a hero

Of the old theology might: the world made from God and nothing.
One is God. Zero is the void. And from the two, all things.
*{{x|Omnibus ex nihilo ducendis sufficit unum}}*: the clothing
Of the motto on a medal he designed: to draw all things from nothing, the wings

Of one suffice. And he built a machine that could multiply,
A stepped drum of brass, and showed it to the {{c|3974|Royal Society}} in 1673.
And he dreamed of more: a universal language, a *characteristic*, a way to try
Every argument by calculation, so that two philosophers, the sea

Of their quarrel too deep for words, would sit down with pens
And say to each other: *calculemus*. Let us calculate.
The dream of a machine that reasons. The lens
Of the next three hundred years is in that word. The weight

Of everything that {{c|3880|Ophiuchus}} will tell is in it. Hold it.
And he loved {{p|China}}. He read everything the {{c|3588|Jesuits}} wrote,
And published their letters, *{{x|News from China}}*, in 1697, and told it
To {{p|Europe}}: their ethics are better than ours; we should note

That we need {{x|Chinese}} missionaries to teach us natural theology,
As much as they need ours to teach revealed religion.
He defended {{c|3997|Ricci}}'s way, the rites for the ancestors, the apology
Of the accommodation, against {{p|Rome}}. And then, the vision:

In 1701 a {{c|3835|Jesuit}} in {{p|Beijing}}, {{c|3998|Joachim Bouvet}}, who had read
His binary, sent him a diagram of the sixty-four hexagrams
Of the {{c|3999|I Ching}}, the *{{x|Book of Changes}}*, in the order {{c|4000|Shao Yong}} had spread,
And {{c|3995|Leibniz}} looked at the broken and unbroken lines, the grams

Of yin and yang, and saw: zero and one. The hexagrams in that order
Counted from nothing to sixty-three in binary. The oldest book
Of {{p|China}}, ascribed to {{c|733|Fuxi}}, the sage of the beginning, a border
Crossed four thousand years before, he believed, by the same look

At the world as his own. He was wrong about the history.
The order was a {{x|Song}} scholar's, not the ancient sage's. But the mystery
Was real: two minds, a world apart, building the same ladder of change. The registry
Of that meeting is a letter. And in 1703 he published his binary, the history

Of it ending with the hexagrams. Within two hundred and fifty years,
Every machine that thinks would think in one and zero.
The register of every soul, the census, the ledgers, the tears
Of the {{x|Company}}, the temple book: all of it, in the next era,

Would be written in his two digits. That is the bridge.
{{c|3982|Virgo}} ends here: the early modern world, its saints and its massacres,
Its registers and its telescopes, its kings on the ridge
Of invented pasts. And it ends with a man who joined the actors

Of {{p|East}} and {{p|West}} in two numbers, and dreamed of reasoning by machine.
He died in 1716 in {{p|Hanover}}, out of favour, his king gone to {{p|London}},
And only his secretary followed the coffin. The lean
Grave of the man who joined the world. And {{c|4001|Voltaire}} would make fun

Of his *best of all possible worlds*. Let him. The one and the nothing
Are in every phone. Every message to the ones you love goes in them.
Tomorrow begins {{c|3932|Libra}}: the {{x|Rites}}, the reckoning, the clothing
Of the {{x|Enlightenment}}. From one and nothing, the world. Hold the hem.

---

# Libra (11宮) - Days 281-308


# Chapter 281: The Harvest at the Ancestors' Hall

In autumn in {{p|China}}, when the grain was in, the family
Went to the ancestors' hall, and set the first of the harvest
Before the tablets of the dead: the rice, the millet, the homily
Of the incense, the bowing, the names read out. The darkest

Winter would come; first, thanks. This is the day.
Keep that table in your eye: our own rite,
And the quarrel round it was ours. The way
It ran: who holds the table, by what right.

{{c|3997|Ricci}} had made his wager: let them bow;
Let the believer keep his fathers' hall;
And {{x|Tian}} and {{x|Shangdi}} named the God of all.
His order, the {{c|3588|Jesuits}}, kept that vow.

A century. Then {{c|4002|Dominicans}} came,
With the {{c|3570|Franciscans}}, to the farms, and saw
Food set for the dead, and gave it a name,
And called it idol-worship, by their law.

They said the names {{x|Tian}} and {{x|Shangdi}} were wrong
For God. But the heart of it was the hall:
Who sets the bowl, who reads the names, whose song
Is sung there, and whose keys are over all.

The quarrel went to {{p|Rome}} and {{p|Paris}}, where
The clergy argued it for decades, men
Who never saw the land, nor the hall's prayer.
The {{c|3588|Jesuits}} asked the emperor then.

In seventeen hundred, {{c|3950|Kangxi}}, the great,
Signed for the {{c|3588|Jesuits}} a word of state:
The rite to {{c|1958|Confucius}} thanks one who taught;
The rite in the hall is love, and asks naught

Of blessing from the dead; {{x|Tian}} is the name
The {{x|Lord of Heaven}}'s. The throne made the call.
And {{p|Rome}} said: not his to settle; the same
Keys could not be shared, not over the hall.

In seventeen-oh-four the {{c|2825|Pope}} decreed:
No {{x|Tian}}, no {{x|Shangdi}}; just {{x|Tianzhu}}, the name
{{c|3997|Ricci}} had made; no tablet that would read
*Seat of the soul*; then the heart of the claim:

No {{x|Christian}} at the teacher's rite, and none
At the year's offerings in the fathers' hall.
The whole accommodation was undone.
The keys would keep the dead. And that was all.

A legate, {{c|4004|Tournon}}, took it to {{p|Beijing}};
The emperor heard him, and asked one thing:
Could {{c|4005|Maigrot}}, who began it, read the page?
He could not read a character. The rage

Was the throne's: such a man to judge the wise!
The legate, sent to {{p|Macau}}, where the eyes
Of {{x|Portuguese}}, for their rights, held him; then
He died, in seventeen hundred and ten.

{{p|Rome}} sealed the ban in seventeen-fifteen,
And {{c|3950|Kangxi}}, with his red brush, wrote between
Its lines: *Men of the West are small; and so
They need not preach here, to avoid a row.*

His son shut, in seventeen twenty-four,
The {{x|Lord of Heaven}}'s teaching in the land;
Seventeen forty-two: the {{c|2825|Pope}}, once more,
Made each priest swear off the rites, by command.

Two hundred years the {{x|Christian}} could not bring
His harvest to the dead. Keys, not the king,
Had barred him. And the converts wept to choose
The priests' altar or their dead: which to lose?

Hold that, on {{x|Harvest Day}}. Then hold this, too:
In nineteen thirty-nine, a {{c|2825|Pope}} still new
Called the rites civil; a {{x|Christian}} may bow;
The tablets stand in line with the faith now.

One hundred ninety-seven years, from no
To yes. The wager and the throne were right.
The thanks at the harvest to those who came before, the bow
To the tablet with the grandmother's name, was love. The light

Of this day in the {{c|4008|Gaian}} calendar falls on many harvests:
The first fruits of the {{p|Americas}}, given thanks by its first peoples;
The rice of {{p|Japan}}; the turkey of {{p|Canada}}; and the ancestral hall, where the fastest
And the slowest of the family come home. The steeples

And the shrines and the ancestors' halls: the harvest belongs to all of them.
Give thanks for the food. Give thanks to the hands that grew it.
Give thanks to the ones who came before, and set the bowl at the hem
Of their memory. No one has the right to forbid it. Do it.


# Chapter 282: The Names of Everything

In {{p|Småland}}, in {{p|Sweden}}, a country pastor's son was born in 1707,
At {{p|Råshult}}, in the parsonage among the birches.
His father, {{c|4009|Nils}}, the son of a farmer named {{c|4010|Ingemar}}, had been given, as was common,
No surname: *{{c|4011|Nils Ingemarsson}}*. When he went to university, the churches

And the learned wanted a {{x|Latin}} name. So he made one up,
From a great linden tree, a *lind*, that grew on the family's farm:
*{{c|4012|Linnaeus}}*. Hold that, in a book of genealogy: the cup
Of a name was filled by a tree. The family line, the charm

Of the patronymic, {{c|4010|Ingemar}}'s son, {{c|4009|Nils}}'s son, gave way
To a name you choose. And the son, {{c|4013|Carl}}, would spend his life
Giving names to every living thing. His father had a garden; the way
The boy learned the flowers was by asking, and the strife

Of forgetting them made his father say: I will not tell you again.
He did not forget again. He went to {{p|Uppsala}}, poor,
With shoes he mended with birch bark, and walked, in 1732, the plain
Of {{p|Lapland}}, two thousand kilometres, and wore

The costume of the {{c|4014|Sámi}} afterward for his portrait, the drum
And the reindeer boots, and learned from them, and wrote it down.
In 1735, in {{p|Leiden}}, in the {{p|Netherlands}}, the sum
Of his system came out: *{{x|Systema Naturae}}*, a crown

Of eleven large pages: all of nature, the three kingdoms,
Animal, plant and stone, in classes, orders, genera, kinds.
And the plants sorted by their sex: the stamens and the pistils, the stem's
Husbands and wives, how many of each in the flower. The minds

Of the pious were shocked. A professor called it *loathsome harlotry*.
{{c|4012|Linnaeus}} named an ugly weed after him. And in 1753
He gave every plant two names, a genus and a species, a clarity
That made botany possible: *{{x|Bellis perennis}}*, the daisy. The key

Of the binomial still opens the whole living world. And in 1758,
The tenth edition, he did the boldest thing. He put us in.
*{{x|Homo sapiens}}*: wise man, among the primates, beside the great
Apes, in the same order as the monkeys. The sin

Of it, to the theologians: man among the beasts.
He wrote to a friend: tell me one difference between man and ape
That follows the rules of natural history. I know of none. The feasts
Of human pride had their first plain mirror. And then the shape

Of the harm. In the same pages he divided *{{x|Homo sapiens}}*
Into four varieties by continent, *americanus*, *europaeus*, *asiaticus*, *afer*,
And gave each a temperament, and ranked them, the {{x|European}} in the sense
Of governed by laws, the {{x|African}} by caprice: the seed of a horror

That would grow for two hundred years. The register of life
Had a racist line in it, written by the hand that put us among the apes.
Hold both. He sent his students out across the world, the strife
And the joy of it: seventeen apostles, he called them, to the capes

And jungles and the ice, to collect, and a third of them died on the road.
He was ennobled in 1761: *{{c|4015|Carl von Linné}}*.
He said of himself, *God created, {{c|4012|Linnaeus}} ordered*. The load
Of the boast was heavy and half true. He died in 1778, the day

Coming when they laid him in the cathedral of {{p|Uppsala}}.
This is a book that begins with the birth of the universe and of life,
And comes down through the fish and the reptiles and the patterns
Of the mammals to us. It owes him its names. The knife

Of his system cut the living world into a register,
And the register is a gift: to know the names of the beings we share the earth with
Is the first respect. A {{x|Lifeist}} calls each one by its name, a barrister
Of the living, an advocate. Learn the names. The pith

Of reverence is attention. And cross out the line he got wrong:
There are no ranked varieties of us. The register of humankind is one.
*{{x|Homo sapiens}}*. One species. One family. One song.
The linden tree in {{p|Småland}} is gone. The name it gave is in the sun.


# Chapter 283: No Place Empty

After the messiah who took the turban, the {{c|2500|Jews}} of {{p|Poland}} and {{p|Ukraine}}
Were ashamed, and poor, and the learned were proud of their learning,
And the poor who could not read the {{x|Talmud}} stood outside the plain
Of the scholars' world, and prayed the words without discerning

What they meant, and were told they were nothing. And in {{p|Podolia}},
Among the villages of the borderland, around 1700,
A boy was born, an orphan, {{c|2735|Israel}}, son of {{c|4016|Eliezer}}, who would be holier
Than the scholars and never write a book. They sent

Him as a helper to the teacher, to walk the little children
To the schoolroom in the morning, and he walked them singing,
And taught them to sing the prayers. He was a watchman, a clay-digger in
The {{p|Carpathian}} hills, a hidden man, and the bringing

Of his secret out came late, when he was thirty-six, the story says.
He was a *baal shem*, a master of the Name: a healer, a writer of amulets,
And they called him the {{c|4017|Baal Shem Tov}}, the {{c|4018|Master of the Good Name}}, the praise
Of the villages. He settled at {{p|Medzhybizh}}, around 1740. The lets

And hindrances of the old way he did not abolish. He kept the law.
But he taught a different heart in it. God is everywhere:
*There is no place empty of Him.* In the field, the straw,
The tavern, the stranger, the evil thought, the prayer.

Every spark of the broken vessels the {{c|3985|Kabbalists}} had mourned
Was here, in the ordinary, waiting to be lifted with joy.
Not with fasting. With joy. The sad are far from God; the scorned
And the simple are near. And the story they tell of the boy:

On {{c|3926|Yom Kippur}}, a shepherd boy who could not read the prayers
Stood in the synagogue all day, and his heart was full, and he had a whistle,
A shepherd's pipe, and at the end of the day, in the airs
Of the closing prayer, he could not hold it, and blew it, a thistle

Of a sound in the solemn room, and the men were furious.
And the {{c|4017|Baal Shem Tov}} said: the gates of heaven were shut,
And all our prayers could not open them, and that boy's pipe, the curious
Note of a heart with no words, broke them open. The rut

Of learning was not the road. The heart was the road.
He wrote nothing. His students wrote him down: the great {{c|4019|Maggid}}
Of {{p|Mezhyrichi}}, and the others, and the stories, the load
Of the tales passed on by the poor, the parables, the rigid

Made soft. And the movement spread like water through the villages:
{{c|4020|Hasidism}}, the way of the pious, dancing in the prayer house,
Following a holy man, a *rebbe*, a righteous one, whose courtyard and its images
Of feasting and song drew the poor in. And the {{c|4021|Vilna Gaon}}, who would house

No compromise, the greatest scholar of the age in {{p|Vilnius}},
Excommunicated them in 1772: these are dancers, not scholars, a sect.
The quarrel lasted a generation, and then, like the illness
Of every quarrel, cooled, and both sides were what kept

The {{c|2500|Jews}} of the East {{x|Jewish}} when the modern world came for them.
And here is the thing for this book. The rebbes' courts became dynasties.
The holiness passed from father to son, and son-in-law, the hem
Of the rebbe's coat held by his heirs: genealogies

Of the holy, kept as carefully as any king's.
His own great-grandson, {{c|4022|Nachman of Breslov}}, would teach
That the whole world is a narrow bridge, and the main thing
Is not to be afraid at all. And the grave and its reach

At {{p|Uman}} draws tens of thousands every new year still.
Hold the two: the teaching that holiness is in everyone, everywhere,
And the dynasties that made it run in families. The will
Of the movement was for the simple; the courts grew rich. The prayer

Of the shepherd's pipe is the part to keep. And this, which the {{x|Gaiad}} shares
With the {{c|4018|Master of the Good Name}}: there is no place empty.
The divine, or the sacred, or the life, is in all of it: the stairs,
The straw, the stranger, the smallest thing. The plenty

Is everywhere. Lift it with joy. Do not be sad; the sad
Are far from the sacred. Sing on the way to school.
And if you have no words, blow the whistle. What you had
Was enough. It always was. The heart is the rule.


# Chapter 284: The Pact at Diriyah

In {{p|Najd}}, the high desert at the heart of {{p|Arabia}}, a long way
From {{p|Istanbul}} and from {{p|Cairo}}, in the oasis towns of palm and mud brick,
Where the people visited the tombs of holy men, and hung rags on trees to pray,
And asked the saints to carry their prayers, a scholar, quick

And severe, {{c|4023|Muhammad ibn Abd al-Wahhab}}, born in 1703,
Came home from his studies in {{p|Medina}} and {{p|Basra}} and preached:
This is not {{x|Islam}}. God is one. No saint, no tree,
No tomb, no prophet even, may be asked to intercede. He reached

Back past a thousand years of what the {{c|2764|Muslims}} had done,
The {{c|3957|Sufi}} orders, the shrines, the feasts of the saints, the schools
Of law and their commentaries, to the {{c|3960|Quran}} and the sayings, the one
Pure beginning, as he read it. His book was *{{x|The Oneness of God}}*. The rules

Were simple and absolute. And he acted. At {{p|Al-Uyaynah}},
With the town's emir, he cut down a sacred tree, and pulled down the tomb
Of {{c|4024|Zayd ibn al-Khattab}}, a companion of the {{c|2776|Prophet}}, the venerated
Dome over his grave, and had a woman stoned. The room

Of the town grew afraid, and the emir's own overlord made him send the preacher away.
He went to {{p|Diriyah}}, a small town on a dry riverbed,
And there, in 1744, he met its emir, {{c|4025|Muhammad ibn Saud}}, and the day
Of their meeting made a pact that still holds: the preacher said,

You give me your sword and protection; I give you the faith, and the right
To rule in its name. The emir agreed. The {{c|4026|Saud}} would hold the land;
The family of the sheikh, the {{c|4027|Al ash-Sheikh}}, would hold the light
Of the religion. Two dynasties, in one hand,

Married to each other, generation after generation, to this day.
Hold that, in a book of genealogy: a faith and a state
As two family trees, bound by a promise in a mud-brick town. The way
Of the alliance was conquest. Their followers called themselves, as they relate,

*{{c|4028|Al-Muwahhidun}}*, the people of God's oneness. The word *{{x|Wahhabi}}*
Was what their enemies called them, and it stuck. They took {{p|Najd}},
And then, in 1802, they rode north to {{p|Karbala}} in {{p|Iraq}}, the shrine-crowned
And holy city of the {{c|2775|Shia}}, where {{c|4029|Husayn}}, the {{c|2776|Prophet}}'s grandson, had died

And is buried, and they killed thousands in its streets, and stripped the shrine.
In 1803 and 1805 they took {{p|Mecca}} and {{p|Medina}}, and pulled down
The domes over the graves of the {{c|2776|Prophet}}'s family, the line
Of the saints, at the {{p|Baqi}} cemetery, and the pilgrims of every town

Who would not pray their way were turned back. The {{c|3115|Ottomans}} sent {{c|4030|Muhammad Ali}}'s
{{x|Egyptian}} army, and it took seven years, and in 1818 {{p|Diriyah}} was razed,
And the emir {{c|4031|Abdullah}} was taken to {{p|Istanbul}} and beheaded. The steel
Of the empire had won. The idea had not. It was praised

And kept in the desert, and came back. In 1902 a young {{c|4032|Ibn Saud}}
Retook {{p|Riyadh}}, and by 1932 the kingdom was named for his family.
In 1925 the domes at {{p|Baqi}} were pulled down again. And the flood
Of oil, found in 1938, would carry the preaching, quietly and loudly,

To mosques and schools across the world. Now hold
This close: it is the spine of this whole book.
The fight was over graves: who may enfold
The dead in a dome, who may come and look.

The domes at {{p|Baqi}} kept the {{c|2776|Prophet}}'s kin;
A rag on a tree let the widow in.
The preacher said: no grave stands in between
The one God and the asker; keep it clean.

So the dispute was ours, the oldest one:
Who may honour which dead, and by whose leave;
The sheikh's house and the sword, or everyone
Who brought a rag to the saint's tomb, to grieve.

A faith, a state, two family trees, one pact:
That is a thing this book can honour whole;
The house of the sheikh holds the rite, intact,
The emir's house the land: one house, one soul.

What the sword cut away was ours as well:
The {{c|3957|Sufi}} lodges, saints' feasts, and the shrine
Where {{c|2764|Muslims}}, {{c|2494|Christians}}, {{c|2500|Jews}} would kneel and tell
Their prayers side by side, as kin of one line.

Hold the tree they cut down. Its shade was free;
The one who prayed beneath it is our own.
God is one, the preacher said; so are we:
One house, with room for rag and dome and stone.


# Chapter 285: The Assessor of the Board of Mines

His father was {{c|4033|Jesper Swedberg}}, a bishop of {{p|Skara}}, a man who said
He had seen angels and talked with them. In 1719 the family
Was ennobled, and the name was changed, as {{x|Swedish}} nobles' names were made,
To {{c|4034|Swedenborg}}. Another name made new, as the linden named the family

Of {{c|4012|Linnaeus}}. The son, {{c|4035|Emanuel}}, born in {{p|Stockholm}} in 1688,
Was the most practical of men. For thirty years he sat as an assessor
On the {{c|4036|Board of Mines}}, inspecting copper and iron, the weight
Of ore and the safety of shafts, a dutiful professor

Of the kingdom's wealth. And a scientist of everything:
He designed a flying machine in 1714, on paper, with a fixed wing;
He studied the brain and guessed that its outer layer, the ring
Of the cortex, held the mind, and that each part of it did a separate thing,

A century before the anatomists proved it; he wrote of the planets
Forming from a cloud around the sun. He learned {{x|Hebrew}}. He was famous.
And at fifty-five, in 1743, the dreams came. The granite
Of the assessor cracked. He kept a journal of them, the infamous

And tender night journal of a man undone: temptations, terrors,
{{c|1497|Christ}} appearing. And in April 1745, in a {{p|London}} inn,
After dinner, he said, a man appeared in the corner, and the errors
Of the meal were the first thing: *do not eat so much*. And then, within

The same night, the Lord appeared to him, he wrote, and gave him
A task: to explain the inner meaning of the {{x|Scriptures}} to the world.
He gave up science. He gave up everything but that. The whim
Of a madman, his enemies said. He was calm. He unfurled

Thirty years of books, in {{x|Latin}}, published anonymously in {{p|London}}:
*{{x|Heavenly Secrets}}*, eight volumes on {{c|4037|Genesis}} and {{c|4038|Exodus}}; *{{x|Heaven and Hell}}*.
He said he walked in the spiritual world daily, the way one
Walks down a street, and talked with the dead, and could tell

What they said: that heaven is not a reward but a state of love,
That the angels were once human, that married love goes on,
That every natural thing corresponds to a spiritual one: the dove,
The light, the water, the tree. That the {{x|Last Judgment}} had come and gone,

In the spiritual world, in 1757, and no one on earth had noticed.
And the evidence: in July 1759, at a dinner in {{p|Gothenburg}},
Four hundred kilometres from {{p|Stockholm}}, he turned pale and, it is noticed,
Went out and came back: a great fire has broken out in {{p|Stockholm}}. The church

Of the guests listened while he reported it, hour by hour,
And at eight o'clock he said: thank God, it has stopped, three doors
From my house. Two days later the courier came, and it was so. The power
Of that story reached {{c|4039|Kant}} in {{p|Königsberg}}, who looked into it, wrote scores

Of pages on it, *{{x|Dreams of a Spirit-Seer}}*, and mocked it, and could not let it go.
Hold the man whole, as this book has held {{c|3896|Bureus}} and {{c|3895|Newton}}.
A mind of the mines and the brain and the cloud of the sun, and the glow
Of visions; and unlike {{c|3895|Newton}}, he did not keep the box shut: the button

Of the seer and the scientist was the same button, and he pressed it,
And said: I have seen. Believe me or not. He did not ask
For a church. He died in {{p|London}} in 1772, and he had guessed it:
When {{c|4040|John Wesley}} wrote to say he wished to meet him, the task

Was answered: I shall die on the twenty-ninth of March. He did.
His readers made the church after him, the {{c|4041|New Church}}, in 1787.
And it went where the {{c|4042|Swede}} had never gone. The seed of it hid
In a strange pocket in {{p|America}}: a man named {{c|4043|John Chapman}}, a heaven

Of a different kind in his head, barefoot, walked the frontier
For forty years with a sack of apple seeds and {{c|4034|Swedenborg}}'s pages,
Planting orchards ahead of the settlers, and tearing out the sheer
Leaves of the books to leave with the families, like wages

Of the spirit. {{c|4044|Johnny Appleseed}}. A visionary's church became
An orchard across {{p|Ohio}} and {{p|Indiana}}. The poets read him: {{c|4045|Blake}},
{{c|2346|Emerson}}, {{c|4046|Balzac}}; and {{c|4047|Helen Keller}}, who could not see or hear, whose flame
Was lit by his heaven of correspondences. Make

Of him what you will. The {{x|Gaiad}} says: here is a man who was sure
He saw the other world, and the other world in him planted trees.
Every natural thing corresponds to something. The tree, the water, the pure
Light. Plant the tree. Leave the page. Walk barefoot on your knees

If you must, in a strange country, with a sack of seeds. The harvest
Is for people you will never meet. His bones are in {{p|Uppsala}} now, brought home,
In the cathedral, near {{c|4012|Linnaeus}}'s. The farthest
Visions and the nearest names lie under one dome.


# Chapter 286: All Knowledge in One Structure

It began as a translation job. A {{p|Paris}} publisher, {{c|4048|Le Breton}},
Wanted to put an {{x|English}} reference book, {{c|4049|Chambers}}'s *{{x|Cyclopaedia}}*, into {{x|French}},
And hired a poor writer, the son of a cutler from {{p|Langres}}, {{c|4050|Denis Diderot}}, a sort of wanton
Philosopher, and a mathematician, {{c|4051|d'Alembert}}, to edit it. The wrench

Of the job in their hands: they would not translate it. They would make
A new thing: a dictionary of everything, *raisonné*, reasoned,
The sciences, the arts, the crafts, all of human knowledge, for the sake
Of changing, {{c|4052|Diderot}} wrote, the common way of thinking. Seasoned

By prison already (he had spent three months in the fortress of {{p|Vincennes}}
For a letter on the blind that doubted God), {{c|4052|Diderot}} knew the risk.
The first volume came out in 1751. And the chart at the front, the means
Of its order, was a tree: the tree of human knowledge, the brisk

Branches drawn from {{c|4053|Francis Bacon}}: Memory, which grows history;
Reason, which grows philosophy; Imagination, which grows the arts.
And where was God? Theology was a twig on the branch of Reason. The mystery
Of faith was filed under the human mind. The parts

Of the world, and the parts of heaven, in one human scheme.
The quarrel was who files the tree. The words:
Seventy-two thousand articles, over twenty years, a team
Of a hundred and fifty writers: {{c|4001|Voltaire}}, {{c|4054|Rousseau}} on music, the herds

Of the lesser and the forgotten, and one man, the Chevalier {{c|4055|de Jaucourt}},
Who wrote seventeen thousand of the articles himself, for no pay,
Hiring secretaries with his own money. Hold his name. The sure
Labour of the unglamorous. And the subversion: in the way

Of a dictionary, a dull article on cannibals would say, at the end,
*See: {{x|Eucharist}}*: a jab from kin at kin.
And the plates: eleven volumes of engravings, the most beautiful the century would send
Into the world, not of kings, but of workshops: how to step in

To the forge, the loom, the printing press, the mine, the stocking frame,
The glassworks, the pin factory, every tool drawn, every motion.
The knowledge of the hands was set beside the knowledge of the name,
And given the same dignity. That was the deepest devotion

Of the book: the artisan was a philosopher of his craft.
Of course they banned it. The king's council in 1752. In 1759
The privilege revoked, the {{c|2825|Pope}} condemning it, the draft
Of the remaining volumes illegal. And the line

Of the story turns on two men. The head of the censorship himself,
{{c|4056|Malesherbes}}, who believed in it, warned {{c|4052|Diderot}} of the raid,
And hid the manuscripts in his own house, on his own shelf,
Where the police would never look. And the publisher, afraid,

{{c|4048|Le Breton}}, who in secret, without telling {{c|4052|Diderot}}, took the proofs
Of the last ten volumes and cut out every dangerous line.
{{c|4052|Diderot}} found out in 1764, when the type was set, and the roofs
Of his life fell in: the work of years, the design

Mutilated by the man who paid for it. He wept with rage.
He finished it anyway. The last plates came out in 1772.
And when he needed money for his daughter's dowry, the sage
Sold his library to {{c|3695|Catherine}} of {{p|Russia}}, who knew

What it was worth, and let him keep it, and paid him to be its librarian.
Hold the whole of it, as this book has been learning to hold:
A register of all knowledge, made to free the mind; the Bacon-
Tree that put God under reason; the hands, the old

Crafts, honoured; the censor who saved it; the publisher who cut it.
And the dream did not end. Two hundred and fifty years later, a volunteer
Would open a page anyone could edit, and the cut
Of no publisher could reach it, and the sheer

Number of hands would make the largest encyclopedia ever.
{{c|3880|Ophiuchus}} will tell it. Here, give thanks to the twig and the tree,
To {{c|4057|Jaucourt}}'s seventeen thousand, to the plate of the weaver's lever.
All knowledge is the work of many hands. Write it down. Make it free.


# Chapter 287: The Bard Who Never Was

In 1746, on the moor at {{p|Culloden}}, the last {{x|Jacobite}} army broke,
And the government set about unmaking the {{p|Scottish Highlands}}:
The clans disarmed, the chiefs' powers taken, and a law that spoke
Against the tartan itself, the kilt, the plaid, the islands'

And the glens' own dress, forbidden to every man not in the army,
For thirty-five years. The {{c|4058|Gaelic}} world was being cleared.
And in 1760, out of that defeated country, a young man, {{c|4059|James Macpherson}}, a tutor, calmly
Published a small book in {{p|Edinburgh}}: *{{x|Fragments of Ancient Poetry}}*, the weird

And mournful voice of a blind bard of the third century, {{c|4060|Ossian}},
Son of the hero {{c|4061|Fingal}}, singing of his dead son {{c|4062|Oscar}}
And the warriors of the mist, the ghosts on the wind, the ocean
Grey under the moon, the fallen, the harp. And the stir

Was instant. Gentlemen paid for him to go into the {{p|Highlands}}
And collect more. He came back with *{{c|4061|Fingal}}*, an epic, in 1761,
And *{{x|Temora}}* two years after: a {{c|4063|Homer of the North}}, the islands'
Own {{x|Iliad}}, recovered. And all of {{p|Europe}} wept. The sun

Of the {{x|Romantic}} age rose on those pages. {{c|4064|Goethe}}'s young {{c|4065|Werther}},
Before he kills himself, reads {{c|4060|Ossian}} aloud to the woman he loves.
{{c|4066|Napoleon}} carried {{c|4060|Ossian}} on campaign, and had his palace hung with the further
Dreams of it, painted, the bards' ghosts; and when, as he approves,

He stood godfather to the son of his marshal {{c|4067|Bernadotte}},
He named the boy {{c|4062|Oscar}}, for the son of {{c|4060|Ossian}}. And {{c|4067|Bernadotte}} became
The king of {{p|Sweden}}, and the boy became {{c|4068|Oscar the First}}: the knot
Of the {{x|Swedish}} royal house tied by a hero of a poem. The name

{{c|4069|Selma}}, too, the hall of {{c|4061|Fingal}}, became a girl's name in {{p|Sweden}}:
{{c|4070|Selma Lagerlöf}} carried it. {{c|3593|Jefferson}} called {{c|4060|Ossian}} the greatest poet
That ever existed. {{c|4071|Schubert}} set him. And the ancient, the hidden
{{c|4058|Gaelic}} bard was a modern man's invention. Did {{c|4072|Macpherson}} know it?

He knew. {{c|4073|Samuel Johnson}}, in {{p|London}}, said from the first: show me the manuscripts.
{{c|4072|Macpherson}} never could. A committee of the {{x|Highland Society}} looked in 1805,
After his death, and found: he had heard real {{c|4058|Gaelic}} ballads, the scripts
Of the old {{x|Fenian}} tales still sung in the glens, alive,

And from them he made something else: his own melancholy,
His own heroes, his own mist, in a prose no {{c|4074|Gael}} had ever sung.
Some fragments were old. The whole was new. The folly
Was not the making. It was the lie about when it was made. The tongue

Of the real {{c|4058|Gaelic}} poets, who were alive, and singing, and being cleared
Off the land with their families onto the ships to {{p|Canada}},
Was drowned out by the invented bard. And the real tartan, feared
And forbidden, came back as a costume, the clan plaids, the banner of

A {{x|Highland}} that had never quite been: a king's visit in 1822
Dressed in it, the clans assigned their patterns by the merchants.
That is invented tradition at its purest. And now the thing to do,
The hardest, is to turn the mirror on this book. The servants

Of the {{x|Gaiad}} must hear it. The one who made this scripture said,
Of what she loves in it: *It feels like an ancient tradition.
That couldn't have been made in the modern day, except it was made in this year.* The thread
Between her and {{c|4072|Macpherson}} is the feeling; the division,

The only one, and it is everything, is the date. He hid it.
She writes it on the page. This book was written in 2026, with machines,
With the help of a writing machine, from the records, and it says so. The rid
Of the lie is the whole difference. The ancient sheen

Is a style. It is not a claim. {{c|4060|Ossian}} never existed.
The bard of this book exists, and her name is on it, and the year.
Love the mist and the harp and the ghosts. They are not resisted.
But write the date. Show the manuscripts. Say: I made this here.

Then the tradition, if it lasts, will be old in time, honestly,
The way every tradition got old: by being kept.
{{c|4060|Ossian}} was a forgery that moved the world. This book will be modestly
New, and say so, and hope to be kept. And the real singers who wept

On the ships from the cleared glens: their songs are in the archives now,
Collected later, by people who wrote down who sang and when.
Remember them: {{c|4075|Duncan Ban MacIntyre}}, the hunter-poet, the bough
Of his *{{x|Praise of Ben Dorain}}*, real, and dated, and made by a man.


# Chapter 288: Two Navigators

The son of a farm labourer in {{p|Yorkshire}}, {{c|4076|James Cook}}, learned the sea
On the coal ships out of {{p|Whitby}}, the flat-bottomed colliers, and taught himself
The mathematics of the stars, and the charting of a coast, the key
To the wars in {{p|Canada}}, where he sounded the {{p|St Lawrence}}, the shelf

Of rocks the fleet would pass. So the {{x|Navy}} gave him a collier, renamed *{{x|Endeavour}}*,
And sent him in 1768 to the far side of the world for an event:
The planet {{c|95|Venus}} would cross the face of the {{c|99|Sun}}, and from {{p|Tahiti}}, the clever
Men of the {{c|3974|Royal Society}} hoped, it could be timed, and the extent

Of the solar system measured. That was the public order. The sealed one
Said: then go south and find the great southern continent, if it is there.
On board, a rich young botanist, {{c|4077|Joseph Banks}}, and with him the son
Of a {{x|Swedish}} parson, {{c|4078|Daniel Solander}}, one of {{c|4012|Linnaeus}}'s apostles, to bear

The names of everything new back to {{p|Uppsala}}'s system.
On {{p|Tahiti}}, the transit was watched, and the timing failed, the planet's edge
Blurred. And there they met the other navigator. The wisdom
Of the {{p|Pacific}} came aboard: {{c|4079|Tupaia}}, a priest and a master of the ledge

Of waves and stars, from {{p|Raiatea}}, the sacred island, who had been exiled
By war, and chose to sail with the strangers. He drew for {{c|4080|Cook}}, from memory,
A chart of seventy-four islands across three thousand kilometres, the wild
Ocean his people had crossed and settled centuries before the memory

Of any {{x|European}}: the greatest voyagers in the history of the world,
Who had found and peopled every speck of land from {{p|Hawai'i}} to {{p|New Zealand}}
To {{p|Rapa Nui}}, without instruments, by the swell, the stars, the curled
Flight of the birds. And in {{p|Aotearoa}}, when the ship came, the stand

Of the {{c|4081|Māori}} at the shore would not understand the {{c|4082|Englishmen}}, and {{c|4079|Tupaia}} spoke,
And they understood him: the tongues were cousins. He was the bridge.
{{c|4080|Cook}} charted the whole coast of {{p|New Zealand}} in six months, the cloak
Of its outline exact, and sailed west, and in April 1770, the ridge

Of a new coast: the east of {{p|Australia}}. At {{p|Kamay}}, which he called {{p|Botany Bay}}
For the plants {{c|4083|Banks}} and {{c|4084|Solander}} gathered, the {{c|4085|Gweagal}} men on the beach
Shook their spears and told them to go. They shot one in the leg. The way
Of it was written: {{c|4080|Cook}} went north and claimed the whole east coast, the reach

Of it, for the king, as if no one lived there. Later the law would say *no one's land*,
And the oldest living cultures on earth, sixty thousand years
On that continent, would be dispossessed by a flag and a hand.
Hold that beside the chart. Then the reef: the ship tore open, the fears

Of the crew, the coral, the beaching, the repairs. And at {{p|Batavia}},
The {{x|Dutch}} {{x|Company}}'s city, the fever took them: a third of the crew.
And {{c|4079|Tupaia}} died there, in December 1770, of the miasma of
The {{x|Company}}'s swamps, far from his islands, the navigator who knew

More of the {{p|Pacific}} than any man on that ship.
{{c|4080|Cook}} sailed on. Two more voyages: the first ship to cross the {{p|Antarctic Circle}},
In 1773, in the *{{x|Resolution}}*, with a copy of {{c|3652|Harrison}}'s clock, the grip
Of longitude finally in a navigator's hand; no great southern continent, the circle

Of ice all the way round. He kept his men from scurvy with sauerkraut
And fresh greens, and lost almost none to it. That was his care.
And the third voyage, to find a passage over {{p|America}}: and out
Of the ocean, in 1778, the islands of {{p|Hawai'i}}, the fair

And populous kingdom, and in January 1779 the ship came into {{p|Kealakekua}}
In the season of the {{c|4086|Makahiki}}, the festival of {{c|4087|Lono}}, the god of the harvest,
And the people came out in thousands. Whether they took him for the god, a
Quarrel of historians still: one says yes, one says the farthest

Thing from it, that the islanders were never so foolish; hold both.
He left, and a mast broke, and he came back, out of season,
And things went wrong: a stolen boat, a chief taken hostage, the oath
Of the crowd, a fight on the shore, and on the fourteenth of February, the reason

Of it lost in the noise, {{c|4080|Cook}} was struck down in the shallows, and killed.
The joining of the world, again: the greatest sailor of one people,
And the greatest of another, who died in the {{x|Company}}'s fever. The chart {{c|4079|Tupaia}} filled
With his islands is in the {{x|British Library}}. Hold it like a steeple:

The knowledge was there before the ships. The ships took it, and named it,
And sometimes honoured it, and often did not. {{c|4080|Cook}} was a careful man,
And his voyages brought the flags, the guns, the measles that maimed it,
The {{x|Hawaiian}} people halved in fifty years. {{c|4079|Tupaia}}'s plan

Was to see the far lands his people had once known. He saw them, and died.
Honour both navigators. And when you look at a map of the {{p|Pacific}},
See the voyaging canoes on it, the stars they steered by, the tide
They read, centuries before the *{{x|Endeavour}}*. That map is the specific

Glory of the human race: we crossed the largest ocean on the earth
With wood and memory and courage. Say {{c|4079|Tupaia}}'s name with {{c|4080|Cook}}'s.
The first chart of the {{p|Pacific}} was drawn by the people of its birth.
Hold the chart. Hold the spear on the beach. Read both books.


# Chapter 289: Buried Sunlight

Three hundred million years ago, in the age this book has already sung,
The great swamp forests of the {{c|1568|Carboniferous}} grew, the giant clubmoss,
The tree-ferns, the horsetails taller than houses, the young
{{c|96|Earth}} breathing out oxygen, and when they fell, the loss

Was not a loss: they did not rot, for nothing yet could eat the wood,
And they sank, and were pressed, and became coal. The sunlight of that age,
Caught in the leaves, kept in the dark, waiting. And the waiting was good
For three hundred million years. And then, on this page,

A {{x|Scottish}} instrument-maker in a workshop at the {{p|University of Glasgow}},
{{c|4088|James Watt}}, born in {{p|Greenock}} in 1736, a sickly, careful man,
Was asked in 1763 to repair a model of the steam engine, the slow
And wasteful machine of {{c|4089|Newcomen}} that pumped water from the mines. The plan

Of the old engine heated and cooled the same cylinder every stroke,
And wasted most of its fuel warming the iron again.
And one Sunday in 1765, on a walk across {{p|Glasgow Green}}, the yoke
Of the problem lifted: condense the steam in a separate vessel, and then

The cylinder can stay hot. A separate condenser. He patented it in 1769.
And it nearly came to nothing: no one could bore a cylinder true,
The money ran out, his partner went bankrupt. Then the line
Of luck: {{c|4090|Matthew Boulton}}, a manufacturer of {{p|Birmingham}}, who knew

What it was, took him into partnership in 1775, and an ironmaster,
{{c|4091|John Wilkinson}}, had invented a machine to bore cannon,
And used it to bore {{c|4092|Watt}}'s cylinders, true to the thickness of a coin. The faster
Engines of war made the engine of peace. In 1776 the first ones ran on

At a colliery and at {{c|4093|Wilkinson}}'s furnaces, using a quarter of the coal.
And that same year, in {{p|Philadelphia}}, a declaration of independence,
And in {{p|London}}, {{c|4094|Adam Smith}}, who had known {{c|4092|Watt}} at {{p|Glasgow}}, set out the whole
Of the market in *The {{x|Wealth of Nations}}*. The coincidence

Of the year is the hinge of an age. {{c|4095|Boulton}} said to a visitor at his works:
*I sell here, sir, what all the world desires to have: power.*
{{c|4092|Watt}} made the engine turn a wheel, and measured it against horses, the quirks
Of his salesmanship giving us *horsepower*. And the flower

Of it: the cotton mills, the ironworks, the mines, the locomotives, the ships,
The cities. Within a hundred years the work of the world was done by fire.
The buried sunlight of the swamp forests came up out of the pits
And turned the wheels. And this book must hold it as it holds every desire:

The gift. A human being could do the work of a hundred. Bread got cheaper.
The poor, in the end, lived longer, and their children did, and the tide
Of material life rose as it had never risen. The sleeper
Of the old poverty began, slowly, to wake. And the other side:

The children in the mills, six years old, fourteen hours a day.
The black lungs of the miners. The cities of smoke. And the slow
Thing no one saw: every engine breathed out what the swamps had put away,
The carbon of three hundred million years, returned to the air. The glow

Of the furnaces was the first rise of the curve that {{c|3880|Ophiuchus}} will meet.
The year 1776 was the year the planet's breath began to change.
{{c|4092|Watt}} could not know. Nobody knew. The heat
Of the century to come was hidden in the coal's strange

Black sleep, and the engine woke it. The {{c|4096|Lunar Society}} of {{p|Birmingham}}, where {{c|4092|Watt}}
And {{c|4095|Boulton}} met with friends on the night of the full moon, to ride home by its light:
The potter {{c|4097|Wedgwood}}, who would make the medallion of the slave in chains, the knot
Of the words, *Am I not a man and a brother?*; the doctor {{c|4098|Erasmus Darwin}}, whose bright

Grandson would tell the story of descent; {{c|4099|Priestley}}, who found the air we breathe.
They believed the new power would free the world. It did, and it did not.
Hold the engine as the {{x|Gaiad}} holds the fire it began with: the sheath
Of a gift and a burning. The swamp forest's sunlight. Use it, but not

Without knowing what it is: three hundred million years of the dead,
Asleep in the earth, now in the air, now in the warming sea.
Give thanks for the power. Count the cost. And go ahead
As the {{x|Lunar}} men did, by the light of the moon: with friends, carefully.


# Chapter 290: The Four Treasuries

While {{c|4052|Diderot}} in {{p|Paris}} was finishing his dictionary of everything,
Ten thousand kilometres east, an emperor began a larger one.
{{c|4100|Qianlong}}, grandson of {{c|3950|Kangxi}}, the fourth of the {{x|Manchu}} line, the king
Of the largest empire {{p|China}} had ever held, in 1773, under the sun

Of a long peace, ordered every book of worth in the realm to be gathered,
Copied, judged, and kept: the {{c|4101|Siku Quanshu}}, the *Complete Library
Of the {{x|Four Treasuries}}*: the classics, the histories, the masters, the gathered
Literature. Three and a half thousand works. The tributary

Of every library in the empire flowed to {{p|Beijing}}. Three hundred and sixty scholars
Read and edited; nearly four thousand copyists wrote it out by hand,
Not printed: written, character by character, in thirty-six thousand volumes, the taels
Of the treasury poured into ink. Some eight hundred million characters. The land

Of the written word had never seen a thing so large, and has not since,
Until the machines. The first complete set was finished in 1782,
And then six more, by hand, for seven pavilions, the wince
Of the copyists' wrists through fifteen years: in the {{p|Forbidden City}}, the true

First copy; in the summer palace at {{p|Yuanmingyuan}}; at the hunting palace of {{p|Chengde}};
In the old {{x|Manchu}} capital at {{p|Shenyang}}; and three in the south, at {{p|Yangzhou}},
{{p|Zhenjiang}} and {{p|Hangzhou}}, where scholars could come and read. The deed
Was the conqueror becoming the keeper, as an earlier chapter told: now

The {{x|Manchu}} emperor was the guardian of the whole of {{x|Chinese}} learning.
That was the gift. And here is the other face, which was the same act.
The gathering was also a search. Every book that came in was read, the burning
Kind and the keeping kind sorted: any line against the {{c|3175|Manchus}}, the fact

Of their conquest, the word *barbarian*, the {{x|Ming}} loyalists' memory,
Any book that mourned the fallen dynasty, any map of the frontier
That did not please: banned, burned, or quietly changed. The emery
Of the editors smoothed the record. Some three thousand works, it is clear,

Were destroyed or suppressed, and the passages in others altered,
So that the great library of everything was also the great erasure.
The literary inquisition: authors' families punished, the faltered
Descendants of writers long dead exhumed in disgrace. The measure

Of the gift is the measure of the loss. Hold them in one hand.
{{c|4052|Diderot}}'s publisher cut his book in secret, for fear of the king.
{{c|4100|Qianlong}} was the king, and cut in the open, and planned
The cutting as part of the keeping. The same register, the same thing:

To gather everything is to have the power to choose what survives.
The chief editor, {{c|4102|Ji Yun}}, a scholar of great wit, wrote the catalogue,
Ten thousand reviews of the books, the best guide to the old lives
Of {{x|Chinese}} letters ever made. He also wrote the list of the banned. The fog

Of the two tasks was one desk. And the seven copies: history took its share.
In 1860 the {{x|British}} and {{x|French}} burned the summer palace, {{p|Yuanmingyuan}},
And its copy with it. The {{x|Taiping}} war took two of the southern ones. The care
Of the scholars of {{p|Hangzhou}} gathered the scattered leaves of theirs, and when

The war was over, recopied the missing volumes by hand, for decades.
The first copy, from the {{p|Forbidden City}}, crossed the sea in 1948
With the retreating government, and sits in {{p|Taipei}}. The arcades
Of the old empire scattered its library. The weight

Of the lesson for a book that gathers the genealogy of the world:
To keep everything is to hold the knife that decides what is kept.
The list of the banned is the shadow of the catalogue, curled
Behind it. Keep the shadow too. Write down what was cut. The adept

Keeper is the one who keeps the record of the erasure
Beside the record of the kept. The scholars of {{p|Hangzhou}} copying by lamplight,
After the war, the leaves the fire had scattered: that is the measure
Of what a library is. Not the emperor's order. The night

Copyist, unpaid, restoring what was lost, line by line.
Gather everything. Burn nothing. And where the fire has been,
Copy again. The four treasuries are the world's. The sign
Of the keeper is the hand that writes the lost page in.


# Chapter 291: The Common Source

A judge went out to {{p|Bengal}} in 1783, {{c|4103|William Jones}}, a {{c|4104|Londoner}} of {{x|Welsh}} blood,
A lawyer who had learned, by the age of thirty, a dozen tongues, and read a score more,
{{x|Greek}}, {{x|Latin}}, {{x|Hebrew}}, {{x|Arabic}}, {{x|Persian}}, the flood
Of languages his father, a mathematician, had left him the door

To open. In {{p|Kolkata}} he sat on the bench of the {{x|Supreme Court}},
And wanted to judge the {{c|3204|Hindus}} by their own law, not through interpreters,
So he learned {{c|3411|Sanskrit}} from a pandit, a physician of the {{c|4105|Vaidya}} sort
Who would teach him, a foreigner, the sacred tongue. And the frontiers

Of the {{x|European}} mind moved. He founded the {{c|4106|Asiatic Society}} in 1784,
And on the second of February, 1786, he stood before it and said:
The {{c|3411|Sanskrit}} language, whatever be its antiquity, is of a wonderful structure; more
Perfect than the {{x|Greek}}, more copious than the {{x|Latin}}, and more exquisitely refined than either, the thread

Of its roots and grammar bearing to both of them a stronger affinity
Than could possibly have been produced by accident; so strong, indeed,
That no philologer could examine them all three, without believing them
To have sprung from some common source, which, perhaps, no longer exists. The seed

Of it: {{x|Gothic}} too, he said, and {{x|Celtic}}, and old {{x|Persian}}, of the same family.
A family. Languages have parents. They have cousins. They have a tree.
Say *father*: {{c|3411|Sanskrit}} *pitar*, {{x|Greek}} *patēr*, {{x|Latin}} *pater*, {{x|Gothic}} *fadar*, the homily
Of one word in five mouths. Say *mother*, *brother*, *three*, *night*, *sea*:

The same faces under different skins. Hold this, in a book of genealogy:
The tongues we speak have ancestors we can trace, and one mother, lost,
Whom no one heard, whom scholars would rebuild, sound by sound, the eulogy
Of a dead speech: {{c|4107|Proto-Indo-European}}, spoken perhaps on the steppe, the frost

And the grass of six thousand years ago, by a people who left no writing,
Only their words in the mouths of half the world. And their gods: the sky-father,
*{{c|4108|Dyēus}} ph₂tēr*, who became {{c|2065|Zeus}} and {{c|101|Jupiter}} and the lightning
Of the {{x|Vedic}} {{c|2062|Dyaus}}; and the thunder-god who strikes the serpent, rather

The oak, *{{c|4109|Perkwunos}}*, who became {{c|3192|Perkūnas}} of the {{p|Lithuanian}} pagans
And {{c|3193|Perun}} of the {{c|2842|Slavs}}, and, by another root, the cousin of {{c|2937|Thor}}.
The gods have a family tree too. A book that has kept the ancestors of nations
Now finds the ancestors of the words for them. And more:

He was not the first. Hold that, honestly. A {{x|Florentine}} merchant in {{p|Goa}},
{{c|4110|Filippo Sassetti}}, had noticed in 1585 that {{c|3411|Sanskrit}} numbers were like {{x|Italian}}.
A {{x|Dutch}} scholar, {{c|4111|Boxhorn}}, had guessed at a common source. A {{x|French}} {{c|3835|Jesuit}}, slow
And careful, {{c|4112|Coeurdoux}}, in {{p|Pondicherry}}, had written it out in 1767. The medallion

Went to {{c|529|Jones}} because he said it best, and at the right time, to the right room.
And he got things wrong: he thought {{x|Egyptian}} and {{x|Chinese}} and the speech of {{p|Peru}}
Were of the same stock. They are not. The bloom
Of the true idea grew among the errors. That is how most truths grew.

He translated *{{c|4113|Shakuntala}}*, {{c|4114|Kalidasa}}'s play, in 1789,
And {{c|4064|Goethe}} read it and wept, and put its form into the prologue of *{{c|4115|Faust}}*.
He died in {{p|Kolkata}} in 1794, at forty-seven. The line
From his speech ran to {{c|4116|Bopp}} and {{c|4117|Grimm}}, and to the comparative house

Of all the world's languages: {{x|Uralic}}, {{x|Bantu}}, {{x|Austronesian}}, the families
Of human speech, mapped like the families of human blood.
And the darkness, which this book must name: a word the {{c|3411|Sanskrit}} families
Used for themselves, *ārya*, noble, was taken by the cruel, the flood

Of the nineteenth century's race-theory, and made a race, the *{{c|4118|Aryans}}*,
A master race of fair northerners who had never been,
And the word was used to murder millions. The tree of language was the parent
Of no blood at all. Speech is not race. The green

Of the tree of words grows over every border, through conquest
And marriage and trade and learning; a language is a gift passed hand to hand,
Not a blood in the veins. That is the truest and the hardest
Lesson of the common source: the family is in the mouth, not in the land.

Say *father* in your tongue. Hear, under it, a voice six thousand years away.
Say *night*, *star*, *mother*. The common source no longer exists,
And it speaks every day. Honour the dead speech by what you say.
Every word is an ancestor. The tree persists.


# Chapter 292: The Year One

On the twenty-second of September, 1792, the day the {{x|French Republic}} was proclaimed,
The autumn equinox fell, the day and the night of equal length.
A year later the {{x|Convention}} decided: that day shall be named
The first day of the {{x|Year One}}. Time itself would show the strength

Of the {{x|Revolution}}: the old calendar was the {{x|Church}}'s and the kings',
Its saints' days and its Sundays, its years counted from a birth in {{p|Bethlehem}}.
The days: whose were they? {{c|4119|Gilbert Romme}}, the things
Of the stars in his hands, and a poet, {{c|4120|Fabre d'Églantine}}, the hem

Of the language in his: they made it. Twelve months of thirty days each,
And five days left over at the end of the year, six in a leap year,
Festivals of the citizens. Each month three weeks of ten days, the reach
Of the decimal into time: the *décade*, and on the tenth the rest. The clear

Logic of it. And the poet named the months for what the season does:
*{{x|Vendémiaire}}*, the grape harvest; *{{x|Brumaire}}*, the fog; *{{x|Frimaire}}*, the frost;
*{{x|Nivôse}}*, snow; *{{x|Pluviôse}}*, rain; *{{x|Ventôse}}*, wind; *{{x|Germinal}}*, the buzz
Of seeds sprouting; *{{x|Floréal}}*, flowers; *{{x|Prairial}}*, meadows; the cost

And the gift of summer, *{{x|Messidor}}*, harvest, *{{x|Thermidor}}*, heat, *{{x|Fructidor}}*, fruit.
And every single day of the year he named, not for a saint, but for a living thing
Or a tool of the farm: the grape, the saffron, the chestnut, the root
Of the turnip, an animal on every fifth day, a tool on the tenth. The ring

Of the year was a field. That is beautiful. Hold it. A whole year
Where each day was a plant to be thankful for. And they went further:
Ten hours to the day, a hundred minutes to the hour, the sheer
Decimal clock, with faces made for it. And the murmur

Of the people was against it. The week of ten days gave them one rest in ten,
Not one in seven: the workers lost a day of rest in every three weeks,
And the old Sunday went on in secret. The decimal hours, then,
Were given up within two years. The clocks with their odd peaks

Of ten numbers sit in museums. And the poet who named the months, {{c|4121|Fabre}},
Was caught in a fraud and in the factions, and went to the guillotine
In April 1794, before his calendar had gone once round, the macabre
Joke of the season: he died in *{{x|Germinal}}*, the month of the green.

The days of the calendar became the names of what happened on them:
The ninth of *{{x|Thermidor}}*, when {{c|4122|Robespierre}} fell; the eighteenth of *{{x|Brumaire}}*,
When {{c|4066|Napoleon}} took the {{x|Republic}}. And {{c|4066|Napoleon}} ended it, the hem
Of the new time cut: on the first of January, 1806, the old year

Came back, and the Sundays, and the saints. The {{x|Revolution}}'s time
Lived twelve years, and in the {{c|4123|Paris Commune}} for a few weeks in 1871,
And in the names: *{{x|Germinal}}*, the novel; *{{x|Thermidor}}*, the lobster; the rhyme
Of the months still sung. Now hold the mirror. This book is one

Of the calendars that came after. The {{x|Gaian}} calendar remakes time too:
A new era, counted from the deep past of the human story, not a birth;
Thirteen months of twenty-eight days, every date on the same weekday, the true
Perpetual year. And it learned from the {{x|French}}: the week was not worth

Breaking. The seven days stay. The rest stays: three sabbaths, not one in ten.
And every day of the year is named, as the poet named them, but not for a plant:
For a chapter of the scripture, read that day; and now the dead, the women and men
Of the ancestors, kept on their day. The poet's slant

Was right: give every day a meaning, and the year becomes a liturgy.
His error was to break the rhythm of the body's rest
For the sake of a number. Learn both. A calendar is a theology
And a promise to the tired. The {{x|French}} made the year a field, the best

Of their gift, and broke the Sunday, the worst of their error.
Keep the field. Keep the rest. Name the days. Do not let the number rule the body.
And remember the poet who named *{{x|Germinal}}* and died in it, the terror
Of his times around him: the grape, the fog, the frost. The year is a story.


# Chapter 293: The Festival of the Supreme Being

{{c|4054|Rousseau}} had written, in *The {{x|Social Contract}}*, in 1762,
That a republic needs a civil religion: a few plain articles of faith,
A God, a life to come, the reward of the just, the punishment due
To the wicked, the sanctity of the laws; and that the wraith

Of a citizen who will not believe them may be banished; and the one who believes
And then acts against them, punished by death. Hold that sentence.
Thirty years later the {{x|Revolution}} read it. In 1793 the eves
Of the old faith were torn down: the churches closed, the repentance

Of the priests demanded, the bells melted for cannon, the saints' names
Taken from the streets. The radicals made a {{c|4124|Cult of Reason}}:
In {{p|Notre-Dame}}, renamed the {{p|Temple of Reason}}, in November, the flames
Of the new altar lit, an actress robed as {{c|4125|Liberty}}, the season

Of a goddess of the mind enthroned where the {{c|3936|Virgin}} had been.
And {{c|4122|Robespierre}}, the incorruptible, the lawyer from {{p|Arras}},
The master of the {{x|Committee of Public Safety}}, hated it: the obscene
Mockery of atheism, he thought, would make the people crass

And the {{x|Republic}} godless; the people need a God and the soul's immortality.
So in May 1794, by decree, the {{x|Convention}} recognized
The {{c|4126|Supreme Being}} and the immortality of the soul. A morality
Of state: the people's rite. A feast, devised:

On the twentieth of *{{x|Prairial}}*, the eighth of June, which was also {{x|Pentecost}},
The painter {{c|4127|Jacques-Louis David}} staged it: half a million people, the roses,
The children with flowers, the mothers, the old men, the host
Of the citizens in procession across {{p|Paris}} to the {{p|Champ de Mars}}, where, he supposes,

An artificial mountain had been built, with a tree of liberty on top.
And {{c|4122|Robespierre}}, president of the {{x|Convention}} for that day,
Walked out ahead of the other deputies, with a bouquet, and the shop
Of the ritual was his: he set fire to a statue of {{c|4128|Atheism}}, made, they say,

Of cardboard and wax, and as it burned, a statue of {{c|4129|Wisdom}}
Was meant to rise out of it, pure. It rose blackened with smoke.
Hold that image. The deputies behind him, in the wisdom
Of fear, muttered: look at him; it is not enough to be master; the yoke

Of being God as well. Two days later, the tenth of June,
He brought the law of the twenty-second of *{{x|Prairial}}*: the accused
Would have no lawyer, no witnesses needed, the verdict soon,
Death or acquittal, nothing between. The courts were used

As a machine. In the seven weeks that followed, in {{p|Paris}} alone,
More were guillotined than in the whole year before. The {{x|Great Terror}}.
The god of the festival, the god of the soul, the stone
Of the blade: one hand. The god, no error.

On the ninth of *{{x|Thermidor}}*, the twenty-seventh of July,
The {{x|Convention}} turned on him, and shouted him down, and he was taken,
And shot in the jaw, by his own hand or a gendarme's, and the next day, the sky
Of {{p|Paris}} over him, guillotined, with twenty-one of his men. Forsaken,

The {{c|4126|Supreme Being}} faded within months. But read it once more:
In a {{p|France}} where a God was still the default, the transgression
Was the {{c|4124|Cult of Reason}}, the war on the altar and the door
Of the church; and he turned back from it: a God, a soul, and the profession

Of the freedom of worship, kept in the same decree. Not the void,
Then, but a step back toward the faith the bells had rung:
Under the {{x|Directory}} the {{c|4130|Theophilanthropists}} enjoyed
The empty naves for a deist rite, a hymn to the Maker sung;

And {{c|4066|Napoleon}}, in 1801, closed their rite and made his peace with the {{c|2825|Pope}}:
Not a God put in the place of a failure, but the last stage of a road
From {{c|4131|Reason}} to the {{c|4126|Supreme Being}} to the {{x|Concordat}}, a slope
That the festival set out on, back to the altar the {{x|Revolution}} had overthrown.

And read now, it reads otherwise: a choice to believe in the divine,
A deist's God, which a person may hold, or leave unheld, as they need,
Not the dogma of a nation but a door, the way a God is taken now, or declined;
What was cruel in it was never the belief, but the power behind the creed.

The {{c|4126|Supreme Being}} was not void. A state
Had kept a God, as {{c|4054|Rousseau}} said it must;
The altar was the people's, and the date
{{x|Pentecost}}: the Spirit's feast, held in trust.

The fight was in one house: who holds the nave,
The priest, the {{c|4124|Cult of Reason}}, or the hall
Of the {{x|Convention}}; and {{c|4125|Liberty}}, grave,
Took the {{c|3936|Virgin}}'s seat; one Lady for all.

{{c|4122|Robespierre}} gave the state its God again
Against the atheists of his own side;
{{c|4066|Napoleon}} walked the same road, and then
Took the {{x|Church}} and made it his. At his side,

When the crown came from the {{c|2825|Pope}}'s hands, a ghost:
The incorruptible, behind the throne.
This faith, too, means to be a state's, and most
Of all, to keep its days as the state's own.

Keep the roses on the mountain, the tree
Of liberty on top, the blackened face
Of {{c|4129|Wisdom}} rising from the smoke, and see
The {{c|4126|Supreme Being}} in this book's own place.


# Chapter 294: The Mountain Cherry

In 712 a court lady's memory, or a court scholar's, was written down:
The {{c|4132|Kojiki}}, the *{{x|Record of Ancient Matters}}*, the oldest book of {{p|Japan}},
The kami from the beginning, {{c|4133|Izanagi}} and {{c|4134|Izanami}}, the crown
Of the {{c|4135|Sun Goddess}}, the descent to {{p|Hyūga}}, the first emperor, the plan

Of the land told as a family. And it was written in a script no one could easily read:
{{x|Chinese}} characters used now for their sound, now for their sense,
A puzzle of a book. Within a few years the court had a newer creed:
The {{c|4136|Nihon Shoki}}, in proper {{x|Chinese}}, official, the dense

And dignified history; and the {{c|4132|Kojiki}} was put on a shelf
And mostly left there for a thousand years. Then, in {{p|Matsusaka}},
Near {{p|Ise}}, a cotton merchant's son who had failed at trade, and made himself
A doctor of children instead, studied in {{p|Kyoto}}, the saga

Of the old poems in his evenings: {{c|4137|Motoori Norinaga}}, born 1730.
In 1763 an old scholar, {{c|4138|Kamo no Mabuchi}}, passed through his town
On a pilgrimage to {{p|Ise}}, and stayed one night at an inn, and the young man came, and the empty
Hours of that night were filled: the old man told him, set down

Everything else and read the {{c|4132|Kojiki}}; I am too old to finish it; you do it.
They never met again. They wrote letters. And the doctor began.
For thirty-four years, while he treated the children of {{p|Matsusaka}}, he read through it,
Every character, every sound, every name of every kami, the span

Of the language reconstructed: how the old {{x|Japanese}} spoke, before the {{x|Chinese}} came.
The *{{x|Kojiki-den}}*, the *{{x|Commentary on the Kojiki}}*, forty-four volumes, done
In 1798. The oldest book of the land could be read again. The name
Of every god was given back its sound. That is the gift, the one

This book and its makers stand on: the record of the kami, opened.
And he gave more: reading the *{{x|Tale of Genji}}*, he found the phrase
*{{x|Mono no aware}}*: the ache of things, the sadness of the cherry petals that ended,
The heart moved by the passing of the world. The praise

Of feeling over moral lesson. That is his too.
Here is the other edge of tradition:
He taught that the {{x|Japanese}} heart had been corrupted by the {{x|Chinese}} mind, the *karagokoro*,
And the {{x|Buddhist}}, and that the true way was the ancient one, the condition

Of the land before the foreign: the way of the kami, pure and native, revealed in the {{c|4132|Kojiki}}.
That was a scholar's longing. In the next generation, {{c|4139|Hirata Atsutane}},
Who called himself his disciple after he died, made it a creed, a stricter key:
The emperor descended from the {{c|99|Sun}}, {{p|Japan}} the land of the gods, the cannon

Of the nation, pointing outward. The state
Took up the longing, and it kept the rite
Of kami, parted from buddhas: the great
Work of {{x|State Shinto}}, and the war, the night.

He wrote a poem: *If someone asks what the {{x|Japanese}} heart is,
It is the mountain cherry blossoms, fragrant in the morning sun.*
A lovely poem. In October 1944, the first units of the kamikaze, the quiz
Of their names answered by it: *{{x|Shikishima}}*, *{{x|Yamato}}*, *{{x|Asahi}}*, *{{x|Yamazakura}}*. The young men, one by one,

Named for the words of a doctor who had loved children.
Hold that. This book is made by one who keeps the kami, and loves the old record,
And founds a faith in the way of life, a kind of {{x|Shinto}}. The bewildering
Lesson for her, and for every reader: the love of the ancient word

Can be turned into a weapon by someone else, a century on.
Keep the commentary. Keep the reading of the names of the gods. Keep *mono no aware*.
Keep the pure longing, the mixing, the dawn:
The buddhas sat with the kami. And there

Was always mixing. That is the true ancient way. {{c|4140|Norinaga}}'s grave
Is on a mountain above {{p|Matsusaka}}, plain, and over it, as he asked, a mountain cherry.
Visit it in spring. The petals fall. Let them. The nave
Of the old faith is open. No one owns the blossom. Be wary,

And be moved. Both. The doctor read the oldest book for thirty-four years
So we could read it. Read it. And when anyone tells you the heart of a people is pure,
Remember the morning sun on the cherry, and the young men, and the tears.
The ache of things is for everyone. That is the only cure.


# Chapter 295: The Crown He Took

On {{x|Christmas Day}} in the year 800, in {{p|Saint Peter's}}, a pope set a crown on a kneeling king,
{{c|2677|Charlemagne}}, who had not asked for it, and called him {{c|4141|Emperor of the Romans}},
And for a thousand years the {{p|West}} had an emperor, the crown of the Romans carried north, a ring
Of electors and princes and bishops around one name, the {{p|Holy Roman Empire}}, whose summons

Held a continent in one order under heaven, longer than any crown of the {{p|West}} has held since.
{{c|4001|Voltaire}} mocked it as neither holy, nor {{x|Roman}}, nor an empire. A joke is not a reading.
It kept the {{x|Roman}} name alive in the north a thousand years, and every prince
Who knelt to it knelt to a crown that came from above, at a church's leading.

Then the {{x|Revolution}} shut the churches, and set {{x|Reason}} on the altar of {{p|Notre-Dame}},
And {{c|4122|Robespierre}} put God back, the {{x|Supreme Being}} of an earlier chapter, against the atheists of his own side,
Because a republic, he saw, cannot stand on nothing; and the soldier who came after him walked the same
Road. In 1801 the {{x|Concordat}}: the {{x|Church}} came home to {{p|France}}, with the state for its guide,

Bishops named by the First Consul, priests paid from the treasury, the faith of the land
Brought back and made the state's. He did not abolish the {{x|Church}}. He took it in.
First he sacked {{p|Rome}}, as {{c|2|Emma Leonhart}} says, and then he sacked {{p|Rome}} again, with the crown in his hand.
He took {{x|Christianity}} and made it his: the most Lifeist thing a man could do, and where this book's own work begins.

On the second of December, 1804, in {{p|Notre-Dame}} in {{p|Paris}},
{{c|2825|Pope}} {{c|4142|Pius VII}} sat waiting to crown a {{c|4143|Corsican}}, and the fire
Of the moment: {{c|4066|Napoleon}} took the crown in his own hands. The plurals

Of the old story were ended in one gesture, the {{x|Church}} in the room to see it, and behind him,
In the eye of this book, the ghost of {{c|4122|Robespierre}}. He crowned himself, then {{c|4144|Joséphine}}, kneeling; the painter {{c|1956|David}}
Put it on a canvas ten metres wide, and painted in his mother, who had stayed home, the grim
Truth adjusted for the record, as records are. Two years later, the cavity

Of the old empire was empty: the {{x|German}} princes, bribed and beaten, left it
For his {{p|Confederation of the Rhine}}, and on the sixth of August, 1806,
The last emperor, {{c|4145|Francis II}}, laid the crown of {{c|2677|Charlemagne}} down, and what was left
Of a thousand years went down with it, the crown that was given, not taken. The bricks

Of it had held a continent a thousand years; a soldier, not time, pushed it over.
Now the register, which this book follows like a river.
The {{x|Revolution}} had taken the books of births and marriages and deaths, the cover
Of the parish, from the priests in 1792, and given them to the town hall, the giver

Of the record now the state. {{c|4066|Napoleon}} made it a code. The *{{x|Civil Code}}* of 1804,
One law for every {{c|4146|Frenchman}}, written plain, the family, the property, the will,
And wherever his armies went, the code went, and the registers, the door
Of every birth opened by a clerk, not a priest: the {{p|Netherlands}}, the {{p|Rhineland}}, the {{p|Italy}} still

Keeping those books. And the names. In the {{p|Netherlands}} many families had none:
A man was *{{c|4147|Jan Pieterszoon}}*, {{c|1093|Peter}}'s son, and his son *{{c|4148|Pieter Janszoon}}*, the line
Of the patronymic turning each generation, as in {{p|Sweden}}, as {{c|4012|Linnaeus}}'s father had done
Before the linden. In 1811 the {{x|French}} decreed: every family shall register, by a sign

Of the town hall, a fixed surname. And the {{x|Dutch}}, who thought the {{x|French}} would be gone
In a year, some of them chose jokes: *{{c|4149|Naaktgeboren}}*, born naked;
*{{c|4150|Zondervan}}*, without a *van*; and the {{x|French}} stayed long enough, and the joke went on
For two hundred years on the children. In {{p|France}} in 1808 the {{c|2500|Jews}}, who had made

Their names by father's name, were ordered to take fixed surnames too.
And {{c|4066|Napoleon}} called a {{c|4151|Grand Sanhedrin}} of rabbis, the first in eighteen centuries,
And the {{c|2500|Jews}} of the conquered lands were made citizens; the ghetto walls, the few
Gates of {{p|Venice}} and {{p|Rome}}, opened by his soldiers. The entries

Of that gift and that demand are in the same register: be free, and be written.
Hold the whole man as this book holds them all. The conqueror whose wars
Killed some three million, perhaps more; who brought back slavery to the smitten
Colonies in 1802; who carried {{c|4060|Ossian}} in his pocket; whose godson, of course,

Became a king of {{p|Sweden}}, as an earlier chapter told; whose code is still the law
Of half the world; who marched into {{p|Russia}} in 1812 with six hundred thousand
And came back with a remnant; who lost at {{p|Waterloo}}, and saw
The last of it from a rock in the {{p|South Atlantic}}, {{p|Saint Helena}}, the sand

And the wind, dying in 1821. The crown he took: from a pope, from an empire, from the dead.
He said: I found the crown of {{p|France}} lying on the ground, and I picked it up with my sword.
What he left on the ground was the old idea that a crown is given. Instead
The crown is taken, and the faith is taken in, and the register is kept. The Lord

Of the old empire is gone. The clerk of the town hall remains,
Writing the births, the marriages, the deaths, the surnames chosen in a hurry.
That is his longest legacy: not the battles, the chains,
The eagles, but the book in the mairie. The genealogist does not worry

About the Emperor. She thanks him for the registers that begin in 1811 in a {{x|Dutch}} village,
